about: Arctic char are the northernmost freshwater fish on Earth — the char of high Arctic lakes and sea-run rivers, in colours that run from silver sea-run fish to spawning males in impossible orange and red. Cold is not a preference for char, it's a gate: spawning runs at just 2–7 °C, slows at 8 and stops by 11, and the research puts their upper lethal limit around 23 °C.

Char live two lives where they can — lake residents that cruise cold depths for fish and crustaceans, and sea-run fish that fatten in the ocean each summer and return to fresh water to overwinter and spawn in fall on lake gravel. Light, not heat, restarts their spring. Anglers travel to the far north to target them, on fly and spoon, for what may be the most beautiful fish in fresh water and one of the strongest.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No lure or technique is named for char in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here: the supported menu is local — littoral benthos such as chironomid larvae and Gammarus, zooplankton where the fish are feeding pelagically, and small fish for the larger residents. Match the offering's size and depth to which of those menus the fish are on.

Keep presentations in the cold band the fish have chosen: prespawn water above the spawn band is still inside the activity plateau that spans roughly 8–16 °C, so ordinary summer-sized offerings are still appropriate early in the fall — shrink and slow only as the water falls toward the spawn temperatures.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the light changes hardest: the full-year telemetry puts the greatest activity at dawn, dusk and in daylight, with dawn and dusk the peaks (both scored 1.0). Be set up on the staging water before the transition, not travelling through it.

Use the long fall light, not the dark, as the main shift — while remembering this fish's unusual floor: char feed at light levels down to 0.001 lux and score 0.55 at night, the highest night floor of any trout or char in the model. A slow pass after dark is a real option here in a way it is not for other salmonids.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the gravel is empty, read the thermometer: above about 8–11 °C the spawn itself is physiologically held up, and the fish are still in prespawn feeding water. Fish deeper and wider until the water falls into the 2–7 °C band.

If staging fish will not take, change depth before pattern: prespawn char split between benthic feeding low in the water and pelagic feeding higher up, lake by lake and morph by morph. A refusal at one level is information about the other.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Offerings matched to the autumn benthic menu — chironomid larvae, Gammarus and other littoral invertebrates — fished low and slow in the cold water beside the beds. No spawn-specific lure is named in the char record, and none is invented here.

Size down as the water falls into the spawn band: feeding continues at 2–7 °C — winter stomachs prove this fish feeds near 0 °C — but nothing at these temperatures is fast, and a smaller, slower offering matches a cold fish's rate better than a summer presentation dragged past it.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The dawn and dusk peaks run the spawn day as they run the year: telemetry activity is greatest at the light changes and in daylight. Cold water and short days compress the useful window — be on the staging edges at first and last light.

Fish slowly and give located fish time: at spawn temperatures the fish are in the lower half of their own dome, and repeated close presentations to a known lie outfish covering water that holds fish you have not found.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the beds look busy but nothing feeds, you may be watching spawners, not feeders: with females spawning only every 2–4 years, the feeding share of the population is elsewhere in the same lake. Move off the gravel to the adjacent feeding water before changing baits.

If the water is still above the band, the spawn has not started, whatever the calendar says — spawning is temperature-gated, slowed at 8 °C and inhibited at 11 °C. Fish it as prespawn until the thermometer, not the date, says otherwise.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Start the year on the winter menu: under-ice diet work found the cold-season diet narrower and benthic — chironomids and Gammarus — and spring fish begin there before the summer's wider menu opens. Small, low, slow benthic-profile offerings are the supported start; no spring lure is named in the research.

As the open-water season builds, add the pelagic option: pelagic-feeding char work zooplankton, and the spring telemetry's vertical movements track that prey's daily migration. An offering fished up in the column at the light changes becomes diet-supported as the season turns, not before.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Let the returning light set the schedule: dawn and dusk are the measured peaks all year, and in spring they lengthen fast. The fish's own resumption is timed to twilight's return — fish the transitions as the season's main event.

Expect a surge, not a ramp, at ice-break: the telemetry year's sharpest activity rise came at ice-break under near-continuous light. The first open days deserve your best water and your full attention; this is one of the year's genuine windows.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If spring fish are silent in the darkest early weeks, that too is in the record: the annual minimum sits in the darkest part of the season, and resumption waits on light. Later — more light, same cold water — is the fix the telemetry itself prescribes.

Check oxygen in a late, depleted lake: char avoid water below roughly 2.3–3.1 mg/L in the field, so spring fish vacate the low-oxygen depths even while those depths are the coldest. Fish the cold water that still carries oxygen.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Feed the generalist: summer char take littoral benthos, zooplankton, molluscs and fish, lake by lake and morph by morph — and larger residents are commonly cannibals, with piscivory beginning around 200–350 mm in the review record. A fish-profile offering for large char is diet-supported; benthic and plankton-sized offerings are the everyday pattern. No specific lure is named in the research, and none is invented here.

Match the level to the menu you are fishing: benthic offerings belong low, on the littoral food; plankton-sized offerings belong up in the column where pelagic fish work zooplankton. A summer char refusal is often a level refusal — the same lake holds both menus at once, at different depths.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work dawn and dusk as the main events (both scored 1.0, above the day's 0.85) and keep fishing into the night with real confidence: this fish feeds at 0.001 lux, stops only in complete darkness, and carries a night score of 0.55 — after dark, slow down and stay on known water, but do not write the night off.

Respect the steepest warm limb in the programme: activity falls from the plateau through 18 °C (about 0.70) and 20.5 °C (about 0.30) to feeding cessation at 21.5–21.8 °C and a lethal family at 23–24 °C. On a hot day, every decision is a depth-and-cold decision first and a presentation decision second.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer fish will not take in warm surface water, they are not being difficult — they are at or past their measured feeding ceiling. Get below the warm layer into the 8–16 °C span, or fish the coldest inflows and spring-fed water, before changing a single offering.

If one part of the lake produces and another never does, morphs may be why: char populations split into littoral and pelagic (and in some lakes profundal) forms with different menus and depths, and the model prices the shared skeleton, not each morph. Treat a blank area as a different menu at a different depth, and test it once that way before abandoning it.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The winter menu is narrow and benthic — chironomid larvae and Gammarus in the subarctic stomach work, prey diversity well down from summer — so small, low, slow offerings are the winter evidence applied to tackle. No winter lure is named in the research.

Keep one fish-profile option in the winter plan even so: larger residents in the High Arctic record ate other char in every season sampled, winter included. Cannibalism does not take the winter off in this species.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Pace the winter by light, not temperature: feeding persists near 0 °C all winter, but the proportion of feeding fish and stomach fullness bottom out in the darkest weeks. The pattern strengthens as light returns in late winter, before the water warms at all.

Fish the light changes inside the short day first — the dawn and dusk peaks persist as the year's skeleton even at winter rates — and give each located pocket real time, because a maintenance-rate fish is not cruising to find your offering.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A dead mid-winter day in the darkest weeks is the annual minimum arriving on schedule, not a tactics failure: the stomach record's lowest feeding sits exactly there. Fish the returning-light end of winter hardest.

If a winter lake is silent everywhere, suspect oxygen: the field avoidance band (below roughly 2.3–3.1 mg/L) does not stop applying under ice, and depleted deep water is water char have left. Move toward better-oxygenated water.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small, low, slow benthic offerings — the winter stomach record is chironomid larvae and Gammarus, with prey diversity well down from summer. No ice-specific lure is measured for char; the winter diet at its smallest is the supported presentation, fished close over the bottom food.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the under-ice light changes first: daily rhythms persist under ice in the lake-resident telemetry, with the day-led shape and dawn and dusk peaks carried into the ice shape (night 0.45 under ice against 0.55 in open water). Expect the exception the telemetry measured — for about two weeks around the winter solstice, activity went much reduced and arrhythmic even though the light stayed bright enough to feed by. That dip is an appetite rhythm, not a light limit, and no presentation fixes it.

Build the late-ice days bigger than the early ones: spring resumption under ice is led by returning twilight at stable, near-zero temperatures — appetite returns on light before it returns on warmth — so the pattern strengthens through late ice for reasons that have nothing to do with the thermometer.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the whole ice pattern is silent, check oxygen before presentation: char avoid water below roughly 2.3–3.1 mg/L in the field and their laboratory lethal band sits at 1.8–2.4 mg/L, so a depleting basin's deep water empties of feeding fish even though the species tolerates low oxygen better than most salmonids. Move toward better-oxygenated water.

Ice catchability itself is not in doubt — a 24.5-inch char came through the ice of Manitoba's Snail Lake in January 2019 — so a blank day in the darkest weeks is the measured annual minimum, not evidence the ice pattern is wrong. Come back as the light returns.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn char are staging for a cold-gated spawn: spawning itself runs at about 2–7 °C, ovulation slows at 8 °C and is inhibited at 11 °C, so while the fall water is still above that band the fish are feeding and gathering, not spawning. Work the gravel areas they will use and the feeding water beside them.

The spawning ground, when it comes, is lake gravel: beds of roughly 3–10 cm gravel in about 0.2–11 m of water, most often around 2.3–5 m deep. Prespawn effort belongs over and around that shallow gravel and its first deep edge, where staging fish can be reached before they are on the beds.

Not every adult is in this season: females commonly spawn only every 2–4 years, so a large share of the fall population is non-spawning feeders in any given year. The prespawn pattern is therefore a mixed one — staging spawners near the gravel, and feeding fish working the same cooling lake more widely.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: The spawn runs September–October in northern populations, later — into November and December — farther south, on lake gravel at about 2–7 °C. Fish are concentrated, shallow and findable: beds in roughly 0.2–11 m, most often 2.3–5 m, over gravel of about 3–10 cm.

Know what kind of season this is in the model: no study has ever measured how much spawning suppresses feeding in lake-resident char, so the spawn carries a modest annotation-grade dip in the season score, not a measured coefficient. Strikes in the spawn window are a mix of feeding fish — remember, many adults are not spawning this year — and fish on the beds, and the entry does not pretend to separate them by formula.

Work the edges of the spawning gravel and the feeding water beside it first, and give the beds themselves room: eggs laid this fall are the next generation, and a concentrated, shallow, cold-gated spawn is the population at its most exposed.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: Spring resumption is led by light, not heat: telemetry fish resumed activity as twilight returned while the water temperature was still stable and near winter values, and the ice-break period brought the sharpest activity surge of the year. Fish the newly open and newly lit water as soon as it exists — this fish does not wait for warmth.

The spring water is still in the cold limb of the dome — activity rising from about 0.35 at 0 °C through roughly 0.50 at 2 °C and 0.70 at 4 °C in the model's anchors — so early fish are cold fish in cold water, feeding at maintenance-plus rates on the winter benthic menu, close to where they wintered.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer is the growth and feeding peak — season values 0.90–1.0 from June through August — inside the coldest dome in the model: the activity plateau spans roughly 8–16 °C, built between a measured preference near 11 °C and a measured growth optimum around 14–17 °C. Fish the water inside that span first, wherever in the lake it sits.

In a warm southern stocked lake — Manitoba's char water is largely stocked parkland lakes such as Snail Lake and Glad Lake — midsummer surface water can pass the fish entirely: feeding ceases at about 21.5 °C. The summer address there is the deep, cold refuge water, and reaching it is the whole pattern.

Choose the refuge by both numbers, not one: the deep cold water must also carry oxygen, because char routinely avoid water below about 2.3–3.1 mg/L. A cold, depleted depth is a place char have left, not a place they are hiding.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter is a feeding season for the lake-resident fish this entry describes — measured, not assumed: stomachs held food in every month of a 9-month ice season at 78°N, and a subarctic lake programme found continuous under-ice feeding at or below maintenance rate. Fish hold where they can feed benthically at low rate, all winter.

The caveat that travels with every winter word here: sea-run char fast all winter by an internal programme — they fast in tanks, at constant temperature, with food in front of them. This winter pattern is the lake-resident form's, and in waters holding native sea-run fish it will overstate feeding. Know which char your lake holds before you fish the winter pattern hard.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: The ice set for Arctic char is ISSUED at Moderate-capped confidence, and the entry carries that flag openly: lake-resident char are measured feeding continuously under ice — stomach programmes at 69–78°N across ice seasons of 6–9 months — and their under-ice activity and daily rhythms are telemetry-measured across a full polar year. No ice catch-rate dataset exists for the species, and the Moderate cap is the price of that gap.

Winter depth is honestly lake-dependent: the subarctic stomach programme found winter fish feeding profundally, while the High Arctic record had fish at their shallowest densities in winter with deep-density peaks in spring and fall. The shared, priced facts are continuous benthic feeding and oxygen — set up where the bottom food and the oxygen are in your lake, and let sonar, not a borrowed depth, settle the rest.

This ice pattern describes lake-resident fish. Sea-run char under the same ice are fasting, and this set will overrate them in winter — the coverage flag says so, and the ice entry repeats it because winter is exactly where the two forms part.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light and dusk; quietest at after dark.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at first light and dusk; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 8–16 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 23 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: Wind, fronts, barometric pressure and moon have never been tested for Arctic char feeding or catch in any source the research could find — and this set parks no proxy points on them at all: the four measured factors (temperature, light, season, oxygen) carry the full rating. There is no front pattern for this fish to sell you; a front matters only as the light and temperature change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The transitions are the measured summit of this fish's day: full-year telemetry found the greatest activity at dawn and dusk, both scored 1.0 against a daylight 0.85. In low light, be already fishing the water you chose in daylight — the peak is short, and travelling through it wastes the best-scored minutes of the day.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is a real shift for char, at a measured floor: the laboratory fish fed at light levels down to 0.001 lux — starlight-level darkness — and stopped only in complete darkness, and the model scores night at 0.55, not near zero. After dark, fish slowly over known benthic and pelagic feeding water, and let the dawn peak, not the clock, end the session.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Bright midday is good, not best, for this fish: daylight scores 0.85 against the dawn and dusk peaks at 1.0, and at 5 °C char out-fed brown trout at every light level in the laboratory comparison while trout took the full-daylight advantage at warmer temperatures. In calm, bright conditions, fish the deeper and shadier side of the feeding water and save the shallowest presentations for the light changes.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais testé pour l'Arctic char — aucun recensement de terrain, aucune télémétrie ou étude contrôlée du vent contre l'alimentation, l'activité ou la capture n'existe pour aucune des deux formes. Zéro par absence (pas un nul mesuré). Bifurcation tranchée 0 plutôt que le précédent d'indicateur du programme : les quatre facteurs mesurés portent le plein 100.
Jamais mesuré pour cette espèce; aucune réponse d'ensemble de front n'existe à exposer. frontExposure : 0. Zéro par absence.
Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou la capture de l'Arctic char dans aucun protocole. Zéro par absence (explicitement pas un nul — aucun analogue Hazzard-&-Clark du char n'existe).
Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou l'activité du char. Aucun résultat lunaire d'aucune sorte n'a été localisé pour aucune des deux formes. Zéro par absence.

Aucune étude NTU/Secchi d'alimentation, de distance réactive ou de capture n'existe pour le char de lac; le seul énoncé de turbidité dans la littérature est une spéculation d'habitat de fjord glaciaire marin (anadrome, eau de mer). turbidity : null — lacune honnête, pas un petit nombre.

Aucune fonction alimentation-contre-débit n'existe pour aucune forme de char; le sujet de l'ensemble est le poisson résident de lac dans les lacs, où le moteur n'a aucune entrée de débit pour cette espèce. Non noté.

L'alimentation est démontrablement structurée par la morphologie et les proies selon le lac (zooplancton pélagique contre benthos contre piscivorie), mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure le champ de proies d'un lac; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.
La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour le char; elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome.
Aucune étude de réponse aux apports/eau de fonte en fin de glace n'existe pour le char. Zéro dans l'ensemble de glace (poids redistribué aux facteurs de glace mesurés).

about: The Arctic grayling is the sailfish of the north — a fish of the salmon family crowned with an enormous, iridescent dorsal fin, living in cold, clear rivers and lakes across the Arctic and subarctic. It is a cold-water fish with a hard ceiling: the research puts its upper lethal point around 23 °C, and its feeding peaks in water of just 10–14 °C.

Grayling live on the move between seasons — overwintering in deep pools, running smaller streams at breakup to spawn over gravel at about 4 °C, then spreading to feeding water where they rise freely to insects. They are delicate-mouthed, surface-oriented and famously willing. Anglers target them with dry flies and tiny spinners in some of the wildest country on the continent, and a big grayling's sail, lit by northern light, is the trophy.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No lure, fly pattern or size is named for grayling in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here: the supported menu is the drift itself — aquatic insects moving in the water the fish are travelling and holding in — presented naturally and close to the fish's line, because prespawn fish are positioning more than chasing.

Size the offering to a cold-water drift feeder at the bottom of its temperature curve: at 1–4 °C the model's activity sits at roughly 0.15–0.45, so small and slow is a temperature conclusion, not a style choice.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the daylight hours first — grayling are sight feeders, feeding mostly during the day, and their ability to locate prey rises dramatically once light passes about 100 lux. A prespawn day is a midday-weighted day.

Cover the staging water thoroughly and move slowly between spots: prespawn migration is temperature-triggered, so a reach that was empty in the morning can hold travelling fish after the day's warming — re-check the best staging water late in the day before you write it off.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If nothing moves, check the thermometer before the tackle: below the first rise toward 1 °C there is no migration stimulus in the record, and below about 4 °C there is no spawning and little feeding — the honest fix is warmer water or a later date, not a new bait.

Cold, dirty water is a double problem for this visual feeder: suitability is already falling by 8 NTU and reaches about 0.3 at 20 NTU, so in stained prespawn water put the presentation closer and slower, or find the clearest water available.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No spawn-specific lure is named in the grayling record, and whether feeding even dips during the spawn has never been measured — so there is no suppression coefficient and no spawn bait to sell. Keep offerings on the measured diet — drifting and surface insects — and fish them as food, not as a provocation, in and beside the spawning shallows.

Territorial males are concentrated and visible in shallow daylight water — that is aggregation, not a feeding rate. An offering taken on the bed may be a defence response; the entry states that plainly rather than calling spawn-season strikes a bite pattern.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Time the effort to daylight, and to midday most of all: spawning movements and activity peak around the middle of the day when the water is at its warmest, and the species feeds by sight. Dawn and dusk still score well in the model (0.85), but the spawn itself is a midday show.

Work slowly and stay off the bed where you can: fish are territorial, adhesive eggs are on the gravel underfoot, and eggs hatch in roughly 186 degree-days — about 2–3 weeks. Wade and position at the edges, fish across the shallows, and leave active beds their room.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shallows look empty, the window may not have opened or may already have closed: the whole event lasts only 2–3 weeks, it needs roughly 4 °C after breakup, and northern ice-out varies — check for travelling fish in the deeper holding water below the spawning ground before concluding the run is absent.

If the spawning reach is running too hard, drop below it: spawning was not recorded above about 1.46 m/s, and feeding positions in fast water cost more than they return — the holding water below the bed is the tough-day address in a high-flow spawn.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Feed them the drift: the measured stream diet is drifting insects taken at the surface and through the column, taken from a held position. Natural insect-profile offerings drifted on the fish's line, at the speed of the water delivering them, are the supported presentation — no specific lure or fly is named in the research, and none is invented here.

In lakes the menu changes and the entry changes with it: lake grayling are facultative planktivores — zooplankton dominates the diet of shallow-water fish (about 80% in the Toolik lake record) — working the water in a stop-and-go search. Small offerings that read as plankton-sized food, fished slowly in the upper water, match that lake diet better than a big drift presentation.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the full day, not just the edges: the diel shape is day-led (day 1.0, dawn and dusk 0.85), because reactive distance rises dramatically above about 100 lux. Postspawn is a daylight feeding pattern — be on the best water when the light is on it.

In current, work the middle velocities hardest: prey encounter rises with flow up to about 46 cm/s, but capture success falls as the water speeds up, and holding effort plateaus around 30 cm/s — net intake peaks at intermediate flow. The fastest water in the reach is not the feeding water, however much drift it carries.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If postspawn fish refuse in dirty water, believe the turbidity curve — it is one of the steepest measured in the whole model: full suitability at 0–5 NTU, about 0.6 at 8 NTU, about 0.3 at 20 NTU, and effectively zero at 30 NTU and beyond. Move to clearer water instead of upsizing the bait.
If the fish have vanished from the spawning area, that is the pattern working, not failing: post-spawn adults leave for feeding areas immediately. Follow them out rather than grinding an empty bed.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer menu is insects at the surface and in the drift, and zooplankton in lakes — small, natural, and sized to that food. Grayling are famously willing surface feeders in the agency canon, consistent with the measured surface diet; no specific lure, fly pattern or size is named in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here.

Know which fish you are rating: this curve is built on adults. Juveniles prefer and grow best near 17 °C — about 5 °C warmer — so in a 15–18 °C midsummer lake the smaller, younger fish may still be feeding willingly while the adult curve is already declining. A day of small fish in warm water is that life-stage split showing, not the model failing.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish daylight first and keep the water clear in your planning: reactive distance collapses as turbidity rises — it falls with the logarithm of turbidity, so most of the damage is done by the first 10–20 NTU. A bright day on clear water is this visual feeder's best condition; a stained day is a close-range day.

Do not save the day for dark: night reactive distance is only about 20–30% of the daytime value and the model's night score is 0.25. Grayling do move at night in summer — the fishpass record shows night passage — but movement is not feeding, and this entry does not sell a night bite the vision record contradicts.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer fish shut down, take the temperature before changing anything: above about 20 °C adults avoid the water, chronic survival failed above 22 °C in the long trial, and the cold-acclimated incipient lethal is 23 °C. There is no presentation fix for water at the top of this fish's range — find cold water, or leave warm-water fish alone.

A hard, roiling wind is a measured problem, not a mood: wind and rain that roil the surface disturb this surface feeder's feeding. On a blown-out day, fish the sheltered shore and the subsurface drift, and expect the surface pattern to be the first thing the weather takes.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The fall menu is the summer menu cooling down: drifting and benthic invertebrates, taken by a fish whose activity now tracks the falling temperature day by day. Smaller and slower as the water drops through single digits is the temperature applied to tackle; no fall-specific lure is named in the research.

Keep offerings on the drift line and in the upper column early in the fall, and lower and slower as fish settle toward winter holding water — the diet does not change its identity in fall, only its delivery speed.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The day-led clock still runs the fall, and it matters more as darkness returns: at northern latitudes the long summer twilight is gone by September, real night is back, and the night score (0.25) applies in full. Concentrate effort in full daylight, when reactive distance is at its measured best.

Start honouring the oxygen rule before the ice does it for you: grayling select water above 4 mg/L when they can choose, and show stress responses at or below it. Stagnant, depleting backwaters that fished well in summer are the wrong late-fall bet.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall fish are gone from summer water, they have not vanished — they have migrated. The overwinter move is the strongest calendar fact in the fall record; fish the routes and the deep winter pools before you conclude the season is over.

In the coldest late-fall water the season value has fallen to 0.30–0.60 and feeding is thinning toward the winter minimum — slow everything down, fish the warmest part of the day, and give holding fish repeated close presentations rather than covering water.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Winter food, where it has been looked for, is invertebrates: the March stomach sample held caddis and other invertebrates, one fish full of invertebrates, sand and algae. Small invertebrate-profile offerings, delivered close and still, are the honest winter tackle story — no winter lure is named in the research, and feeding is minimal, so presentation has to arrive at the fish.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish winter as a low-rate pattern, because that is the measured description: the agency record says grayling feed minimally in winter and conserve energy, while the habitat synopsis says they apparently feed through it, probably limited by poor visibility under snow and ice. Both lines point the same way — slow, close, patient, in the aggregation.

Keep the day-led habit even in winter: this is a sight feeder whose reactive distance depends on light, and winter light is the scarcest of the year. The brightest part of the short day, over the located aggregation, is the winter window.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a winter spot is dead, suspect oxygen before presentation: a basin or pool that has slid toward the stress line at 4 mg/L and below will hold surviving fish that are not feeding. Move toward better-oxygenated deep water.

Know the honest limit of the season: winter feeding has never been quantified for this species — there is no winter catch-rate record behind any winter claim. A blank winter day is inside the evidence, not a surprise the entry hid from you.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small invertebrate offerings, fished close and still over the aggregation: the only direct winter food evidence is invertebrates in March stomachs — caddis and other invertebrates, one fish full of them. No ice-specific lure or presentation is measured for grayling; small and slow is the winter record applied honestly.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the brightest part of the short day first: the under-ice diel shape has never been measured, so the timing here is the measured open-water day-led shape (day on top, night at 0.20 under ice) carried across and labelled as a transfer. Give each hole over the aggregation real time — winter fish move little and feed minimally.

Treat a located aggregation as the whole pattern: winter fish compress into a small share of their summer water, so searching away from the deep, slow, oxygenated holding water is fishing where the fish are not.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Mid-winter silence is usually oxygen or rate, not bait: feeding is minimal all winter even where fish are present and surviving well. Move toward better-oxygenated water before changing presentations — and know that a provisional set means exactly this: the winter pattern is real, its size is unmeasured.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn is a migration season before it is a feeding season: the first rise toward 1 °C starts fish moving from overwintering water toward smaller spawning streams, and adults are travelling, not settled on summer feeding ground. Fish the travel routes and the holding water just below the spawning reaches, and expect the pattern to build as the water climbs toward 4 °C.

Overwintering fish come out of deep, slow, well-oxygenated water — lakes and the deeper pools where they aggregated — so early prespawn effort belongs where that deep winter water meets the spring routes, in water still carrying more than 4 mg/L of oxygen where you have a choice. Stress begins at or below that 4 mg/L line in the winter record.

On the stream side, prespawn adults stage below the shallow spawning gravel rather than on it: spawning itself will run over gravel, sand and rubble in about 0.15–0.91 m of water, and the approach water is where travelling fish can be met without fishing the spawning bed itself.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs for about 2–3 weeks after breakup once the water reaches roughly 4 °C — typically mid-May to mid-June in the north — with activity intensifying toward 10 °C. It is a short, daylight event, peaking near midday when the water is warmest, and males defend territories on the spawning ground.

Lake fish are part of this season, not an exception to it: lake-resident grayling leave the lake to spawn, entering outlet and inlet streams after breakup, then return to feeding water when the 2–3 weeks are done. The stream mouths and the first holding water inside them are the lake-side interception points.

The spawning address is shallow and specific: adhesive eggs are broadcast over gravel — also sand and rubble — in about 0.15–0.91 m of water, at sites where the measured optimal flow is roughly 0.34–1.19 m/s and no spawning was recorded above about 1.46 m/s. Fish the edges of that shallow gravel rather than standing in the middle of an active bed.

movementSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: Post-spawn adults move to feeding areas immediately — that is the chronology line — so the pattern flips quickly from the spawning shallows to summer feeding water. Start where the spawning ground empties into deeper holding and feeding water, then follow the fish out as the days pass.

The water is now climbing through the adult curve's sweet band: field occupancy peaks at 10.8 °C and stays high from about 6.9–14.7 °C, with the model's plateau at 10–14 °C. Postspawn fish in this band are the most catchable grayling of the spring — feeding fish, in warming water, still close to the spawning routes.

In streams, postspawn fish settle into the drift-feeding order: dominant fish take the positions with the highest predicted net energy intake, and modern field video had fish holding a focal position about 81% of the time. Fish one good holding position thoroughly — the best fish in the reach is likely parked on the best drift line, not cruising.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer is the peak — the model's July and August values are 1.0 — but it is a cold-water peak: adult field occupancy tops out at 10.8 °C, the plateau runs 10–14 °C, stress physiology begins above about 16 °C, and fish are stressed at about 17 °C and avoid water over 20 °C. In a warm summer, fish the coldest inflow, outlet and spring-influenced water first; in a cold northern summer, ordinary surface water is already in the band.

In lakes, summer fish feed visually on zooplankton and on surface and terrestrial insects where column prey is thin — a stop-and-go, saltatory search through the upper water. Work the upper column over and beside the feeding flats rather than dredging deep water the diet does not support.

Summer stream fish are drift specialists holding ranked, defended positions: dominant fish hold the spots where drift delivery minus holding cost is best, fish held a focal point about 81% of the time in the field-video record, and only about 14% of the time was spent actively foraging away from it. Cast to positions, not to water.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall feeding continues into the migration: fish build fat stores for winter while the season curve is still high in September (0.90), then the overwintering migration — usually September, running August to December — pulls them toward lakes and deep, slow pools. Early fall is feeding water; late fall is travel and arrival water.

As the water falls through the plateau and out the bottom of it, follow the fish toward the winter address: deeper, slower, well-oxygenated holding water. The temperature that ends the summer pattern is the same signal that starts the winter aggregation.

In streams the fall move is downstream and deliberate: fish leave summer feeding reaches for the deeper, slow-current pools of medium and large water, where winter fish in one telemetry study all held inside just 3.5 km of river, in near-zero flow with cover. Late-fall stream effort belongs in and above those deep pools, not spread over summer runs.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter fish are aggregated, not scattered: grayling overwinter in lakes and in deep, slow pools, packed into a small fraction of the water they use in summer. Find the deep, slow, covered winter water and you have found the population; the rest of the system is mostly empty of them.

Oxygen is the winter address inside the address: adults select deeper, more oxygenated water when they can, stress begins at or below about 4 mg/L, and yet the survival physiology is remarkable — the adult 24-hour LC50 is 0.75 mg/L at 1–3 °C, and winter survival ran 0.95–0.97 in the lake study despite near-anoxic bottom water. Fish the oxygenated layer over the deep holding water, not the bottom of a depleting basin.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: The ice set for grayling is PROVISIONAL, capped at Moderate confidence, and the entry carries that flag openly: overwinter habitat, aggregation and the oxygen gradient are measured for this species, and March stomachs show low-level winter feeding — but winter feeding rate has never been quantified, the under-ice timing below is the open-water day shape carried under ice as a labelled transfer, and no ice catch-rate record exists. Fish the deep, slow winter water where fish aggregated in the fall.

Oxygen decides the winter map: fish select water above about 4 mg/L when they can, stress responses start at or below 4 mg/L, and adults survive far lower — a 24-hour LC50 of 0.75 mg/L — by holding in the oxygenated layer. Set up over deep holding water that still carries oxygen, not over the deepest, most depleted bottom.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at midday; quietest at after dark.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at midday; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 10–14 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 23 °C, from the species' research file.
Wind: this species' feeding holds up best with wind 0–10 km/h — its own measured wind curve, not a generic one.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: Fronts, barometric pressure and moon have never been tested for grayling feeding or catch in any source the research could find — not measured nulls, plain absences. There is no front trick for this fish: what is measured is temperature, light, clarity and season, and a front matters here only as the temperature, wind and turbidity change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Wind is the one weather mechanism this species actually has on record: wind or rain that roils the surface disturbs surface feeding. In a hard chop, drop the offering below the disturbed surface, work the sheltered shore, and expect the surface pattern to be the casualty — the direction is measured; no wind-speed dose exists, and none is claimed.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Dawn and dusk score 0.85, close to the day's 1.0, for a physical reason: low northern light still clears the roughly 100-lux knee where reactive distance rises dramatically, for much of a summer shoulder period. Fish the transitions as real feeding time, not as bookends.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is a measured floor, not a mystery: reactive distance at night is about 20–30% of the daytime value and the model scores night at 0.25. Fish left after dark should fish slowly and close in known holding water — and plan the day so the best water gets daylight.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais testé pour l'Arctic grayling — aucun recensement de terrain, modèle d'enquête ou expérience contrôlée pression-alimentation n'existe. Zéro par absence (pas un nul mesuré).
Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai du grayling. Le frai/la migration sont conditionnés par la température, la glace et la profondeur dans chaque étude qui a mesuré leurs déclencheurs.

Le régime est démontrablement divisé (dérive de rivière contre planctivorie de lac, contraste du lac Toolik ~80% contre <10% de zooplancton — Jones et al. 2003; O'Brien & Evans 1992) mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure la dérive ou l'offre de zooplancton d'un plan d'eau; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.
La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour le grayling; elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn is a migration season before it is a feeding season: the first rise toward 1 °C starts fish moving from overwintering water toward smaller spawning streams, and adults are travelling, not settled on summer feeding ground. Fish the travel routes and the holding water just below the spawning reaches, and expect the pattern to build as the water climbs toward 4 °C.

Overwintering fish come out of deep, slow, well-oxygenated water — lakes and the deeper pools where they aggregated — so early prespawn effort belongs where that deep winter water meets the spring routes, in water still carrying more than 4 mg/L of oxygen where you have a choice. Stress begins at or below that 4 mg/L line in the winter record.

On the stream side, prespawn adults stage below the shallow spawning gravel rather than on it: spawning itself will run over gravel, sand and rubble in about 0.15–0.91 m of water, and the approach water is where travelling fish can be met without fishing the spawning bed itself.

Fish the daylight hours first — grayling are sight feeders, feeding mostly during the day, and their ability to locate prey rises dramatically once light passes about 100 lux. A prespawn day is a midday-weighted day.

Cover the staging water thoroughly and move slowly between spots: prespawn migration is temperature-triggered, so a reach that was empty in the morning can hold travelling fish after the day's warming — re-check the best staging water late in the day before you write it off.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs for about 2–3 weeks after breakup once the water reaches roughly 4 °C — typically mid-May to mid-June in the north — with activity intensifying toward 10 °C. It is a short, daylight event, peaking near midday when the water is warmest, and males defend territories on the spawning ground.

Lake fish are part of this season, not an exception to it: lake-resident grayling leave the lake to spawn, entering outlet and inlet streams after breakup, then return to feeding water when the 2–3 weeks are done. The stream mouths and the first holding water inside them are the lake-side interception points.

The spawning address is shallow and specific: adhesive eggs are broadcast over gravel — also sand and rubble — in about 0.15–0.91 m of water, at sites where the measured optimal flow is roughly 0.34–1.19 m/s and no spawning was recorded above about 1.46 m/s. Fish the edges of that shallow gravel rather than standing in the middle of an active bed.

Time the effort to daylight, and to midday most of all: spawning movements and activity peak around the middle of the day when the water is at its warmest, and the species feeds by sight. Dawn and dusk still score well in the model (0.85), but the spawn itself is a midday show.

Work slowly and stay off the bed where you can: fish are territorial, adhesive eggs are on the gravel underfoot, and eggs hatch in roughly 186 degree-days — about 2–3 weeks. Wade and position at the edges, fish across the shallows, and leave active beds their room.

spawningSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: Post-spawn adults move to feeding areas immediately — that is the chronology line — so the pattern flips quickly from the spawning shallows to summer feeding water. Start where the spawning ground empties into deeper holding and feeding water, then follow the fish out as the days pass.

The water is now climbing through the adult curve's sweet band: field occupancy peaks at 10.8 °C and stays high from about 6.9–14.7 °C, with the model's plateau at 10–14 °C. Postspawn fish in this band are the most catchable grayling of the spring — feeding fish, in warming water, still close to the spawning routes.

In streams, postspawn fish settle into the drift-feeding order: dominant fish take the positions with the highest predicted net energy intake, and modern field video had fish holding a focal position about 81% of the time. Fish one good holding position thoroughly — the best fish in the reach is likely parked on the best drift line, not cruising.

Fish the full day, not just the edges: the diel shape is day-led (day 1.0, dawn and dusk 0.85), because reactive distance rises dramatically above about 100 lux. Postspawn is a daylight feeding pattern — be on the best water when the light is on it.

In current, work the middle velocities hardest: prey encounter rises with flow up to about 46 cm/s, but capture success falls as the water speeds up, and holding effort plateaus around 30 cm/s — net intake peaks at intermediate flow. The fastest water in the reach is not the feeding water, however much drift it carries.

spawningSources.citation: Chronologie saisonnière (frai ≥4 °C après la débâcle, mi-mai–mi-juin, 2–3 sem., lumière du jour sur gravier; pic d'alimentation juill.–août; migration d'hivernage sept.) — Larocque et al. 2014; Hubert et al. 1985; Stewart et al. 2007. Le frai est une annotation — aucun coefficient de suppression n'existe
Terme générique d'eau de fonte (la débâcle printanière est le déclencheur de frai du grayling, mais le terme lui-même est le générique du programme)

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai du grayling. Le frai/la migration sont conditionnés par la température, la glace et la profondeur dans chaque étude qui a mesuré leurs déclencheurs. (Monographie de l'Arctic grayling §4/§5)

about: The black bullhead is the toughest of the bullheads — the turbid-water specialist, built for warm, shallow, silty water over soft bottoms with little vegetation, where low oxygen and murk shut out most competitors. It's a heat-tolerant fish whose feeding peaks in the high twenties Celsius in the rating model, spawning May through July once the water passes about 20 °C.

Black bullheads are night feeders and nest guardians, fanning eggs in soft-bottom shallows and herding their black fry balls through early summer. They'll eat nearly anything — insects, snails, dead fish, dough — and bite when nothing else will. Anglers target them for guaranteed action on farm ponds and prairie lakes, for fish fries, and as the fish that keeps a slow evening honest; big black bullheads from clean water are genuinely good eating.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Scent-led and still, on the genus mechanism — taste working as a distance sense, measured in the experiment where bullheads themselves were the subjects (no primary taste-bud count exists for black bullhead; the 'about 100,000 receptors' figure in secondary accounts has no primary source and is not used). Offerings sized to the measured diet — detritus and chironomids lead the pond diet work — are the supported shape. No lure is named in the black bullhead literature, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Slow and close to shelter, with one black-specific comfort in hard winters: this is the family's low-oxygen end-member — the historic resistance experiments used it as exactly that, showing a tolerance of combined low oxygen and high carbon dioxide the other test fish didn't match — so in a winterkill-prone shallow lake, this is the bullhead most likely to still be there. Survival, again, is not a feeding promise; it is a reason to keep the lake on your list.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If cold black bullhead won't go, you may simply be past this fish's studied year — its winter feeding has never been measured, and the secondary accounts lean toward stopped, not slow. The library's honest cold-season bullhead is brown bullhead; black in deep winter is a gap, and the entry leaves it one.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The benthic menu, broadly: this is a wide benthic omnivore — insects and larvae, crustaceans, molluscs, worms, detritus, plant material, fish. One measured prespawn-adjacent lesson from the diet work: when water rises and floods new ground, the diet swings hard to terrestrial prey (56% by volume in the rising-water period of the reservoir study) — after a spring rise, offerings that read as drowned terrestrial food are fishing a documented switch, not a hunch.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the whole day more honestly than the other bullheads allow (see the summer entry for the measured reason) while weighting dusk and dark. Prespawn black bullhead are a warming-shallows pattern with a real daytime component — a combination neither cousin offers you.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the turbid shallows are quiet, check that the water has actually warmed — the spawn below is temperature-gated at about 20 °C, and a cold turbid flat is still a winter flat. Warmth first, then the shallows.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No spawn-specific presentation is measured for this species. The scent-led bottom offerings of the feeding seasons, worked around the nesting shallows, are the supported approach.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: One discipline this entry keeps on purpose: whether guarding suppresses feeding has never been observed in black bullhead at all, and no other species' spawn story is borrowed here as a black fact — expect the spawn window to fish on this species' normal clock (night-led, with its genuine daytime component) and let your own results, not a cousin's study, describe its spawn bite.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the nesting shallows are dead, work the first deeper soft-bottom water off them before leaving — post-spawn and non-nesting fish in a sedentary genus are a short move away, and the turbid shallows' edges fish in daylight for this species in a way they don't for its cousins.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the night menu and the day menu as the diet work separates them: offshore summer fish caught at night in the reservoir study were 98% Chaoborus (phantom midge larvae) — a tiny, mid-water night food — while the pond diet work has detritus at about half the diet with chironomids the dominant animal prey. Small, soft, scent-led bottom offerings cover the documented core; the Chaoborus result argues for keeping one small offering off the bottom at night over deeper soft flats. Taste does the finding (the genus mechanism, measured on bullheads themselves); no lure is named in this species' literature, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Here is this species' measured difference from its cousins, and the reason its entries read differently: black bullhead feeds by day in a way brown bullhead measurably does not. The field tradition says adults feed almost exclusively after dark — and then the controlled evidence qualifies it twice: video-recorded scavenging experiments found activity higher at night but substantial daytime activity also recorded (larger fish more active, especially at night), and a high-density pond population fed across the day with three peaks, at 08–11, 13–15 and 19–22 h. That pond was a stunted, high-competition population, which is not a lake — the entry carries the caveat — but two independent results break strict nocturnality for this species, so its rating's day value sits near double brown's. The practical shape: night and dusk are still the peak, and a black bullhead trip does not have to wait for dark — a summer midday on turbid shallows is a real shift for this fish, where for brown it is the documented off shift. (The juveniles' midday school-feeding in the secondary accounts is noted and not modelled; these entries describe adults.)

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the turbid shallows won't go at night, fish them again in daylight before you move lakes — with this species that is a measured pattern, not optimism. And in a hot, still, low-oxygen spell that empties a shallow lake of everything else, remember the ranking: this is the fish built to be the one still feeding there — slowly, and mostly after dark.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer bottom menu, slower. The fall diet breadth stays wide — a benthic omnivore in cooling water is still a taste-led fish, and scent remains the presentation the genus mechanism supports.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Keep both halves of this species' day while the water holds warmth: dusk and night as the peak, daylight as a genuine second shift on the turbid shallows. As the water falls toward the low teens, weight the dark hours more and the day less — the daytime evidence comes from warm-season studies, and the entry doesn't extend it into the cold.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A fall flat emptying is more likely temperature than departure in a sedentary genus — follow the warmest shallow, sheltered, soft-bottom water before you follow the fish anywhere else. Below that, you are in the cold entry's honest territory: low cap, winter unmeasured.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice presentation exists for black bullhead, and the winter accounts give no feeding pattern to build one from.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: If you fish this species through the ice, know that its ice season is past its evidence entirely. Its open-water facts (warm turbid shallows, soft bottom, a night-led clock with a real day shift) are open-water findings if you use them, not ice findings.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Black bullhead under ice is unstudied water, and the library's answer is to say so rather than to borrow a cousin's winter.

movementSeasons.heading: Eau froide
lines: Start with what this entry is, because the cold season shows it plainest: black bullhead's rating is a derived set, its confidence capped at Low — the lowest cap in this genus package. Its temperature and oxygen curves are built from black's own measurements; its winter is not. Black's own winter material is secondary-only: accounts of decreased or ceased feeding and of fish buried in shoreline debris with their gills exposed, unreplicated and graded as claims, not findings — and if anything they describe a fish that stops. Fish the warm, shallow, soft-bottom water this species owns, near shoreline debris and shelter, and hold your confidence at the cap.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Fish the warming shallows this species is built for: warm, shallow, turbid water over soft bottoms with little vegetation is its documented niche — the turbid-water specialist of the genus, at the opposite end from yellow bullhead's clear gravel. In shallow turbid lakes its bottom-feeding actively sustains the turbidity it prefers (in the macrophyte-impact study its effect ran about half of common carp's at median catch rates), so the murkiest warm shallows in the system are not a compromise for this fish; they are its address.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs May through July (April–June in some accounts) once the water passes about 20 °C, with a core band of 20–24 °C on consistent secondary-grade evidence. Nests are small saucers, 15–35 cm across, at about 0.6–1.2 m deep, in the shallow soft-bottom water. Care is biparental with variable roles between the sexes in the syntheses. Fish the shallows around the nesting water.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer black bullhead are the warm, shallow, turbid, soft-bottom pattern at full strength — little vegetation, high turbidity tolerated and preferred beyond either cousin, and an agency ranking that has this species persisting and flourishing in warm, low-oxygen, silted water lethal to nearly everything else. The temperature frame is black's own: no preferendum exists for this species, but its growth was measured insensitive to temperature across 18–29 °C — that broad, cool plateau is what its rating carries — with feeding and growth commencing near 10 °C, best weight conversion at 23–24 °C, and black's own ceiling above it: an upper incipient lethal of 35.4 °C and a critical thermal maximum of 37.5 °C, with a 1953 measurement of 35.0 °C (24-hour, 50% mortality) independently agreeing with the lethal bound across 57 years. A fish-culture tradition running this species at 23–25 °C is a plausibility check that its productive band includes the mid-20s — a husbandry range, not an optimum, and the entry quotes it as nothing more.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is thin water for this species: its cooling-season behaviour has never been measured, and no other fish's fall slide is substituted for it. What is black's own is the growth logic — growth across its populations correlated significantly and positively with temperature in the meta-analysis, so cooling water means slowing fish. Shorten the search toward shoreline shelter and debris as it cools; the winter-burial accounts wait at the bottom of this season.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: Not covered — and for this species the absence argues in one direction. No winter feeding or under-ice study of black bullhead exists, and the only winter material there is — secondary accounts of fish ceasing to feed, buried in shoreline debris — points away from borrowing any other species' ice shape. ICE mode for this species reports not-covered.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light and after dark; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at first light and after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 18–29 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 37.5 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The weather file for black bullhead is a blank shared by the whole genus: front, pressure, wind and moon have never been measured in any bullhead — pressure and moon carry zero weight in this rating as data, not omissions, and the one front-adjacent claim in the canon (a modern synthesis repeating wind-blown-bank lore for this species) is Grade C background, not a study. The rating carries no front term for this fish at all — none has ever been measured. Fish the temperature change a front brings; there is no black bullhead barometer rule, and anyone selling one has no study to show you.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is still this species' peak — the field study's adults fed almost exclusively after dark, and in the scavenging experiments the larger fish were most active at night. Fish it as the main shift; just don't make it the only one (see the daylight overlay, which is where this species parts company with brown bullhead).

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Evening is one of this species' three measured feeding peaks in the pond work (19–22 h) and the front edge of its field-observed night pattern — dusk on the turbid shallows is the most reliable single window the black bullhead day offers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: This overlay is the species' signature, and it is deliberately the opposite of the brown bullhead entry across the page: bright daylight is a genuine feeding shift for black bullhead. Substantial daytime activity is a controlled-experiment result for this fish, and a wild population fed in distinct morning (08–11 h) and afternoon (13–15 h) peaks — caveated as a high-density pond population, but real. Do not import brown bullhead's near-zero daylight picture into this species: if you only have a midday, fish it, on the warm turbid shallows, with more confidence than bullhead folklore allows any of them.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Wind honesty for the genus, with this species' one footnote: no wind study exists for any bullhead; a modern angling synthesis repeats the wind-blown-bank claim for black bullhead specifically, and it remains untested canon (Grade C). Fish a windward turbid shore if it fits your water — as lore you chose, not a finding you were given.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais mesuré pour aucune espèce de bullhead (alimentation, activité, mouvement ou capture). Zéro est une donnée, pas une omission.
Jamais mesuré pour aucune espèce de bullhead. Le travail d'éclairement de Peters (100–1,400 lx) n'est PAS extrapolé au clair de lune.
Aucune étude de télémétrie ou de réponse au débit n'existe pour aucun bullhead; le modèle de lac ne porte aucun terme de débit pour ce genre.
Le régime est une omnivorie benthique large chez les trois espèces; aucune étude d'impulsion ou de fenêtre de proies n'existe à paramétrer.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Fish the warming shallows this species is built for: warm, shallow, turbid water over soft bottoms with little vegetation is its documented niche — the turbid-water specialist of the genus, at the opposite end from yellow bullhead's clear gravel. In shallow turbid lakes its bottom-feeding actively sustains the turbidity it prefers (in the macrophyte-impact study its effect ran about half of common carp's at median catch rates), so the murkiest warm shallows in the system are not a compromise for this fish; they are its address.

Fish the whole day more honestly than the other bullheads allow (see the summer entry for the measured reason) while weighting dusk and dark. Prespawn black bullhead are a warming-shallows pattern with a real daytime component — a combination neither cousin offers you.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs May through July (April–June in some accounts) once the water passes about 20 °C, with a core band of 20–24 °C on consistent secondary-grade evidence. Nests are small saucers, 15–35 cm across, at about 0.6–1.2 m deep, in the shallow soft-bottom water. Care is biparental with variable roles between the sexes in the syntheses. Fish the shallows around the nesting water.

One discipline this entry keeps on purpose: whether guarding suppresses feeding has never been observed in black bullhead at all, and no other species' spawn story is borrowed here as a black fact — expect the spawn window to fish on this species' normal clock (night-led, with its genuine daytime component) and let your own results, not a cousin's study, describe its spawn bite.

spawningSources.citation: Aucune forme défendable sur 12 mois n'existe : les deux propres études saisonnières de régime du black se contredisent sur l'ordre d'intensité d'alimentation (Sikora et al. 2022 — alimentation minimale en octobre; Snow et al. 2017 — alimentation maximale en hiver), alors le facteur est porté PLAT au neutre 0.60 plutôt que résolu par emprunt. La bande de frai 20–24 °C, mai–juill. est propre au black (synthèses de grade secondaire; le groupe 19–21 °C des guides de terrain s'accorde à l'extrémité basse).

about: Black crappie — speckled, dark-mottled panfish — are the crappie of clearer, cooler, more vegetated water, and in the north their spring run can lag into late May. Spawning starts at 13–14 °C and peaks in the mid-to-high teens, in nest colonies in the vegetated shallows, and telemetry has caught them staying shallow well into summer when the generic crappie calendar says they should be deep.

Black crappie hold around weed edges, brush and docks, feeding in schools on minnows and insects, most actively in low light and through the ice. They are delicate biters and soft-mouthed fighters — finesse fish, caught on tiny jigs and live minnows. Anglers target them for the spring shallows run, for hardwater slabs, and because a two-pound black crappie is one of panfishing's great prizes.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small offerings matched to the plankton-and-minnow forage, fished at the schools' depth. The direct experiments are the colour story here: black crappie ate least in clear water and showed no clear-water preference in any test — the draw is vegetation and structure, not clarity, so don't pass up stained, vegetated water for a clear flat.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the edges slowly at school depth. Adults already run a dusk-and-night clock, so prespawn evenings on the staging edges outfish the midday hours.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the vegetated edges are quiet, check the first deeper break — staging fish hold a step off the shallows until the temperature says go.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small, slow, at nest depth in the vegetation. Nothing in the spawn evidence supports big or fast; the colonies are the location, and small forage-matching offerings are the presentation.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the protected shallows methodically while the window runs, and weight your effort to dusk — the adults' feeding clock peaks then even in the spawn season.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If one colony is quiet, move along the protected shore rather than deeper — spawning colonies are patchy, and the next sheltered stretch can be loaded while yours is empty.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Plankton-and-minnow forage matching, at exact school depth. Turbidity is a tested non-story for this species — three experiments converge on no turbidity preference — so clarity should never talk you out of a vegetated spot.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The adult clock: dusk and night elevated, a midday trough, juveniles peaking at dawn — competent studies conflict on the exact peak hour, and the library keeps that conflict visible rather than picking one. What doesn't conflict: low light is when adults feed, so build the trip around dusk.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A dead midday is this fish's trough, not a verdict on the spot. Fish the same vegetation at dusk before you move lakes.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small forage-matching offerings at school depth, slowing as the water drops through the teens Celsius.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Keep the dusk emphasis and start checking the deeper edges near the summer vegetation — the winter move is a short one in this species, from shallow structure toward the nearest deep, oxygenated water.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall spots empty, follow the oxygen logic early: the fish are setting up where winter oxygen will hold, not where summer put them.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small and slow at the schools' depth. Open-water oxygen response was never measured for this species — the winter gate is the measured anchor, and the open-water entries don't pretend otherwise.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Locate first, fish second: winter schools are tight, and the difference between a school and empty water can be a short move. The under-ice entries below carry the detailed pattern.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: In a low-oxygen winter, technique is not the problem — basin choice is. Move to the deepest, best-oxygenated water in the lake before changing a single bait.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small offerings at the schools' exact depth. The under-ice evidence is about location, oxygen and timing — it does not name a lure, and the entry won't invent one.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the clock the ice evidence gives: under-ice feeding peaks in the creel synthesis include a midnight-to-2 a.m. window, matching the nocturnal plankton (Chaoborus) mechanism — a synthesis at Grade C, labelled as such, but it's the only under-ice diel guidance that exists for this fish. Dusk remains a primary window.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If early-ice fish won't go, verify the basin's oxygen story before the bait: below the gate, there is no presentation fix.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small and slow, presented at the school's level in the basin. Mid-winter black crappie are a location problem solved on electronics, then a patience problem.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Keep the low-light and night windows — dusk, and the late-night window the synthesis reports. Bright midday under thick ice and snow is the trough of this fish's day.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A silent mid-winter basin is usually an oxygen verdict. Move basins, not baits.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The small school-depth offerings of mid-winter, fished a step more actively as the fish start travelling.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Check shallower every trip now. Late-ice black crappie are moving one direction — toward the spawn — and staging fish on the edges are the catchable ones.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the edges are quiet, they're still deep — but re-check the shallows at dusk before you leave; the move can happen within days at late ice.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Black crappie stage toward the spawning shallows as the water climbs toward 13–14 °C. Within a lake they hold shallower and on steeper, more vegetated water than white crappie — fish the vegetated shallows' edges and the first breaks off them.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning starts at 13–14 °C and peaks at 16–20 °C, in nest colonies in the vegetated shallows — in the north the run lags, into late May in Manitoba. One measured detail worth fishing: wind matters to the nests, not the day — colonies favour wind-protected sites, so the sheltered side of the spawning shallows is the percentage water.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Ignore the calendar canon here — telemetry from Kentucky Lake has black crappie staying shallow into summer after the spawn, the opposite of the generic crappie calendar and of white crappie in the same water. Fish the shallow vegetation and structure, suspended at the schools' level.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall fish use the same shallow vegetation and structure story, cooling toward the winter pattern: deeper as it gets cold, with oxygen becoming the address that matters most as winter approaches.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter black crappie are an oxygen story with a hard number: under ice, about 2 mg/L is the gate. Fish the deep, oxygenated basins near the summer structure — and in a winterkill-prone lake, the fish are wherever the oxygen survives.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace précoce
lines: Black crappie is a genuine ice species — one of the few in this library with A-grade under-ice evidence for the species itself. Early ice: the deep, oxygenated water near the summer vegetation and structure, with oxygen already the governing fact (the gate sits near 2 mg/L).

movementSeasons.heading: Glace de mi-hiver
lines: Mid-winter is the oxygen squeeze: stay on the deepest oxygenated basins, and expect fish to have shifted toward whatever water still carries oxygen as the season's depletion runs.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace tardive
lines: Late ice loosens the pattern: fish slide from the deep basins back toward the vegetated shallows they'll spawn in, as light and meltwater return. Fish the route — the first breaks and edges between basin and spawning shallows.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 16–24 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 33.3 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The one real pressure finding in crappie belongs to this species — and it is about movement, not feeding: rapid pressure change, either direction, correlated with fish moving more (r = 0.75 in the South Dakota telemetry). Whether moving fish feed more or less has never been tested, in either crappie. So a pressure swing is a reason to expect fish to have relocated and to re-find them — not a promise about the bite, in either direction.

weatherOverlays.heading: Avant l’arrivée d’un front
lines: Same honest limit ahead of the front: pressure change predicts movement in this species' one telemetry study, and nothing about feeding has ever been measured. Fish your found fish while you have them, and plan to relocate them after the swing.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Adults feed at night — that part of the diel evidence is consistent even where the exact peak hour is disputed. A dusk start that fishes into dark is this species' measured window.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Wind honesty, in this species' own data: wind speed and direction were tested against black crappie movement and came back non-significant. There is no wind pattern for daily fishing here — wind only enters this fish's year as shelter for the nest colonies in spring.

weatherNotCounted.reason: TESTÉ NUL — Guy et al. 1992 ont testé le vent contre l'activité du crapet de roche et n'ont trouvé aucun effet. Zéro est la mesure.
Non porté — aucune mesure lunaire pour l'alimentation du crapet de roche dans la base de preuves.
NUL VÉRIFIÉ par trois expériences indépendantes (succès d'alimentation / distance de réaction insensibles sur la turbidité testée) — poids zéro, délibérément.

lines: Black crappie stage toward the spawning shallows as the water climbs toward 13–14 °C. Within a lake they hold shallower and on steeper, more vegetated water than white crappie — fish the vegetated shallows' edges and the first breaks off them.
Fish the edges slowly at school depth. Adults already run a dusk-and-night clock, so prespawn evenings on the staging edges outfish the midday hours.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning starts at 13–14 °C and peaks at 16–20 °C, in nest colonies in the vegetated shallows — in the north the run lags, into late May in Manitoba. One measured detail worth fishing: wind matters to the nests, not the day — colonies favour wind-protected sites, so the sheltered side of the spawning shallows is the percentage water.
Work the protected shallows methodically while the window runs, and weight your effort to dusk — the adults' feeding clock peaks then even in the spawn season.
