about: The brook trout — speckled trout in the east — is a char, not a true trout, and it is the native fish of cold spring water: its Latin name, fontinalis, means “living in springs.” It is strictly a cold-water fish, native below about 16 °C with an ideal in the single digits to mid-teens, and in the rating model its feeding peaks at 13–16 °C.

Brook trout live where the cold comes in — spring-fed creeks, headwater streams, beaver ponds and the spring holes of northern lakes — feeding on insects, crustaceans and smaller fish, and spawning in fall over gravel where groundwater wells up. They are famously beautiful, famously willing, and famously fragile where waters warm. Anglers target them with fly and light tackle for the colours, the wildness, and the wild places you have to walk into to find them.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Match what is on the water — the books' first rule: study the insects along the stream and make up your cast accordingly. Small and plain beats large and gaudy on most streams; for educated fish, the smallest flies on No. 12–18 hooks, on gossamer leaders. The old standard cast: Professor, Queen of the Water, Grizzly King, the Drakes, Montreal, Silver Doctor, Coachman — and hackles.

For big lake fish, think smelt: the great Rangeley streamers — Carrie Stevens's Gray Ghost first, the Supervisor (tied to mimic the finger smelt), the Black Ghost — and Don Gapen's Muddler Minnow, invented in 1936 to imitate the slimy sculpin for the giant brook trout of the Nipigon River.
If they won't rise: 'fear not to use bait' — minnows, red worms, white grubs, grasshoppers. A dead bait must be fresh and sweet; brook trout will not eat carrion.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Stealth is the whole technique with this fish. No other fish is so affected by shadows: the shadow of your body, your raised rod, or your line across a quiet pool is instant alarm. Crawl to the pool noiselessly on all fours. Slide rather than step when you wade. It's concussion they hear — a voice doesn't disturb them, but a toe scratched on the boat bottom or a careless tread on the bank empties the pool.

Most trout are taken within 30 ft — long casts are seldom needed. Working a rise: cast a little short of it first, then a little further. Let flies fall lightly, and let a dry fly drift down into a foamy pool with the current now and then — that drift took one classic author's largest fish.

For big lake fish: cast a straight line, let the fly sink a foot or two, then draw it toward you with short pauses. From a boat at a brook mouth, cast toward the mouth and draw the flies slowly across the ripples — and where big fish are known, use one fly only.

Strike with the wrist alone, swiftly but delicately — swift because a trout ejects a fly in a fraction of a second (in rapids, instantaneously; in a quiet pool, the slow striker wins), delicate because the arm is never needed. And don't land a hooked fish hastily: most escapes are lost through undue haste.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Clear, low water under bright skies is the books' hardest condition — the answer is more stealth and finer presentation, not a different lure. And fish unlikely water thoroughly: 'Never think that you know a brook until you have fished it thoroughly — the best trout are sometimes taken in the most unlikely spots.'

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: At a cold tributary mouth, a fresh minnow is the classic bait; in the spring-fed lake shallows in spring, big char chase minnow shoals and a live minnow takes fish daily.

In swift water they tolerate more warmth than in sluggish water — fish the runs and riffles with streamers (the Gray Ghost, the Muddler) and small plain flies. At a cold tributary mouth, a fresh minnow is the classic bait.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: All the stealth rules double in warm, clear, low water: crawl, slide, keep your shadow off the pool, cast short of the fish first. Warm water holds the wariest fish in the coldest corners — fish those corners like they're made of glass.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the home water is warm everywhere, the honest book answer is to travel to the cold: spring holes — brook trout gather about springs in the bottoms of lakes and ponds in warm weather. There is no presentation that fixes warm water for a brook trout.
If the home water is warm everywhere, the honest book answer is to travel to the cold: tributary mouths and high-gradient runs. There is no presentation that fixes warm water for a brook trout.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Streamers for the lake fish: Gray Ghost, Supervisor, Black Ghost, and the Colonel Bates — Stevens's pattern recorded as successful particularly in stained water.
Ordinary trout flies, fished in the river, take the big autumn fish — the standard cast of the classics.
Trolling with the spoon, the phantom minnow or a dead-fish bait is very successful on the big lake fish in fall — they'll take a very large pike spoon.
On off days on the river, the phantom minnow usually does the work.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the foot-of-falls pools and the outlet rivers with the full stealth rules — shadow and concussion discipline matters more with these fish the bigger they get. Dusk is coming into its own: feeding peaks as the dark gathers.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: On the days they won't rise in the river, the phantom minnow is the classic's own fallback. And remember the season's oddity — spawning fish fast; if a pool full of fish ignores everything, they may be spawners, and the feeders are in the next pool down.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice lure for brook trout is book canon. Anything you read elsewhere about tip-ups and spoons for brookies is modern magazine material, not the books this app is built on — and the app won't dress it up as book teaching.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: What the books do give you is the season around the ice: after ice-out, the fish aren't commonly taken until the water and the morning air are nearly the same temperature — and the early-spring trolling streamers earn their keep then, on fish hungry after a winter under the ice. If brook trout are the goal, that's the sourced season to plan for.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: For hard-water fishing, the honest move is to target the species the ice books actually cover — walleye, pike, perch, lake trout, burbot — and save the brook trout for the cold open water they're made for.

movementSeasons.heading: Eau fraîche
lines: Brook trout are strictly cold water — native below 60 °F, ideal 35–55 °F — and the name says the address: fontinalis, 'living in springs.' In lakes, the spring-fed water and the mouths of cold tributaries. In warm weather the fishing moves to the mouths of streams.

Brook trout are strictly cold water — native below 60 °F, ideal 35–55 °F — and the name says the address: fontinalis, 'living in springs.' In streams, the deep pools and eddies where they can lie concealed under grassy banks or logs and see without being seen. In warm weather the fishing moves to the mouths of streams and the swift, aerated water.

On the big lakes the seasonal round runs: shallows and points as the water warms in June, the cool depths in the heat of summer, the pools again in September. Big lake fish live deep and feed under the surface — they are not surface feeders.

movementSeasons.heading: Eau chaude
lines: The water is past what this fish calls home — above the mid-teens Celsius it's a relocation problem, not a tactics problem. Go where the cold is: the mouths of cold tributary streams and the spring-fed depths of the lake. Brook trout gather about springs in the bottoms of lakes and ponds in warm weather.

The water is past what this fish calls home — above the mid-teens Celsius it's a relocation problem, not a tactics problem. Go where the cold is: the mouths of cold tributary streams and the swift, aerated water.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Autumn is the spawning movement: in the great Quebec lake country the pattern is famous — through summer the giants stay in the cool spring-fed depths, then in late August they descend into the outlet river.

Autumn is the spawning movement: from September into November the fish move up nearly to the sources of the spring brooks, preferring fast water over gravel. In late August they descend into the outlet river, and through late August and all of September big fish rise freely to ordinary trout flies there. Note the old teaching: in the spawning season the fish take no food at all — fish the feeders at the edges of the movement, and the pools they rest in.
On the Nipigon pattern: the best fishing of the year runs mid-July through August and September, at the foot of the falls and chutes — excellent fishing at the foot of all of them.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: We have to be honest with you here: none of the brook trout books behind this app — and we read the classics cover to cover — covers fishing for them through the ice. There's no book-taught ice pattern for this species to pass on.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at midday; quietest at after dark.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at midday; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 13–16 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 25.3 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The old books are blunt about weather for this fish: 'Neither a low barometer nor an electric storm are conducive to success in fishing.' But the same page finishes the thought — 'a change of weather is often the prelude to good luck in fishing.' The day the weather breaks is a day to be on a brook trout stream.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Dusk is this fish's feeding peak: hunger approaches its maximum as dusk gathers, the insects are most abundant, and fish feed on into the dark — they were taken up to midnight, on dark and moonlit nights alike. After dark: the white miller and light-coloured flies, and the black hackle has proven attractive. For fish sipping tiny midges on the surface, a gray-midge fly on a No. 18 or 20 hook. Evening fish lie along bushy banks and are excessively fond of crickets and grasshoppers.
At the other end of the day: be on hand early — 'the first rays of the sun are often death to your success,' in a famous guide's teaching. The dawn window is short; be fishing before it starts.

weatherOverlays.heading: Couvert
lines: One of the classic's best evenings came under a dull, grey sky with a southerly breeze rippling the water ahead of a coming storm — the fish rose freely in numbers. Grey, rippled water is brook trout weather; fish it with confidence.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: They feed after dark — to midnight, dark nights and moonlit ones — but not in the rapids: night fish are in the pools and along the bushy banks. White miller, light-coloured flies, black hackle; crickets and grasshoppers along the banks.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Bright sun is this fish's hardest light — that's when the stealth rules earn their keep: no shadow on the pool, no concussion, flies falling like feathers, and casts kept within 30 ft. Fish the aerated water and the shade of the banks at midday, and save the open pools for the light change.

about: The brown bullhead is the hardy, whiskered panfish of warm lakes, ponds and slow rivers — a small catfish that shrugs off conditions that defeat fussier fish, tolerating heat into the high thirties Celsius in the research and feeding at temperatures where others sulk. It's one of the earliest spring feeders in its community, already feeding at 6.5 °C in the Ontario field work behind this entry.

Brown bullheads spawn in late spring, in one of the best-documented bullhead seasons in the literature — most egg-laying inside a tight couple of weeks — with nests guarded by one or both parents, and the fry herded in black clouds through early summer. They feed at dusk and after dark on insects, snails and small fish. Anglers target them for easy, family-friendly action and honest table fare, often as the first catfish a kid ever catches.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Scent-led, still and on the bottom. The genus locates food by taste at a distance — measured in the experiment where brown bullhead itself was a subject (Bardach, Todd & Crickmer 1967) — so a bait that puts scent into still water is fishing the measured sense. Match the measured diet at its smallest cold-season size: chironomid larvae and other aquatic insects, small crustaceans, worms. No lure is named in the brown bullhead literature, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Keep the night shift even now — especially now. In controlled winter trials this species preyed at temperatures as low as 3 °C, almost exclusively at night, with consumption rising steeply from 3 °C to 4.5 °C. A buried cold fish is not an immobilised one (disturbed fish emerge), but it is not looking for a midday bait either: fish slow, fish close to shelter, and weight the dark hours.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Two opposite claims about this fish in cold water are both wrong as absolutes. 'Dormant and does not feed all winter' is contradicted by stomachs with food in them from fish netted under the ice at 4 °C, and by the 3 °C night-predation trials — which also supersede the older published claim that feeding ceases at 3.5 °C. And 'active all winter' ignores the measured collapse in spontaneous activity below 7 °C. The honest cold pattern is a real but low, nocturnal, opportunistic one.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The full benthic-omnivore menu is back in play as the water warms: chironomids and other aquatic insects, crustaceans, molluscs, worms, detritus and plant material, fish and fish eggs all appear in the diet work. Bottom presentations sized to that menu, scent forward, are the supported tackle story — the studies name the food, not a lure.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the climb, not the calendar: activity is steady through the teens, and the spawn season below is gated by temperature (onset around 18 °C, core 20–25 °C), so prespawn effort pays hardest on warming trends toward that band. Keep the species' clock — dusk and night over midday — even in spring.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If prespawn shallows are silent, check the temperature before the bait: below about 7 °C this species' spontaneous activity measurably falls away, and a cold snap puts the shelter-and-wait half of its winter behaviour back in charge until the water recovers.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No spawn-specific bait is measured for this species. Keep the scent-led bottom presentations of the feeding seasons and work them along the nesting banks and the first soft-bottom feeding water off them, where the fish that are feeding actually are.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: This species carries the programme's only directly observed spawn-feeding suppression in a catfish — and it is sex-specific: in Blumer's field work the males, the principal care-givers, did little or no feeding through breeding and care (care runs up to about 20 days after the eggs are laid, at most about 29), while the females increased their feeding over the same period. How much that lowers the population's bite has never been quantified, so the entry carries the dip as real but unmeasured in size: expect an uneven spawn bite, fish the edges and the females' feeding water, and don't read a guarding male's refusal as the whole lake turning off.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the banks are dead, slide off them to the nearest feeding flats rather than working the nests harder — and ignore the popular line that this fish spawns only once the water reaches 80 °F (27 °C): every primary source contradicts it (the Michigan field spawn, the 21.1 °C compilation optimum, a measured European spawning population at 15–21 °C). That figure is a growth value misfiled as a spawn threshold, and the library lists it as do-not-use.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish by smell, theirs: searching behaviour guided by taste alone — over distances of many body lengths, in turbid water and clear — was measured with brown bullhead itself as a subject (Bardach, Todd & Crickmer 1967), and the behaviour was the same in every bullhead tested. No brown-specific taste-bud count exists, and none is claimed here. What is brown's own is the diet: a broad benthic omnivore — insects, crustaceans, molluscs, worms, detritus, fish. Scent-forward bottom offerings sized to that menu are the supported presentation; the literature names no lure for this fish.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Night is not a preference in this species, it is a measured threshold. In the scotokinesis experiments the fish shelter by day and start exploring only when the light drops hard — a relative illuminance drop of 95% or more triggers the response (in as little as 3 seconds), weaker drops get no response at all; at a scotophase illuminance of 1,400 lx locomotor activity fell to near zero, and time-to-feed was fastest at about 100 lx. Daylight fish adopt a sleep posture with slowed heart and breathing and reduced response to sound and touch. So build the summer trip backwards from dark: be set up on the feeding water before the light fails, and treat a bright midday as this fish's off shift, not a bait problem. One caution against over-reading the warm dome: in pairwise feeding trials on chironomids, this species' efficiency was lower at 25 °C than at 18 °C against a competitor — the plateau is a preference-and-growth structure, not a promise that feeding rate peaks at the top of it on every prey.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer fish won't go in daylight, believe the experiments and wait for the drop in light rather than cycling baits — the trigger is the darkness itself. If nights on good water still fail in a heat wave, check where the water sits against the low-30s stress band before changing anything else.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer scent-led bottom menu, smaller and slower as the temperature drops. Cooling shortens this night fish's already-dark feeding day; nothing in the fall evidence supports bigger or faster.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Concentrate everything into dusk and the first dark hours, and give each sheltered spot real time — a cooling brown bullhead near its cover is catchable, but it is not travelling to a bait. As the water crosses below about 7 °C, expect the cold pattern (previous entry) to take over within days.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A fall spot going quiet week over week is usually the temperature story, not an emptied spot — this is a sedentary, home-ranging fish in everything the literature records (no telemetry study exists for any bullhead, so no migration is claimed here). Move toward warmth and shelter before you move lakes.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice presentation is measured for this species. Small, scent-led, still bottom offerings are the open-water evidence carried under the ice as a labelled transfer — nothing stronger can honestly be claimed.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the night shape, knowing exactly where it comes from: in controlled winter trials at 3–4.5 °C this species preyed almost exclusively at night — laboratory fish, not fish under lake ice, and the distinction is kept on purpose. The dormancy physiology fills in the rest of the day: spontaneous activity and willingness to arouse fall as temperature falls, and buried fish respond when disturbed but are not roaming. Slow, close to shelter, after dark is the provisional pattern; bright midday under the ice is its trough.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Treat a silent provisional pattern as an open question, not a failed one — the evidence under this set is sampling and laboratory work, and your lake is allowed to disagree with it. The proven cold-season brown bullhead fishing is the open-water cold entry: low, erratic, and nocturnal, on a fish that never fully stops.

movementSeasons.heading: Eau froide
lines: Cold water splits this fish into two documented halves, and the entry keeps both: spontaneous activity holds relatively constant from 17 °C down to 7 °C and then falls away, with fish burying in mud and dropping into a sleep-like, discontinuous-breathing state — and yet feeding itself does not stop there. Fish the still, soft-bottomed, vegetated water where they shelter, and expect a low, erratic bite, not a shut-down one and not a summer one.

Oxygen is rarely the cold-season address it is for other fish: in the winterkill syntheses, bullheads and fathead minnows are the most tolerant guild in the lake, and chronic-winterkill basins become bullhead-dominated. That tolerance is a survival record, not a feeding measurement — no study measures this species feeding against dissolved oxygen at any concentration — so use it to keep a low-oxygen basin on your list, never as a promise the fish in it are feeding.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: This is among the earliest spring feeders in its community: in the Ontario field work, brown bullhead feeding was already under way at 6.5 °C when the study started, while pumpkinseed and rock bass in the same water waited until 8.5 °C. Fish the warming, still, vegetated shallows and soft-bottom feeding water as soon as the water climbs past the mid-single digits — the spring shallow and inflow concentration the agency material describes (expert consensus, Grade C) fits that measured head start.

In creeks and slow river water, the same rule in miniature: the early feeding the field work recorded was creek fish in slow water. Fish the pools, backwaters and soft edges, not the current — no flow response has ever been measured in this genus, and still water is its documented address.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The best-documented bullhead spawn in the literature: in the four-year Michigan field study, spawning ran late May into early June, with most egg-laying inside a tight 10–15-day window; the compilation's optimum spawning temperature is 21.1 °C, and the model's core band is 20–25 °C, May through July in the north. Nests are saucers excavated in sand, gravel or mud under roots, logs and vegetation. Fish the water around the nesting cover — because of who is and isn't eating there (see How).

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: A warm fish, measured three ways: the compilation's final temperature preferendum is 26.2 °C and its optimum growth temperature 30.0 °C, so the productive plateau runs 26–30 °C — individual preferendum studies spread 23.5–31.0 °C by season and method, which is why this entry fishes a plateau and never quotes one point as 'the' optimum. The controlled bioenergetics work measured consumption and growth across 10–30 °C, the backbone under that dome. Summer addresses are the species' own: still, muddy or silty, vegetated water over soft bottom. Above the plateau the fall is steep — an upper incipient lethal of 33.4 °C and a critical thermal maximum of 37.9 °C bracket the low-to-mid 30s as stress water, not feeding water.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is the long slide between the two measured halves of this fish: spontaneous activity holds from 17 °C down to 7 °C, then the burial and sleep-like behaviour grows as the water falls below it — cold-acclimated fish given a gradient still moved to water above 25 °C within a day, which tells you the preference doesn't change, only the fish's willingness to go and get it. Fish the warmest still, sheltered, soft-bottom water your lake offers, close to cover, and shorten your search radius as it cools.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: PROVISIONAL — and the flag is part of the entry, the way this library carries lower-confidence ice sets. Brown bullhead is the only bullhead with any under-ice evidence at all: fish netted from under the ice at 4 °C in an Ontario lake included individuals with food in their stomachs (feeding described as erratic), and its winterkill record puts it among the last fish alive in a depleting basin. What does not exist is any observation of free fish under a lake's ice — no telemetry, no under-ice diel curve, no snow-or-light response — so this set is built from under-ice sampling, laboratory winter trials and dormancy physiology, and it is flagged provisional wherever it appears. Fish deep, still, soft-bottom water near shelter; oxygen is a weaker location rule here than for any other ice species in this library, on survival evidence only.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 26–30 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 37.9 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note: no study of any design has ever measured a front or a pressure effect in any bullhead — pressure carries zero weight in this fish's rating because it has never been measured, not because it was tested and failed, and the same is true of moonlight (the light experiments worked at 100–1,400 lx; nobody has extrapolated them to moonlight, and this entry won't either). The rating carries no front term for this fish at all — none has ever been measured. Fish the temperature change a front actually delivers; there is no bullhead barometer trick to sell you.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: You're fishing the measured peak of this species' existence: fastest time-to-feed at about 100 lx, predation almost exclusively nocturnal even at 3 °C in the winter trials, and field work in the wild matching the laboratory's night-led pattern. Everything in these entries bends toward this window because everything in the fish does.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The light changes are the trigger, literally: this fish's exploration starts on a drop in illuminance of 95% or more, so the dusk fall-off is the day's starting gun — be fishing before it, not arriving during it. Dawn runs the film backwards (fish returned to shelter within about 75 seconds of full light in the experiments), so weight the evening end of low light well above the morning end.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Bright, calm daylight is this species' documented off shift: shelter-seeking, a sleep posture with slowed rhythms, and locomotor activity driven to near zero at high illuminance. A midday trip is not impossible — the rating's day value is low, not zero — but it is the hardest hours this fish offers, and no presentation change in the literature turns a sheltering fish into a feeding one. Save the effort for the light drop.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Being straight about wind: no study measures a wind effect in any bullhead. The canon claim — wind-blown banks concentrate food and feeding fish — is expert opinion only (Grade C/D), never tested in this genus. Fish a windward shore if your water fits it, but know it is lore, not a finding.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais mesuré pour aucune espèce de bullhead (alimentation, activité, mouvement ou capture). Zéro est une donnée, pas une omission.
Jamais mesuré pour aucune espèce de bullhead. Le travail d'éclairement de Peters (100–1,400 lx) n'est PAS extrapolé au clair de lune.
Aucune étude de télémétrie ou de réponse au débit n'existe pour aucun bullhead; le modèle de lac ne porte aucun terme de débit pour ce genre.
Le régime est une omnivorie benthique large chez les trois espèces; aucune étude d'impulsion ou de fenêtre de proies n'existe à paramétrer.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: This is among the earliest spring feeders in its community: in the Ontario field work, brown bullhead feeding was already under way at 6.5 °C when the study started, while pumpkinseed and rock bass in the same water waited until 8.5 °C. Fish the warming, still, vegetated shallows and soft-bottom feeding water as soon as the water climbs past the mid-single digits — the spring shallow and inflow concentration the agency material describes (expert consensus, Grade C) fits that measured head start.

In creeks and slow river water, the same rule in miniature: the early feeding the field work recorded was creek fish in slow water. Fish the pools, backwaters and soft edges, not the current — no flow response has ever been measured in this genus, and still water is its documented address.

Fish the climb, not the calendar: activity is steady through the teens, and the spawn season below is gated by temperature (onset around 18 °C, core 20–25 °C), so prespawn effort pays hardest on warming trends toward that band. Keep the species' clock — dusk and night over midday — even in spring.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The best-documented bullhead spawn in the literature: in the four-year Michigan field study, spawning ran late May into early June, with most egg-laying inside a tight 10–15-day window; the compilation's optimum spawning temperature is 21.1 °C, and the model's core band is 20–25 °C, May through July in the north. Nests are saucers excavated in sand, gravel or mud under roots, logs and vegetation. Fish the water around the nesting cover — because of who is and isn't eating there (see How).

This species carries the programme's only directly observed spawn-feeding suppression in a catfish — and it is sex-specific: in Blumer's field work the males, the principal care-givers, did little or no feeding through breeding and care (care runs up to about 20 days after the eggs are laid, at most about 29), while the females increased their feeding over the same period. How much that lowers the population's bite has never been quantified, so the entry carries the dip as real but unmeasured in size: expect an uneven spawn bite, fish the edges and the females' feeding water, and don't read a guarding male's refusal as the whole lake turning off.

spawningSources.citation: Blumer 1985 (lac Munro : frai fin mai–début juin, fenêtre d'oviposition de 10–15 jours); Blumer 1986a/b (les mâles qui gardent s'alimentaient peu ou pas — observé, AUCUN coefficient de population n'existe; le creux de frai est étiqueté non mesuré en taille); Hasnain OS 21.1 °C.

about: The brown trout is Europe's gift to the world's trout water — wary, golden, red-spotted, and the longest-lived challenge in many a river. It is a cool-water fish with no single neat optimum: the research puts its growth plateau around 13–18 °C, its feeding peaks in spring and fall, and its avoidance line near 19 °C, above which browns relocate rather than feed.

Browns spawn in autumn, cutting redds in gravel runs, and the biggest fish turn nocturnal and piscivorous — eating mice, sculpins and their own kind — while younger fish feed on the insect drifts all day. Stream browns hold lies with a banker's precision and inspect flies like auditors. Anglers target them precisely for that difficulty: a big wild brown, taken on a fly at dusk, is trout fishing's graduate degree.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the measured diet: drift invertebrates are the staple of the stream work, and the growth experiments themselves ran on invertebrate prey (Gammarus) — small, natural invertebrate presentations are the supported menu. No lure, fly pattern or size is named for this species in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here; the one presentation fact that is measured is about profile, not pattern — previously-fished browns were more easily scared and required smaller, low-profile flies (Young & Hayes 2004).

Large fish are facultative piscivores — the second growth experiment ran entirely on fish prey, and evacuation in big piscivorous browns was measured on fingerling fish prey (He & Wurtsbaugh 1993) — so a fish-profile presentation for the largest browns is diet-supported in a way it is not for the other trouts. Treat it as the big-fish option, not the default.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Time the day by this species' own clock, because it is the night fish of the trouts: activity peaks at dusk, stays high overnight and is lowest by day across telemetry in Belgium, Michigan, Idaho and Norway, and its dark-adapted visual threshold — about 0.005 lux, half the rainbow's — lets it forage through all twilight and under average night light (Rader et al. 2007). In cold spring water the day compresses further: at mean temperatures of 4.7 and 7.3 °C the early hours of night were the ONLY feeding period measured; a second, daytime period only appeared at 10.8 °C (Elliott 1973). Put your best spring hour at dusk and into the first hours of dark.

Fish an educated water like it remembers you, because it does — that part is measured, not folklore: two anglers caught 11–23% of the population of a heavily fished river against up to 47% of a naïve one at comparable density, disturbed fish hid and were rarely seen for days, and fished-for fish needed smaller, low-profile presentations (Young & Hayes 2004). On pressured spring water, rest a lie you have disturbed and come back to it another evening.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a spring lie is dead by day, that is the species working as measured — near-zero daytime activity was the large-fish telemetry pattern (resting at home sites by day, moving at night, back by morning). Do not change baits at noon; change hours. The same lie at dusk is a different fishery.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Match the season's own rotation: in the one long lake record (Lake Sorell, Tasmania), the summer and autumn diet specialised on Daphnia while winter and spring ran to fish prey (Stuart-Smith et al. 2004), and in the Norwegian lake the large browns' summer food was surface insects and large insect larvae, with fish-eating rare (Amundsen & Knudsen 2009). Summer is the invertebrate season for this fish at every size — small, natural, invertebrate presentations lead, and the fish-profile option belongs to the cold seasons. Still no lure is named in the literature; the menu above is the whole supported tackle story.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Dusk is the peak and night is nearly its equal — the proposed clock for this species, built from its own telemetry and nothing else's, runs dusk 1.0, night 0.95, dawn 0.85, day 0.55. Social rank sharpens it: dominant fish fed mainly at dusk and early night, the most beneficial times, while subordinates were displaced to other hours (Alanärä, Burns & Metcalfe 2001) — so the biggest fish in a lie are the most dusk-bound of all, and a subordinate feeding at an odd hour is not evidence the clock is wrong.

Keep the retrieve honest about digestion: gastric evacuation sets how often this fish can feed — measured at roughly 7%/h at 4.5 °C rising to roughly 29%/h at 22.5 °C in piscivorous fish (He & Wurtsbaugh 1993) — and drift availability, not appetite, sets when it feeds (Elliott 1973). In warm plateau water the meals turn over fast; a lie that refused at dusk can genuinely be feeding again later the same night.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the plateau water is quiet, check the clarity before the presentation: this is the one trout with a measured turbidity cost — as Lake Sorell's turbidity climbed from 26 to 141 NTU, mean stomach-content volume fell to one sixth and prey diversity fell from over six species per stomach to one (Stuart-Smith et al. 2004), with reduced feeding observed as low as 7.5 NTU in the older stream work. Dirty water is a measured brown-trout problem; the clearest inflow or the clearest margin is the fix, not a bigger offering.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: In avoidance-band water the presentation question is secondary and this entry will not pretend otherwise: the diet menu is unchanged (invertebrates for most fish, fish prey for the largest), fished only in the cold refuges above. Warm water also punishes the catch itself — catch-and-release mortality rises at 23 °C and above in the carried evidence — so the supported warm-water tackle decision is the short one: fish the cold water, handle anything caught there fast, or leave this species alone today.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Compress everything into the dark: the night-heavy clock (dusk peak, night 0.95) is the warm season's whole tactic, and at raised temperatures the dominant fish stayed nocturnal in the rank experiments even as lower-ranked fish shifted into the day (Alanärä, Burns & Metcalfe 2001). The fish worth catching in warm weather are the ones that will not move until dark — be on the cold refuge at dusk, not on the warm flat at noon.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the whole system is at or past 19–20 °C with no cold refuge reachable, the study's answer is the brook trout answer in this species' own numbers: there is no presentation that fixes avoidance-band water for a brown trout. Travel to the cold, or wait for the cooling — the fall entry below is this fish's other great season, and it is coming.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The fall tackle story has two honestly different tiers. The diet tier: large browns are facultative piscivores and the fish-prey option is diet-supported (Elliott & Hurley 2000). The canon tier, labelled as canon and nothing more: guide and angling literature holds that pre-spawn browns turn territorial and strike large streamers aggressively in the weeks before spawning — widely repeated, Grade C, and with no measured feeding or aggression coefficient anywhere behind it. Aggression at an intruder is not feeding; fish the streamer if you fish it as a provocation at a territorial fish, not as a meal it wants.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the change, not the level: the migration evidence says day-to-day VARIATION in temperature and water level together move these fish — and the controlled test tempers any simple rule, because across eleven experimental freshet releases, freshets did NOT stimulate or facilitate spawning migration, and one headwater study found no flow effect at all (Baker et al. 2020; Slavík et al. 2012). So rising water alone is not a brown-trout trigger anyone has measured; a swinging temperature-and-level week inside 10–12 °C is the supported staging signal, and it is a stream result — nothing in this paragraph is a lake feeding rule, because no flow study in this species measures lake feeding.

Moonlight belongs in this entry only to be put in its place: two solid studies show the moon timing brown trout MOVEMENT — spawning-migration distance was highest at new moon and lowest at full moon (Slavík et al. 2012), and lake fish moved more as the moon waned (Finlay et al. 2020) — while the only feeding test of moon phase is a null. Dark nights may time the run; no study says they time the bite, and this entry does not claim they do.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If staging fish ignore everything in daylight, you are fighting the clock, not the menu: fall telemetry made these fish more crepuscular, not less — autumn and winter activity concentrated at the day's edges with dusk predominant (Ovidio et al. 2002). Fish the last hour into dark on the staging water and let the midday hours go.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Nothing spawn-specific is measured for this fish — no redd presentation, no egg pattern, no lure is named in the spawning literature behind this entry, and none is invented here. The supported offering on the staging edges is the ordinary fall one: the diet menu (invertebrates, fish prey for the largest fish), with the streamer remaining what the entry above labelled it — Grade C canon about territorial aggression, not a measured spawn tactic.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the movement's timing, which IS measured: the spawning movements are overwhelmingly nocturnal and timed to darkness — migration distance peaked at new moon and bottomed at full moon, and detection odds rose as the moon waned and the water rose and clouded (Slavík et al. 2012; Finlay et al. 2020), consistent with a fish that can see at about 0.005 lux moving when it is hardest to see. Dusk into dark, on the approaches to the gravel, is the spawn season's supported hour; males arrive first, so the earliest movement fish are males, with the females following.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A reach full of visible fish that will not eat is the spawn working as described, not a puzzle to solve with a new fly: spawning fish are not on a feeding pattern anyone has measured, and pestering redds is not a tactic this library teaches. Drop to the next staging pool or margin down — the feeders are the fish between the redds and the deep water, before their turn and after it.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Winter stream food is the drift the fish shelter beside — the invertebrate menu at its smallest and slowest. The lake winter diet is covered in the ice entry; in open winter water, no winter-specific lure or bait is named in the research, and the supported statement is the diet itself.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: One window, all winter: the dark. At cold temperatures the night feeding period was the only one measured even in the open-water experiments (Elliott 1973), and the winter stream telemetry is a full dark-to-dawn activity pattern. A winter brown fished for at midday is being fished at its measured zero; the same lie an hour after dark is the season's real fishery.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the winter lie is dead after dark as well, accept the arithmetic rather than inventing a fix: a fish feeding at a tenth to a sixth of its summer rate, losing condition as it goes, gives an angler a small number of honest chances per night. Shorten the session to the first hours of dark, fish one lie perfectly, and save the long efforts for the spring climb toward the plateau.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The under-ice diet inverted for big fish, and it is the ice season's one firm tackle fact: small browns under 20 cm ate insect larvae, while large browns over 20 cm were predominantly PISCIVOROUS on Arctic charr in winter — fish-eating that was rare for those same fish in summer (Amundsen & Knudsen 2009). Small, insect-larva presentations for ordinary fish; a fish-profile presentation for the largest browns is the diet-supported winter choice, the reverse of the summer rule. No ice lure, jig or bait is named in the study, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: They feed all winter, slowly: consumption ran at roughly a tenth to a sixth of the summer peak, continuously, with no growth and declining condition — so fish patiently and expect the take to be a maintenance decision, not a feeding frenzy. The diel shape under ice is NOT measured in a lake, and this entry says so rather than borrowing one silently: the nearest evidence is the winter-stream pattern (fully nocturnal, dark to dawn — Heggenes et al. 1993), transferred here as a flagged inference and tempered by a juvenile flume result in which young browns actually took MORE drifting prey by day when surface ice was present (Watz et al. 2023). Night-leaning is the honest lean, held loosely — the first hours of dark are the best-supported single window, not a proven curve.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the littoral is silent, the supported move is along it, not off it: winter movement in this species was minimal except during high discharge or ice break-up — the species-measured basis for checking inflow and current edges late in the ice season, when meltwater starts to move, before anywhere else. And if the whole lake is quiet, the winter arithmetic from the open-water entry applies under ice too: a fish at a sixth of its summer ration is a few-chances fishery on its best night.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: Spring is one of this fish's two measured feeding peaks — feeding rates were highest in spring and fall in the classic drift-feeding study (Bachman 1984) — and the water is climbing toward the growth plateau from below. Fish the feeding water the temperature is improving into, not the coldest water in the system: browns position where the temperature, oxygen and prey trade is best, and that trade improves steadily through spring.

In streams the address is the drift line at a home site: wild adults were sit-and-wait foragers 86% of foraging time, feeding mainly on drift from a held lie (Bachman 1984), and telemetry fish held small, confined home ranges — a median of 131 m against a rainbow's 606 m in the same Idaho water (Young et al. 1997). Work one good lie thoroughly instead of covering water; this fish does not roam to find you.

In lakes, fish the littoral margins: radio-tracked browns in New Zealand's Lake Otamangakau used the weedy littoral margins, held confined home ranges and were less mobile than the rainbows in the same lake — and the famous day-to-shallow, night-to-margin commute in that study belonged to the rainbows, not the browns (Dedual et al. 2000). A brown's spring lake address is a margin it lives on, not a route it travels.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer water inside the plateau is this fish's prime season, and the plateau has to be stated honestly because there is no single optimum temperature for a brown trout: growth peaked at 13.9 °C on an invertebrate diet and at 17.0 °C on a fish diet in the same laboratory programme (Elliott & Hurley 2000, 2001), so the supported prime band is the whole 14–18 °C span between those two measured optima. Fish the water in that band first — this is also the warm-tolerant trout of the set: in Jocassee Reservoir, browns selected 7.5–21.9 °C where the rainbows beside them stayed at 8.3–13.4 °C.

Lake browns stay a littoral fish even in summer — in the subarctic Norwegian lake study they were almost exclusively littoral in the open-water season as well as 100% littoral in winter (Amundsen & Knudsen 2009), and the New Zealand telemetry put them on weedy littoral margins year-round (Dedual et al. 2000). Work the margins and the first water off them before you probe the deep basin.

Summer stream range expands measurably: the summer daily home range was 3.2 times the winter range and was exploited 2.5 times more intensively, with activity scaling with temperature and day length (Ovidio et al. 2002). Summer stream fish are findable across more of the reach than at any other season — but they are still home-site fish by day, so the expansion is in how much water a dusk pass can cover, not in midday roaming.

movementSeasons.heading: Eau chaude
lines: Above the plateau this becomes a relocation problem, stated with the study's own numbers: browns avoided water over 19 °C in the New Zealand telemetry (Dedual et al. 2000), growth stays positive only to 24.74 °C, and the experimentally measured incipient lethal temperature is 24.7 °C (Elliott 1981) — note the honest discrepancy the research prints rather than blends: a habitat-suitability synthesis carries about 27 °C, in the ultimate-lethal family, and it is not the conservative number this entry fishes by. Find water back inside 14–18 °C: the coldest inflows, the deepest littoral the lake offers, the layer where the temperature–oxygen trade still works — free-swimming browns tolerated dissolved oxygen of 5.0–5.5 mg/L, and selected water generally at or above 5.0 mg/L, which is why the cold layer remains fishable for them longer than a threshold rule would suggest.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is the second measured feeding peak (Bachman 1984: feeding rates highest in spring and fall) running into the spawning movement, and the movement has a compound trigger worth fishing by: in the Belgian telemetry, seven of nine fish migrated 5.6–22.95 km upstream between 7 October and 15 November, set off by the COMBINATION of high day-to-day variation in water temperature AND water level, inside a thermal window of 10–12 °C (Ovidio et al. 1998). Before that window, pre-October movements were 300 m a day or less. Fish the staging water below the spawning reaches while the fish are still feeding, and expect the addresses to change suddenly once temperature and level start swinging together.

Lake fish run later than stream fish: the Irish lake-to-stream study found peak movement near the winter solstice, males arriving before females, and the movements overwhelmingly nocturnal (Finlay et al. 2020). On lake water, the fall pattern is a long staging season on the littoral margins the fish already live on — do not abandon the margins for the tributary mouths until the water is properly cold.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: This is the spawn itself: northern-hemisphere spawning runs September to December, peaking October–November, on shallow gravel — on Minnesota's Straight River it began at 5.68–6.36 °C, every redd was on gravel and 78% were associated with cover, with a trigger range of 6–12.8 °C carried by the habitat synthesis. The honest framing comes first: no measured feeding-suppression coefficient exists for this species in any system, so what follows is an availability entry, not a feeding entry — fish in the act of spawning are on the redds and on the spawn's business, and the feeders are the fish not yet on, or already off, the gravel at the edges of the spawning reaches.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter is this fish's measured floor, and the number is stark: under-ice consumption ran at 0.3–0.5 against a summer peak of 2.8–3.4 in the same lake — roughly a tenth to a sixth of peak — the season value sits near 0.3, the fish grew not at all, and condition declined across the winter (Amundsen & Knudsen 2009). In open winter water that means the coldest-season browns are persisting at or below maintenance, not feeding up: fish the lies they already hold, at the hours below, and expect few chances rather than none.

Winter stream fish hold the cost-minimising pattern: passive shelter in substrate and vegetation by day — fish under 25 cm were almost never active in daylight — and activity on and above the substrate throughout the night, dark to dawn, all winter, with night feeding continuing (Heggenes et al. 1993). The winter stream address is a sheltering lie with a night feeding lane beside it, and movement stays minimal except during high discharge or ice break-up (Brown et al. 2001, Grand River, Ontario).

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: PROVISIONAL — stated up front, in the study's own terms: this species has exactly one direct lake under-ice study, and it is a good one (a subarctic Norwegian lake, a full winter, monthly sampling plus December, March and May under-ice work), but there is no under-ice telemetry, diel or catch-rate study, so this whole ice entry is provisional in a way the open-water entries are not. What the study does measure is unusually clear: browns were 100% littoral under ice — and almost exclusively littoral in summer too — in littoral water at 0.6–0.7 °C. Fish the littoral, all winter; the basin is not this fish's winter address on its only evidence. Manitoba anglers do take stocked browns through the ice, so the fishery is real even where the science is thin.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 13–18 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 24.7 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: After dark is this species' home water, on its own measurements: a dark-adapted threshold of about 0.005 lux — half the rainbow's and cutthroat's — is sufficient for foraging through all twilight and under average night light (Rader et al. 2007), large telemetry fish moved at night and were back at their home sites by morning, and the early hours of night were a major feeding period in the experiments, the ONLY one in cold water. Fish the night session as the main session: arrive for the dusk peak, stay through the first hours of dark, and work the home-site lies the fish left at sunset — they feed a short move from where they rested all day.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Dusk is the single peak of this fish's day in every telemetry programme that watched around the clock — most active at dusk in all seasons in the Belgian work, activity rising dramatically at dusk in the Michigan work, dominant fish feeding mainly at dusk and early night in the rank experiments — with dawn a real but second peak (0.85 against dusk's 1.0 and night's 0.95 on the study's own clock). If you fish one low-light window, fish the evening one; the dawn window is the subordinate shift, and it fishes like it.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Bright, calm midday is this fish's measured minimum — day scores 0.55, the lowest quarter of its clock, with large fish resting at home sites and activity near zero — and brightness compounds the wariness that is measured in this species itself: fished-for browns hid for days after disturbance and demanded smaller, low-profile presentations (Young & Hayes 2004). Fish bright midday only if you fish it like a stalking exercise — low profile, small offering, first cast counts — or bank the hours and spend them at dusk, when the same fish become the most catchable trout in this library.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: This is the spawn itself: northern-hemisphere spawning runs September to December, peaking October–November, on shallow gravel — on Minnesota's Straight River it began at 5.68–6.36 °C, every redd was on gravel and 78% were associated with cover, with a trigger range of 6–12.8 °C carried by the habitat synthesis. The honest framing comes first: no measured feeding-suppression coefficient exists for this species in any system, so what follows is an availability entry, not a feeding entry — fish in the act of spawning are on the redds and on the spawn's business, and the feeders are the fish not yet on, or already off, the gravel at the edges of the spawning reaches.

Fish the movement's timing, which IS measured: the spawning movements are overwhelmingly nocturnal and timed to darkness — migration distance peaked at new moon and bottomed at full moon, and detection odds rose as the moon waned and the water rose and clouded (Slavík et al. 2012; Finlay et al. 2020), consistent with a fish that can see at about 0.005 lux moving when it is hardest to see. Dusk into dark, on the approaches to the gravel, is the spawn season's supported hour; males arrive first, so the earliest movement fish are males, with the females following.

about: The burbot is the odd one out: a freshwater cod, complete with a single chin barbel, mottled eel-like body and a taste for the coldest, darkest water in the lake. It does its living upside-down compared to everything else — feeding and spawning in the dead of winter, then retreating to deep, cold holes for the summer, where it keeps company with lake trout and whitefish.

Burbot spawn under the ice in mid-winter, balling up over sand and gravel in the shallows, and feed hardest after dark on fish, crayfish and whatever the bottom offers. Most are caught by ice anglers fishing set lines at night, surprised by the pull. Those who know, target them on purpose: the flesh is firm, white and sweet — poor man's lobster — and a big winter burbot is a genuine trophy of the dark months.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The open-water standard from the agency guidance: a glow jig or spoon sweetened with cut bait, fished on bottom at night — glow, noise and scent are the whole attraction package for a fish that hunts by smell and feel as much as sight.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish it after dark, on bottom, near rocky shore structure. Let scent do the work — burbot follow their noses to a still bait.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: As the water warms, go deeper or wait for fall — a summer burbot is a deep, cold, night fish, and spring's shallow window closes fast.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Glow jig or spoon with cut bait on the bottom. Freshness is the rule from the agency guidance: fresh bait, never spoiled — burbot will not feed on rotten food.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Anchor over the rocky depth, fish after dark, and give a spot time — scent trails build. Trolling or bottom-bouncing near deep structure works but is the less common route; still bait at night is the standard for a reason.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer burbot are the goal and the deep night bite won't go, the honest advice is seasonal: this fish is made for the cold months. The fall shore pattern and the ice season are burbot season; summer is the off-season you fish through, not the one you plan around.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Glow jigs and jigging spoons, 1/4–1/2 oz on 2/0–4/0 hooks, tipped with a small skin-on strip of sucker or chub meat — plenty of scent without swamping the jig. Charge the glow hard with a UV light; bites often come right after a fresh charge.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Spread lines across a rocky point from about 10 ft out to 50 ft first, find the depth band that produces, then consolidate into it. Fish the dusk rise — that's when they come up onto the shelves.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: After you catch one, get back down fast — burbot travel in small schools and the second fish is usually right there. Give a dead spot about 15 minutes, then move the line.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Big, heavy, noisy, glowing — that's the system. Jig the same lures you'd use for walleye, doubled or tripled in size: a 3/4-oz flasher jig, up to a 1½-oz jigging spoon for burbot where the walleye versions are 1/4–1/2 oz. Colour: 'glow in any shade is king,' hot fluorescents — pink, orange, chartreuse — second.

The bait is steaked ciscoe belly — 'burbot candy': steak the belly into roughly seven 1/4-in pieces and hook each through the tendon at the bottom of the U; it moves, flashes and gives off scent. Anything meaty works — beef heart, salted shiners, scented plastics — but fresh beats everything; burbot refuse rotten bait.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Pounding bottom is the signature: rip the lure as high as you can reach, let it crash to the bottom — a thud on soft bottom, a whack on rock — then bottom-dance it, then pause it about 2 ft up and watch the sonar. The noise is the point: spawning burbot drum their swim bladders to communicate, anglers traditionally mimicked it by banging the rocky bottom, and the modern version is this jig. When a fish moves in, dance it gently on bottom or creep it up a couple of feet to seal the deal.

Tackle for the heavy work: pike/walleye-class gear — a 32-in medium-heavy rod in the shack, a 42-in heavy rod for running and gunning; 20-lb braid, a 4-ft leader of 17–20 lb fluorocarbon, and a barrel swivel between them. The swivel is also a landing tool: burbot roll and often won't come through the hole straight, so grab the swivel and hold the fish until it relaxes and slides up.
Fish it at twilight and after dark. Drill your holes in the afternoon — auger noise after dark costs fish — and be set up and quiet before dark.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Searching is a tip-up job: string them from the shallow shoal, down the drop-off, onto the basin flat — plain 3/8-oz 'do-nothing' jigs dropped to bottom with chunked ciscoe (hook exposed) or a jumbo salted shiner cut in three and skewered. When you check a line, hand-jig it a few times: burbot can swallow a bait without ever tripping the flag.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The same oversized glow system: 3/4-oz flasher jig or 1½-oz spoon, steaked ciscoe belly. On the spoon side, the In-Fisherman pick is a heavy 3/4-oz rattling spoon with shiners gobbed on the hook — crash it into bottom to stir mud; the noise calls them. A 3/4- to 1-oz jig or spoon, glow-painted, tipped with a minnow or a strip of cut fish, is the standard.

Chumming, where legal: the ciscoe parts left over from the steaks, cut finger-length, or cut ciscoe, sardines or shiners. Chum a spot before you head home and a burbot 'stuffed with chum' may be waiting in the morning; multi-day chumming slowly pulls numbers into an area. A powerful scent gel on the bait is the no-chum shortcut — garlic-crawfish is the reported producer.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Pound, dance, pause 2 ft up — the full sequence, eyes on sonar the whole time. Once a fish comes in to play, dance gingerly or creep the bait up. Stay mobile with the electronics until you find biters, then work the spot hard.

Darkness discipline is a real tactic here: drill before dark, stay quiet after it, and recharge the glow every time you check a line — a glow lure dims in 15–20 minutes, and bites commonly come right after a fresh charge.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Run the two-phase system: one rod pounds and rattles to attract; the second is a motionless scented presentation — dead minnow or cut bait on a plain hook lying on bottom, or a tip-up with bait just off bottom. They follow the vibration in, then commit to the still bait. Some nights they hit only right after a re-glow; some nights only the deadstick wins. Keep both within inches of bottom.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The heavy glow system, unchanged — but the fish are shallow now, so the drops are shorter. Steaked ciscoe belly on the 3/4-oz flasher jig is still the call. Note: chumming stops working at last ice — fish on the shoal to spawn don't respond to it, so spend the effort on position instead.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The exception to every burbot rule: on the spawning shoals, a genuine daytime bite develops and lasts the rest of the ice season — fish in a dark tent over the shoal and you can watch them maul baits. Individual fish make several spawning forays and feed heavily between runs, and after the peak the groups hold 'sentry duty' on the shoals against ciscoes, perch and shiners — which is why the daytime bite persists.
Heavy pounded jigs are also the tool for making daytime action happen away from the shoals.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shoal edge is quiet, the fish are between forays, not gone — they make several runs. Stay on the travel lane, keep a line soaking, and fish the dark hours for the spawning movement itself.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: In spring, burbot move into shallow water along the shore — then, as the water warms, they retreat to the deep holes and cold water and largely stay there until autumn. Spring shore water at night is the last of the shallow season.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer burbot live deep and cold, in the same water as lake trout and whitefish — cold, well-oxygenated depths (their comfort tops out in the low-to-mid teens Celsius; about 74 °F is their upper limit). They're a night fish on top of a deep fish: the standard open-water pattern is bottom fishing at night over 20–50 ft near rocky bottom, with fish moving shallower after dark to feed.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall brings burbot shallow along the shore again, and toward the spawning season: the agency-taught prespawn pattern (from Wyoming's Flaming Gorge water, mid-October into November) is rocky points and benches — burbot rise out of deep water at dusk to forage on the rocky shelves where the slope eases, not in the deep water in front of sheer cliffs.

Fall brings burbot shallow along the shore again, and toward the spawning season: the agency-taught prespawn pattern (from Wyoming's Flaming Gorge water, mid-October into November) is river arms, rocky points and benches — burbot rise out of deep water at dusk to forage on the rocky shelves where the slope eases, not in the deep water in front of sheer cliffs.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace précoce
lines: First ice is tied to the fall cisco spawn: burbot feed on the spawning and spent ciscoes, their eggs, and everything sharing that bounty. Best water: deep, rocky main-lake points and the first major drop-offs near current areas — carefully, current ice is thin ice early. The best bite comes out of the deepest holes, the same holes holding first-ice walleye, and burbot usually start biting after the walleye quit for the night. Tip-ups set just past the deepest holes even produce daytime burbot now.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace de mi-hiver
lines: Mid-winter, burbot scatter through the whole basin and get hard to pattern. Two patterns hold: deep rock structure and current areas. Fish them early, late and at night, learn the travel routes and the spot-on-the-spot features, and GPS-mark them — they produce year after year. Pre-spawn is the hardest period of the season to pattern them, and it's when chumming (where it's legal) helps most.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace tardive
lines: Late ice is the spawn, and it's the season's best fishing. After the first windy thaw in February the fish set up for the rest of the season on shallow main-lake flats and bars of rock, gravel and coarse sand near deep water. On the chart, look for the biggest main-lake feeding flats jutting into the deepest part of the lake, and camp on the edge where the shallows fall away steep — the daily travel lane, where the groups concentrate and the biggest fish can be intercepted. The spawn can run February through April; spawning itself happens at night over shoals 3–15 ft deep on sand, gravel and small stone, males first, about a week of it.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 10–14 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

about: The channel catfish is the sport fish of the big warm rivers — fork-tailed, smooth-skinned and armed with whisker-like barbels that taste the bottom for food. It is a heat-lover: the rating model peaks its feeding at about 27 °C, among the warmest plateaus in this library, and channel cats stay active through the hottest weeks of summer when other fishing slows.

Channels live in river holes, snags and current seams by day and prowl the shallows to feed at night, spawning in cavities — undercut banks, hollow logs, rock crevices — guarded by the male. They eat anything from cut bait to live minnows, and Manitoba's Red River grows them to famous sizes. Anglers target them for heavyweight fights on summer nights and for some of the most reliable big-fish action in the country.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Scent is this fish's long-range sense — taste works as a distance sense in this genus, and bile-salt (carrion) chemistry is its most sensitive channel of all. A still, scented bait soaking in the hole is the cold-water presentation the physiology supports.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Feeding is greatly reduced at and below about 10 °C, and cold taxes the signature sense itself — the measured palatability response to food flavours disappears in cool water. Slow right down, fish one good hole thoroughly, and expect a small number of real chances.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: They are not dormant — winter feeding is documented, and the flathead's 'shuts down completely' line belongs to a different species and was rejected for this one. Stay on the wintering holes and let scent build; moving often is the cold-water mistake.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish are feeding consistently again once the water is past the low teens and heading for 21 °C — this is a feeding window, not just a migration. Scent-forward baits match how this fish finds food at any temperature.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Cover the routes slowly and fish the staging water near where they'll nest. The Manitoba telemetry behind this entry — 161 fish in the Lake Winnipeg basin — shows fish using the whole river network seasonally, so think connected water, not single spots.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the routes are quiet, the run hasn't reached your water yet — drop back toward the wintering holes and fish the deep water on the way. The move is temperature-timed; cold snaps stall it.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No spawn-specific bait is measured for this species. Keep to the scent-led presentations that work on feeding fish and work them along the nesting banks and the first deeper water off them.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Expect the spawn window to fish unevenly: the fish on nests are guarding, not feeding, and the catchable fish are the ones between nests and along the edges. That is the honest pattern the monograph supports.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the banks are dead, slide deeper and slower — post-spawn and non-nesting fish hold off the banks, and canon describes a compensatory feed after the male's fast (expert opinion, not a measured schedule).

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish by smell, theirs: this genus locates food by taste at a distance, so baits that put scent into the water are fishing the measured sense. Vision is a real secondary channel, not absent — they are not blind in clear water, and muddy water does not switch them off either.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the deep holes and structure through the day and the shallows after dark. On oxygen: appetite holds until the daily minimum dissolved oxygen falls toward roughly 2.5–3 mg/L; in the 1.5 mg/L band, measured consumption dropped by a fifth to nearly half — on a still, hot, low-oxygen night, expect the bite to sag with the oxygen.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer fish won't go, check the hour before you change the bait — the dusk move into the shallows is the day's most reliable window, and a bait soaking on the shallow edge at dark fishes it exactly.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The same scent-led baits, fished slower as the water drops. Canon adds one useful trigger (expert opinion): several days of warm, stable fall weather can reactivate fish in the wintering holes.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Follow them down, don't wait for them to come back up. Fish the deep holes on the route and the wintering water itself, thoroughly and slowly.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a fall spot dies, it has probably emptied rather than turned off — relocation is the season's story. Move toward the deep wintering water before you change anything else.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice presentation is study-backed for channel catfish. The open-water evidence supports only the general shape: deep wintering water, scent-led bait, slow.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: If you fish them through the ice, you're fishing the winter-aggregation fact — deep holes, patience — as an experiment, and the library says so plainly rather than dressing it as a pattern.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: The proven cold-season channel catfish fishing is the open water of late fall and early spring, on the wintering holes. Save the ice effort for the species the ice studies actually cover.

movementSeasons.heading: Eau froide
lines: Cold water gathers channel catfish rather than scattering them: telemetry shows a fall downstream shift into deep wintering holes, and winter fish aggregated in the deep water. Fish the deepest holes you know, not the summer shallows.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: The best-documented seasonal behaviour in this species is the spring move: pre-spawn movement rises as the water climbs through the teens toward 21 °C, with fish pushing up toward tributaries and spawning water. Fish the travel routes and the water below the spawning banks.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs from about 21 °C through 29 °C, in cavities: undercut banks, hollow logs, rock crevices, muskrat burrows, riprap voids. The male selects and cleans the nest and guards it — and guarding males are off feed. How much that suppresses the bite has never been measured, so fish the water around the nesting banks, where the feeding fish are, rather than expecting nest fish to eat.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: This is a warm-water fish at its best: feeding and growth peak around 27 °C. The agency pattern is deep holes by day, with movement and feeding around sunrise and sunset and into the shallows at night — but don't over-read the night story: daytime gut fullness equals nighttime in the diet check, and this species feeds by day more than the other catfish do.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall relocation comes at about 15.5 °C: fish shift downstream toward the wintering water — in the Platte telemetry, two-thirds of fall movements ran downstream and every winter movement did. Feeding continues while the temperature holds, and late-fall fish stay catchable in the wintering holes.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: We have to be honest here: no under-ice study of channel catfish exists. Agency ice guidance and winter sampling show the fish present, aggregated in deep water and still feeding in winter — but there is no measured ice pattern for this species to pass on, and the app won't borrow one from another fish.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water about 27 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 38.6 °C, from the species' research file.
Wind: this species' feeding holds up best with wind 15–30 km/h — its own measured wind curve, not a generic one.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: One honest note, in the perch style: no study of any design has ever measured a front or pressure effect in channel catfish — the weather canon for this species is entirely unmeasured, and there is no barometric trick to sell you. What is measured is temperature, oxygen and season; fish those, and treat a front only as the temperature change it actually brings.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: After dark is a measured part of this fish's day — displacement was greatest at night in every season in the river telemetry, and the shallows the fish leave by day are feeding water at night. Fish shallow after dark with confidence, but keep a day spot honest too: this species feeds by day more than its reputation says.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Being straight about wind: no study measures a wind effect in channel catfish. The canon claim — wind-blown shores and current concentrate the fish — is expert opinion only (Grade C), never tested. Fish it if your water fits it, but know it's lore, not a finding.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: The best-documented seasonal behaviour in this species is the spring move: pre-spawn movement rises as the water climbs through the teens toward 21 °C, with fish pushing up toward tributaries and spawning water. Fish the travel routes and the water below the spawning banks.

Cover the routes slowly and fish the staging water near where they'll nest. The Manitoba telemetry behind this entry — 161 fish in the Lake Winnipeg basin — shows fish using the whole river network seasonally, so think connected water, not single spots.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs from about 21 °C through 29 °C, in cavities: undercut banks, hollow logs, rock crevices, muskrat burrows, riprap voids. The male selects and cleans the nest and guards it — and guarding males are off feed. How much that suppresses the bite has never been measured, so fish the water around the nesting banks, where the feeding fish are, rather than expecting nest fish to eat.

Expect the spawn window to fish unevenly: the fish on nests are guarding, not feeding, and the catchable fish are the ones between nests and along the edges. That is the honest pattern the monograph supports.
