about: The cisco — tullibee across the prairies — is a small, silvery member of the whitefish branch of the salmon family, and one of the most important forage fish in northern lakes: whole food webs of lake trout, pike and walleye run on cisco. It is a narrow cold-water specialist, holding a tight band in stratified lakes — night tracking in the research found them schooled at 10.8–13 °C — and squeezed hard when warm summers shrink that layer.

Cisco feed on zooplankton and insect larvae in open water, school deep by day, and gather in fall to spawn over the shoals as the water cools. Few anglers target them directly, though they take small presentations in cold water and are prized smoked; their real angling importance is as the baitfish behind the big predators — find the cisco schools and you've found the lake.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the visual planktivore's menu: cisco feed by sight on zooplankton in open water, with large eyes built for picking individual prey — small presentations sized to large zooplankton are the diet-supported shape. No lure, size or presentation is named in any controlled cisco study, and the well-known controlled feeding-versus-light experiment in this corner of the library belongs to kokanee, a different genus; it is not borrowed here, and no cisco tackle claim is built on it.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish position over timing, because the daily movement pattern is a lake-level outcome for this species: across the tracking programmes, normal vertical migration, no migration, and reverse migration are all documented, sorted by temperature, oxygen, prey and predation risk in each system. Spring migrations in the Lake Superior work were less extensive than summer and fall ones. Locate the school on the day, in the water the temperature and oxygen sections describe, and let its depth — not a clock rule — set your presentation depth.

Work the climb into the adult plateau: the occupied band centres on 8–13 °C, built on the adult final preferendum of 10 °C and two modern field programmes, so warming spring water is at its best for this fish while it still holds in the low teens. The laboratory numbers that look better — a juvenile preferendum of 16.5 °C and a juvenile growth optimum near 14.5 °C — are age-0 fish, sit roughly 5 °C warmer than where adults actually live, and are quarantined in the study as do-not-use for adult fishing.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the spring shallows are empty, the school has likely already taken its deep address — a pelagic, schooling fish is found by searching open water over depth, not by refining a shallow presentation. Drop to the cold band below the shallows and search for the school itself before changing a single bait.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small zooplankton-sized presentations, fished at the school's exact depth in the cold band: a visual planktivore feeding on copepods and large cladocerans is a depth-and-size pattern, and a presentation running above or below the tracked band is not fishing the school no matter how well it matches the menu. No summer lure is named in the cisco research, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Carry the lethal boundary as the pair it actually is, never as a single temperature: field kills fitted a boundary running from 23.8 °C at 8 mg/L of dissolved oxygen down through 22.9 °C at 3 mg/L to 20.0 °C at 1 mg/L (Jacobson et al. 2008), and a 48-year simulation validated a constant survival pair of 22.1 °C at 3 mg/L against observed kills and survivals (Fang et al. 2016). Warmer water is survivable only with more oxygen; cooler water tolerates less. The practical summer rule follows the protective benchmark — full habitat at 6 mg/L or better (Lyons et al. 2017), a survival knee at 3 mg/L — and any one-number lethal temperature quoted for adult cisco is wrong in a way the primary literature fixed in 2008.

Let the school's depth tell you which daily pattern your lake is running: some populations rise toward the surface at dusk to feed, some hold deep all day, and some do the reverse, and the study programmes that measured all three could sort them only by each system's prey, predators, temperature and oxygen. There is no species-level dusk rule for cisco, and this entry will not sell you one — find the migration, if your lake has one, by watching where the band sits at the light changes across a few trips.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the cold band is empty in midsummer, suspect the squeeze before the tackle: warm surface water above and low-oxygen deep water below can compress this fish into a band only a few metres thick, higher and warmer than its preference — across 32 lakes, as the squeeze tightened, cisco were caught higher, in a narrower band, at higher minimum temperatures and lower minimum oxygen (Grow et al. 2022). Search the narrow oxygenated layer that remains, and if the deep water has gone truly low in oxygen, expect the fish to have abandoned it entirely rather than to be feeding slowly inside it.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The zooplankton menu, unchanged — nothing fall-specific is measured in this species' diet, and the entry does not borrow a fall pattern from any other fish. On the staging edges, small presentations at the school's depth remain the whole supported tackle statement.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the cooling as the schedule: spawning is temperature-triggered into the low single digits (broodstock are taken once the water drops below 6.0 °C in the culture record, and the Alberta account puts spawning at about 5 °C falling to 2 °C), so each cold step moves staging schools closer to the nearshore ground. Work progressively toward the spawning areas as the surface temperature falls through the plateau toward 6 °C, and expect the feeding pattern to give way to the aggregation pattern in the next entry once the window opens.

Use the light changes as sounding checks in fall, when daily movement is at its most extensive in the tracking record — the Lake Superior programme found spring migrations less extensive than summer and fall ones — so a fall school's depth at dawn and at dusk can genuinely differ. In a lake running the classic pattern that is a feeding ascent to intercept; in any lake it is the cheapest way to learn where the school spends the dark hours.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall schools seem scattered, remember what a school is in this species: a moving, depth-shifting aggregation whose address is set by temperature and oxygen on the week, not by fixed structure. Search the cold band systematically across depths before concluding the lake is between patterns — a missed school is usually a missed depth, not an absent population.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Nothing spawn-specific is named in the cisco literature — no egg presentation, no spawning lure — and none is invented here. At the edges of the grounds, the supported offering remains the zooplankton menu at the school's depth, presented to fish that are moving and staging rather than spawning.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the window's length rather than a predicted peak night: the season runs for weeks from late October into December, males arrive first, and deposition happens at night — a schedule that rewards returning to a known spawning area across the window. Do not convert that night deposition into a night feeding claim: spawning at night is measured, feeding at night during the spawn is not, and the entry keeps the two separate on purpose.

As December runs on, fish the transition rather than the ground: the season values ease from the November aggregation value to the winter floor (0.60 to 0.55) as the late spawn ends and schools settle into the deep winter pattern described in the winter entry. The last weeks of the window are a move from shallow rock toward deep holding water, and the staging depth at the edge of the ground deepens with it — follow that slide instead of holding a November depth into the new year.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Dense schools sitting on known shoals that will not respond are the spawn working as described — aggregation is a distribution fact, not a feeding fact, and a packed school is not a promise of a bite. Slide off the rock to the staging depth at its edge; if the edges are also quiet, the window is long enough that the post-spawn schools will be feeding again on the winter pattern within weeks.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The winter menu is the narrowest of the year and it is measured: overwintering copepods, size-selected — in the March stomachs, zooplankton were the entire diet and the fish preferred larger zooplankton while selecting against small copepods and immature stages. Small presentations that read as the larger end of that winter plankton are the supported shape; the broader spring menu is not a winter claim.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish deep and patiently, without a clock pattern, because the measured winter pattern is the absence of one: no vertical migration means no dawn or dusk movement to intercept, and winter success is school location repeated accurately. Give a located deep school real time — a fish feeding selectively on overwintering plankton in near-freezing water is browsing, not chasing, and presentations need to arrive at the school rather than call it over.

Let the late-winter weeks carry a little more confidence than the first ones, at canon strength and labelled as such: the March stomach record is itself a late-winter feeding proof, and the Minnesota ice tradition holds that some of the best tullibee fishing of the year occurs in February and March. Early winter and late winter share the same measured floor in the model; the fishery record simply says the late end of it has been producing for a long time.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A quiet winter session is usually a missed school, not a refused bait: a non-migrating, deep, schooling fish offers few accidental encounters, so a blank at one depth is worth a systematic move through the deep band before it is worth a presentation change. And hold the limit honestly — no study measures a winter feeding rate against conditions for this species, so the floor values here are a distribution-based estimate, and your lake's winter pace is genuinely new information.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small presentations sized to overwintering zooplankton, fished at the school's depth and kept close: the March stomach record says the winter diet is large copepods, selectively taken. The Minnesota ice tradition's spoon-and-dropper presentation is carried as what it is — Grade C guide canon, not a measured tactic — and the Manitoba canon likewise describes a visual fish that will rise many feet toward a flashed lure and then take with an exceptionally light bite. Canon can shape a session here; it is labelled canon every time it appears, and nothing stronger exists for cisco ice tackle.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish a near-flat clock, because that flatness is measured rather than assumed: with no winter vertical migration, the ice diel values sit close together (day 0.90, dawn 0.85, dusk 0.85, night 0.75), and day is deliberately not penalised — the Manitoba and Saskatchewan ice canon independently reports best action often at midday in bright sun, with a slower dawn and dusk bite. A midday session on a located school is a first-choice pattern for this fish under ice, not a compromise.

Carry the oxygen sensitivity into late ice at its proper weight: no cisco winterkill dataset exists, so the ice oxygen term is this species' measured warm-season oxygen sensitivity — full habitat at 6 mg/L or better, a survival knee at 3 mg/L, always as a temperature pair rather than a lone temperature — applied to the general late-ice oxygen decline, and labelled as that construction. In a shallow, depleting basin late in the season, better-oxygenated deep water is the supported move, on the boundary evidence rather than on any winter measurement.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a deep basin set is silent, move with the school logic before changing baits: winter cisco roam as a school over basin structure in the canon record, and a non-migrating fish still relocates between days. Re-find the school at a neighbouring basin edge at the same depth band — depth first, then distance — and treat a full blank across bands as the provisional set's honest limit: winter feeding is proven for this species, its rate on your lake on your day is not something anyone has measured yet.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: Start with what kind of entry this is: cisco's rating is a DERIVED set, confidence capped at Low, and every curve in it is built from distribution — occupied temperatures, a fitted survival boundary, and vertical-migration tracking — because no measured adult feeding-rate response exists for this species at any factor. What these entries can honestly tell you is where the schools demonstrably are and how they demonstrably move; they claim nothing finer. In spring the annual cycle climbs out of the winter floor: season values rise from 0.60 in March through 0.70 in April to 0.85 in May.

Spring is the shallow feeding phase in the standard accounts — the species' most active shallow period, graded as expert consensus and used only as season shape: fish come shallow and the diet broadens beyond the winter zooplankton base to crustaceans, mayflies and occasionally small fish. Treat the shallows as a spring address held at consensus strength, and expect the schools to slide back toward cold, deep holding water as stratification sets up.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer cisco hold a narrow cold band in stratified water, and three programmes converge on it: in Lake Simcoe's Kempenfelt Bay, night tracking found fish in a 5–8 m band at 10.8–13.6 °C, sitting just below a 15–17 °C thermocline and tracking its internal-wave movement; Wisconsin summer netting put them mainly in metalimnetic water at 8–12 °C. Fish that cold band where it intersects the open water the schools travel — its depth is set by the stratification on the day, not by last month's mark.

The second address rule is oxygen, and for this species it is not a preference, it is a survival boundary (see How): when the cold deep water loses its oxygen, cisco leave it outright — in the Amisk Lake oxygenation experiment, fish entirely avoided their preferred cool deep layer while it was low in oxygen, and returned to deep use when oxygenation restored it (Aku et al. 1997). Summer searching therefore targets cold water that still carries oxygen, in that order, every trip.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is the squeeze releasing and the spawn approaching, in that order: season values step down from 0.90 in September to 0.80 in October as the feeding season gives way to aggregation, and cooling restores the deep cold water that summer oxygen loss took away. Fish the schools in the re-opening cold band early in the fall, and expect addresses to shift toward the spawning areas as October advances — Lake Superior aggregations form in October ahead of the late-fall spawn.

Know the spawning address before the window opens: spawning runs over rocky nearshore ground, with eggs deposited at night, males arriving on the grounds before females and leaving first. The staging schools hold in cold open water off that hard, shallow ground — fish the deep edge of the nearshore spawning areas while the water is still above the spawning trigger.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: The spawn is a late, cold, nocturnal aggregation: across the range it runs late October through December, peaking in November–December below about 6 °C, with eggs deposited at night. The honest framing matches the rule this library uses for every fall spawner: feeding suppression across the spawn has never been measured in cisco, the season model's November value of 0.60 is flagged in the study as its softest number, and this is therefore an aggregation entry, not a feeding entry — the fish are concentrated and findable, and whether the ones on the ground are feeding is a question the research does not answer.

The spawning ground itself is shallow and hard: Lake Ontario spawning was targeted over shallow hard substrate at 2–5 m in December, and the range-wide account puts egg deposition over rocky nearshore substrate at night. Fish the first deep water at the edge of that shallow rock for the staging and travelling fish — the defensible target around an aggregation — rather than over the spawning ground itself.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Open winter water is an active season at a moderate floor for this fish — season values hold at 0.55 through January and February — and that activity is measured, not assumed: through-ice stomach work (covered fully in the ice entry) found cisco feeding selectively in March, and the year-round tracking study found winter fish present and deep all season. In open cold water, fish the deep cold band the schools occupy and expect a steady, unspectacular rate.

Winter position is the year's simplest: in the one year-round study, cisco did not migrate vertically at all in winter, staying deep day and night in what the authors describe as low-risk, low-reward conditions at all depths. A winter school's address barely moves on the day — find it once, at depth, and it is found for the session.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: PROVISIONAL — flagged the way the study flags it: winter feeding for cisco is directly measured and winter movement is directly measured, which is more than most provisional sets have, but no under-ice feeding rate or catch-against-conditions study exists, so the ice rating stays provisional at the set's Low cap. The feeding measurement is a good one: 38 cisco collected through the ice at the Apostle Islands on 9 March 1994 held zooplankton as their entire diet and were feeding selectively — preferring larger zooplankton, especially the copepod Diaptomus sicilis, and selecting against small copepods and immature stages (Link et al. 1995). Selective foraging in March is deliberate feeding, not gut residue.

Manitoba's own ice fishery confirms the target at home: tullibee are a recognised provincial ice target, with Big Whiteshell Lake called out as a top Master Angler tullibee destination and repeated winter records from Lake Winnipeg. The Saskatchewan and Manitoba guide account, graded as expert canon, puts winter schools over basin edges at 30–50 ft, roaming as a school — use that depth band as one productive lake class's description and as a starting search area, not as a species parameter.

Winter depth barely negotiates: the year-round tracking found no vertical migration in winter, with fish deep day and night, so the through-ice address is the deep basin band the school already occupies — there is no shallow winter move to wait for in this species on its only year-round evidence.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 6–13 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for cisco is a documented blank: wind, fronts, barometric pressure and moon have never been tested against this species' feeding, activity or catch in any source the research could find. The wind results in its literature are recruitment effects on larvae and a physical effect in which wind-driven internal waves move the cold band the fish track — neither is an adult feeding response, and neither is used as one. Every weather factor carries zero weight in this rating by absence. A front matters here only as the temperature and light change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The light changes are when a migrating population moves — the tracking programmes agree that diel light change is the proximate trigger for vertical migration, and in a lake running the classic pattern, the school ascends at dusk into the window where light still lets a visual planktivore feed. Fish the transitions to find your school's depth on the day: a dusk ascent on your sounder is your lake telling you which regime it runs, which is worth more than any species-level rule, because other lakes run the reverse pattern or none at all.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night holds moderately high in the model (0.85) on the normal-migration record: populations that ascend at dusk feed in shallow water at night, and spawning fish deposit eggs at night in season. Hold that value at its evidence — it describes the lakes where the classic pattern was measured. In a lake whose fish were tracked doing the reverse, night is a deep-water pattern instead, and the first night's sounding, not this paragraph, should set your depth.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Aucun test du vent contre l'alimentation, l'activité ou la capture du cisco adulte n'existe par aucune méthode. Les résultats sur le vent dans la littérature sont des effets de recrutement sur les larves et un effet physique d'ondes internes sur la profondeur de la thermocline — ni l'un ni l'autre n'est une réponse d'alimentation adulte. Zéro par absence.
Aucun test de front n'existe par aucune méthode. Zéro par absence.
Aucun test de pression n'existe par aucune méthode. Zéro par absence (pas un nul mesuré).
Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai du cisco. Le frai nocturne de décembre garantit des coïncidences lunaires parasites; la coïncidence n'est pas un signal. Zéro par absence.

Aucune étude NTU/Secchi d'alimentation, de distance réactive ou de capture n'existe à aucun stade de vie. L'association d'occurrence en eau claire est confondue avec la productivité/l'oxygène (les lacs eutrophes sont troubles ET hypoxiques), alors la noter compterait le facteur oxygène deux fois. turbidity : null — lacune honnête, pas un petit nombre.

La densité de proies réorganise démontrablement la stratégie de mouvement du cisco (Ahrenstorff et al. 2013), mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure le champ de zooplancton d'un lac et aucune fonction densité-de-proies-contre-taux-d'alimentation n'est ajustée. La construction de couche de daphnies d'une autre espèce est une construction différente et n'est pas empruntée. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.
Les eaux servies du cisco sont des lacs; l'espèce est lacustre-pélagique et aucune fonction alimentation-contre-débit n'existe. Non noté.
La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour le cisco; elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome.
Réponses de transmission de lumière neige/glace et d'eau de fonte non mesurées pour le cisco — non ajustées (les poids de glace portent phase/oxygenRisk/iceDiel/température/photopériode seulement).

Do not convert that night deposition into a night feeding claim: spawning at night is measured, feeding at night during the spawn is not, and the entry keeps the two separate on purpose.

As December runs on, fish the transition rather than the ground: the season values ease from the November aggregation value to the winter floor (0.60 to 0.55) as the late spawn ends and schools settle into the deep winter pattern described in the winter entry. about: The common carp is the world's most travelled freshwater fish — Eurasian by birth, now at home on every continent but Antarctica, and in North America both a scorned “rough fish” and, increasingly, a respected game fish. It's a big, warm-water bottom feeder whose spawning gate is the sharpest seasonal fact in its file: spawning starts at 17–18 °C, in flooded shallows where whole bays boil with rolling fish each spring.

Carp root along the bottom for insects, crustaceans, seeds and molluscs, using barbels and a fine sense of taste, and their feeding clouds mud in a way that marks the spot for watching anglers. They are wary, powerful and long-lived — big carp test tackle like few freshwater fish. Anglers target them with bait, bow and increasingly fly rod, sight-casting to tailing fish on flats like bonefish of the muddy water.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: This is a chemosensory, bottom-feeding fish, and prespawn tackle follows from that alone: taste carries the final feeding decision — yearling carp discriminated attractive, neutral and deterrent taste substances at sub-microgram levels, and fish rendered unable to smell responded to taste unchanged (Kasumyan & Morsi 1996). No lure is named in the common carp literature, and none is invented here — small, natural bottom offerings the fish can find by taste and scent in the sediment are the whole supported story.

Keep the offering on the bottom and in the feeding zone: the feeding apparatus is a protrusible suction mouth with sediment winnowing and barbels carrying taste buds, built for picking benthic food out of the bottom rather than chasing it through the water.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Time the day by the feeding clock, which is night-led in every feeding line the research holds: wild carp feed largely at night, demand-fed carp chose the night with intake highest at 22:00 and lowest at 10:00, and competition landings rose from sunset to a peak at sunrise. Be fishing the staging shallows from dusk onward, and stay for the sunrise peak.

Respect the graded cold floor while the water is still cold: intensive feeding fades below about 15 °C and pond tradition puts practical feeding cessation at about 5–8 °C, yet telemetry proves some foraging at 3.1 °C. Cold prespawn fish are a dimmer, not a switch — slow down, fish the warmest shallow water, and give a spot real time.

Use repeat visits deliberately: wild carp learned the location of a newly introduced food reward within four nights and returned to it nightly with precision, in turbid water and without visual landmarks. A staging spot that is quiet on the first evening is not a written-off spot for this species.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shallows are empty, check the thermometer before the tackle: below about 8 °C you are at the practical feeding floor, and below 5–10 °C the spring migration itself may not have started. Drop back to the deep wintering water and its first staging edge and wait for the water rather than changing baits.

If daytime produces nothing, that is the measured shape, not bad luck — the day value in the model is 0.55 against a night peak of 1.0. Move the session to dusk, night and dawn before you move lakes in your mind.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No spawn-specific lure or technique is named in the carp literature, and none is invented here. Keep the supported pattern — small, natural bottom offerings worked by taste and scent — and fish it at the edges of the spawning shallows, where feeding fish work between bouts, rather than expecting a feeding response from fish in the act of spawning.

Batch spawning is the tackle-relevant fact: spawning repeats in batches across April to July in temperate systems, so at any moment in the window some fish are spawning, some are between batches, and some are still feeding toward it. The between-batch fish on the margins are the catchable ones.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the night movement into the shallows: in the Pearl River spawning-season telemetry, tagged carp were detected more during the night than the day and moved into shallow shoreline habitat more frequently at night. Set up on the spawning margins before dark and fish through the first hours of night.

Keep the sunrise in the session: across 14 European competitions, landings built from sunset through the night and peaked at sunrise, then fell toward midday. A dawn finish on the margins is this species' own measured pattern, in the spawn window as in summer.

Do not read a quiet midday on the beds as a failed spot — the diel shape (dawn 0.85, day 0.55, dusk 0.90, night 1.0) says the middle of the day is the trough even at the peak of the season. Presence in the shallows is high all day; feeding is not.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the spawning shallows themselves will not produce a feeding fish, that is the honest expectation the research sets — feeding is displaced by spawning, not bonused by it, and no spawning feeding coefficient exists in either direction. Step off the beds to the adjacent deeper feeding water and fish the fish that are not spawning today.

If the temperature has run past about 26 °C, the main spawning is declining on the measured gate, however active the shallows still look. Fish it as a post-spawn feeding pattern — margins and nearby benthic feeding water — rather than waiting for another wave at the top of the band.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the benthic menu from the bottom: this is a benthic omnivore gated by the bottom fauna of the water it is in, feeding by suction and winnowing with a taste system that discriminates attractive from deterrent substances at trace levels. No lure is named in the common carp literature, and none is invented here — natural bottom offerings, placed where the fish are rooting, are the supported pattern.

Oxygen rarely rules this fish out of a spot: carp survived 0.5 mg/L for seven days with energy reserves maintained, and tracked fish extensively used bottom water below 1.1 mg/L, largely at night. In a still, warm basin where other species have left the bottom, carp may still be feeding on it — the model's oxygen curve is the shallowest in the library because the measurements say so, reaching full value only at the 5 mg/L growth-preference bound.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Night is the peak and it is not close on the feeding evidence: night 1.0, dusk 0.90, dawn 0.85, day 0.55. Wild telemetry, self-timed demand feeding and 14 competitions of landings all point the same way. Build the summer session around dark, and treat the daytime as a real but secondary shift.

Carry the disclosed conflict honestly: one long locomotor telemetry series found fish less active at night, resting deep, and juvenile tank studies found day grazing — movement and juvenile lines, against four feeding lines. That dissent is exactly why the day score sits at 0.55 instead of near zero. Day fish are catchable; they are just not the main event.

Work a found feeding area across repeat evenings: carp learned a new food location in four nights or fewer, the knowledge spread socially through the tagged group, and competition landings rose across days as fish learned the baited spots. For this species, returning to a swim is a measured behaviour, not a superstition.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer fish will not take in the heat, check which side of the plateau you are on: the curve holds full value to 28 °C, then declines — 0.90 at 30 °C, 0.75 at 32 °C. On the hottest water, fish the night in the coolest feeding water you can find and leave the midday basking shallows alone; the preferendum is not the feeding peak.

If a clear, bright flat is dead, try the murk before you try a new bait: this fish's food-finding does not run on sight, and turbid, low-oxygen and dark water are all smaller costs to carp than to anything else in this library. The spots other entries tell you to abandon are often this fish's spots.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer benthic pattern, a step slower as the water cools: natural bottom offerings, found by taste and scent, presented in the feeding and gathering water. No fall-specific lure is named in the carp literature, and none is invented here.

Size the effort to the temperature, not the calendar: feeding holds while the water is in the teens, fades through the fade zone below about 15 °C, and approaches the practical floor near 8 °C. The same offering fished patiently in cold fall water outperforms a changed offering fished fast.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The night-led clock runs into fall unchanged — night and twilight carried the highest activity in the pond telemetry, with the day kept open at 0.55 by the disclosed locomotor dissent. Fish the light changes and the dark over the gathering water.

Once aggregation starts below 10 °C, finding fish replaces covering water as the skill: grouped fish in known gathering water are worth repeated, patient sessions, while empty summer shallows are worth one check and a move. The groups also move, so a located group is a starting point for the next session, not a permanent address.

Watch the temperature trend, not just the reading: activity tracked water temperature directly in the winter telemetry winters, and the fall limb is where that relationship does its work. A warming spell in October is a genuine feeding window for this species; a hard cold snap is the aggregation signal.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the fall shallows have gone silent, the fish have likely started the move, not stopped feeding — drop to the deep gathering water off the summer shallows and fish the grouped fish there. Below about 8 °C, expect the practical floor: residual feeding continues, but sessions are won by location and patience, not presentation changes.

If a gathering spot produces once and then dies, relocate the group rather than resting the spot: tracked aggregations moved frequently through the cold season. Search the nearby deep, still water close to shore before you search new water entirely.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small, natural bottom offerings, delivered close to located fish and left for them: winter feeding is real but residual — the temperature curve sits at 0.25 at 6 °C and 0.15 at 4 °C — so the presentation has to arrive at the group. No winter-specific lure is named in the carp literature, and none is invented here.

Oxygen is seldom the reason a winter spot fails for this species — the most hypoxia-tolerant fish in this library, with survival measured at 0.3–0.5 mg/L. One honest caution from the telemetry: where aggregations sat within a wintering water was not explained by temperature or dissolved oxygen, so oxygen tells you a basin can hold carp, not where in it they are.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the temperature, literally: winter activity correlated positively with water temperature in two of the three telemetry winters. The warmest stable water, and any mild spell that lifts it, is the winter window — the coldest snaps are for locating, not for expecting.

Give a located aggregation time, then move with it: winter fish forage at low rates and the groups relocate often, so a session is locate, fish patiently, and re-locate. Dawn and dusk keep a small edge in the flattened winter shape the model carries, but winter is the season where the diel contrast is weakest in the evidence.

Expect a fraction of summer, and plan for it honestly: at 2–4 °C the model's temperature value is 0.08–0.15 — non-zero because the telemetry forbids zero, and low because the same telemetry shows a fish conserving, not feeding hard. Short, well-placed sessions over known groups beat long hopeful ones.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a winter spot is dead, move along the gathering water before you change anything else: aggregation position was not predicted by temperature or oxygen in the telemetry, so the warmest, deepest guess can simply be the wrong pool. Search the deep, still water close to shore systematically.

Know the honest limit of the winter pattern: foraging at 3.1 °C is proven, a winter feeding rate is not. A fishless session over correctly located winter carp is within what the evidence predicts — this is a low-rate season, and the entry says so rather than selling a winter trick.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice-specific presentation is measured for common carp, and none is borrowed to fill this space. The honest application of the winter evidence is small, natural bottom offerings fished close and still over a located aggregation — the open-water chemosensory pattern at its slowest. The commercial under-ice netting in the record proves presence and vulnerability to nets; it is not an angling pattern and is not presented as one.

One angler-grade record in the file deserves its label: schooled carp watched on camera through ice were moving very slowly and did not really appear to be feeding. Expect presentations to need to arrive at nearly stationary fish, and expect refusals that have nothing to do with the offering.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The timing below is a labelled transfer, and says so: the under-ice diel shape in the model is the open-water night-led shape flattened — dawn 0.80, day 0.60, dusk 0.85, night 0.95 — supported only by the finding that the diel cycle essentially disappears through the cold months in open-water telemetry. Fish the light changes first, but treat the whole short day as fishable in a way summer never is.

Fish the temperature trend through the ice season: winter activity tracked water temperature in the telemetry winters, so mild stretches are the windows. And relocate relentlessly — tracked aggregations moved frequently all winter, which is why control programmes find them with tagged fish rather than fixed marks.

Treat oxygen as a basin question, not a spot answer: this species tolerates oxygen down to levels no other fish in this library survives, and its aggregation position was not explained by oxygen in the telemetry. A low-oxygen basin can still hold its carp; where inside it they sit has to be searched, not calculated.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Mid-winter silence over located carp is within the evidence, not a tactics failure: feeding under ice is proven occasional — foraging at 3.1 °C — and never quantified, and the one direct angler observation describes slow, apparently non-feeding schools. Move with the aggregation, fish the mild spells, and know the ice season is this entry's provisional edge.

If the whole basin seems empty, question the basin before the bait: wintering choice is concentrated — most adults in a watershed picked a single wintering water. A winterkill-resistant deep basin nearby is a better next move than a new presentation in a basin the fish never chose.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Spring starts with a movement threshold, not a spawning one: overwintering aggregations break up and, in the Minnesota watershed study, 82–98% of adults migrated toward shallow spawning water once temperatures reached 5–10 °C. Fish the routes out of the deep wintering water and the first shallow, vegetated staging water beyond them — the migration is under way well before any spawning temperature arrives.

In spring the tracked pattern is shallow vegetated aggregations (Penne & Pierce 2008), against scattered use of shallow cover through the summer that follows. Work the vegetated shallows the fish are gathering into, close to the deeper water they wintered in.

In flowing water, expect the same break-up on the same thermometer: fish leave the deep, still winter holding water as the temperature climbs through 5–10 °C and stage toward shallow, vegetated spawning margins. Fish the quiet staging water off the deep holding pools first.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The spawn gate is the sharpest seasonal fact in this set: onset at 17–18 °C, the main batch spawning at 18–23 °C, declining by about 26 °C and stopping near 28 °C in the St. Lawrence tradition. The address is shallow, vegetated water — often freshly flooded margins, 25–50 cm deep on the Danube flood meadows in the record — with adhesive eggs laid on vegetation. In Manitoba the window runs late, May into June.

Fish the shallow vegetated margins themselves and the feeding water immediately beside them. Spawning is carried in the model as a location annotation with no feeding bonus — spawning carp are catchable by presence in the shallows, but spawning is not feeding, and this entry will not dress it up as a bite peak.

Wild running-water populations spawn on flooded terrestrial vegetation, and rising discharge is what moves fish sideways onto that flooded ground. When the water is up and the margins are flooded, fish the newly covered vegetation at the edges rather than the deep water the fish left.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer is the feeding plateau, and its centre is lower than the folklore says: the one controlled feeding-rate function peaks at 24 °C, growth was already depressed at 28 °C in juveniles, and the model's plateau runs 20–28 °C inside the agency growth bands of 23–30 and 23–26 °C. The laboratory and field preferenda of 27–32 °C — where carp sit when offered a gradient — are recorded in the research and deliberately not used as the feeding plateau. Fish where the fish feed best, not where they bask warmest.

Through the summer the tracked pattern is fish scattered in shallow vegetated cover (Penne & Pierce 2008), working benthic food. Cover the vegetated shallows and soft-bottom feeding water thoroughly rather than camping on one spot — summer carp are spread across the feeding habitat.

Turbid water is not a problem to solve for this species: carp live and feed at turbidities beyond 200 units with visibility under 8 cm, were tracked across 1–113 NTU with no avoidance reported, and find food by taste and smell. Do not abandon a summer spot for murk that would end the day for a sight-feeding fish.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall feeding runs on the temperature limb: the season score holds 0.85 through September and 0.65 in October as the water cools off the plateau, and the location story turns at about 10 °C — aggregation begins as temperatures descend below 10 °C, and grows particularly dense below 5 °C. Early fall, fish the summer feeding shallows; late fall, fish the gathering water.

The winter address is chosen in fall at a watershed scale: over three winters, more than 90% of adults in a 12-water Minnesota watershed overwintered in a single deep water less susceptible to winterkill. As the temperature falls through the single digits, concentrate on the deep basin water the local fish are gathering into, close to shore in the tracked lakes.

In flowing water the fall move is the same gathering in reverse order: out of the scattered summer feeding water and toward the deep, still holding water before winter. Fish the deep still pools on the cooling limb, and expect the fish to be grouped rather than spread.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter carp do not sleep through the season, whatever the pond-culture picture says: across three winters of radio telemetry the fish were relatively active throughout, activity rose with water temperature, body-weight loss was minimal, and the authors report foraging at 3.1 °C. The winter address is the dense aggregation — forming below 10 °C, particularly dense below 5 °C — in deep water that resists winterkill.

The tracked under-ice position is specific: aggregations held just below the ice, at about 1.5 m, close to shore, and moved frequently. In open winter water read that as the top of the deep gathering water near shore — and keep searching along it, because the group you found last week has probably shifted.

Winter movement in running water is minimal — except during high discharge or ice break-up, when tracked fish moved their longest distances, generally downstream, and shifted into still backwater areas (Brown et al. 2001). After a winter flow pulse, re-find the fish in the still water off the main flow rather than assuming the old holding pool still has them.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: The ice set for common carp is provisional, capped at Moderate confidence, and this entry carries that flag openly: winter movement, under-ice aggregation and foraging down to 3.1 °C are all measured for this species — a stronger winter file than most provisional sets rest on — but the under-ice diel shape has never been measured, no ice catch-rate dataset exists, and Manitoba carp are netted under ice commercially while remaining a rare, difficult ice-angling target. Fish the dense cold-season aggregations: below 5 °C they hold just under the ice at about 1.5 m, close to shore, and they move frequently.

Start the search where the fall gathering put them: the deep wintering water that resists winterkill, near shore, at the top of the basin. Watershed telemetry says the great majority of adults choose one such wintering water — find that water first, then find the group inside it.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 20–28 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for common carp is an absence, and a famous one: no front or barometric-pressure test of carp feeding or catch exists in any source the research could find, in either direction — the extensive carp pressure lore, falling-barometer rules and optimal-pressure charts included, is angling canon with no dataset behind it. Wind carries no term in the rating at all — it has never been measured for this species — and the one wind result in the record is temperature-mediated movement, not feeding. There is no front trick for this fish to sell you: a front matters here only as the temperature and light change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The light changes are the shoulders of this species' peak: dusk at 0.90 carries the sunset-to-sunrise build the competition landings measured, and dawn at 0.85 carries the sunrise landing peak and the morning activity the pond telemetry found. Be set up on the feeding water before the transition, not travelling during it.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is this species' measured peak, full stop: the model's night value is 1.0, wild carp feed largely at night, self-timed demand feeding peaked at 22:00, and tracked fish even used oxygen-poor bottom water extensively at night. Darkness is cover for a fish that finds food by taste and smell — after dark, fish the same benthic feeding water you located by day, slowly and on the bottom.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais testé pour la carpe commune — aucun recensement de terrain, aucune expérience contrôlée pression-alimentation, aucun modèle d'enquête avec une covariable de pression n'existe. Toute la littérature de pression de la carpe est du folklore de pêcheur (règles de baromètre tombant, tableaux « optimal hPa ») sans jeu de données. Zéro par absence (pas un nul mesuré).

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai de la carpe commune. Le registre de frai lunaire de la rivière Halda concerne les grandes carpes indiennes (catla/rohu/mrigal) dans une rivière tidale confondue par les crues — un résultat d'espèces différentes qui n'est pas transféré. Les calendriers de capture par phase lunaire de la carpe sont grade D.

L'alimentation adulte est conditionnée par la faune benthique et guidée par l'apprentissage selon le lac (mesuré), mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure la faune benthique ou l'historique d'amorçage d'un lac; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché (l'apprentissage contamine aussi les données de capture, Žák 2021).
La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour la carpe; elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Spring starts with a movement threshold, not a spawning one: overwintering aggregations break up and, in the Minnesota watershed study, 82–98% of adults migrated toward shallow spawning water once temperatures reached 5–10 °C. Fish the routes out of the deep wintering water and the first shallow, vegetated staging water beyond them — the migration is under way well before any spawning temperature arrives.

In spring the tracked pattern is shallow vegetated aggregations (Penne & Pierce 2008), against scattered use of shallow cover through the summer that follows. Work the vegetated shallows the fish are gathering into, close to the deeper water they wintered in.

In flowing water, expect the same break-up on the same thermometer: fish leave the deep, still winter holding water as the temperature climbs through 5–10 °C and stage toward shallow, vegetated spawning margins. Fish the quiet staging water off the deep holding pools first.

Time the day by the feeding clock, which is night-led in every feeding line the research holds: wild carp feed largely at night, demand-fed carp chose the night with intake highest at 22:00 and lowest at 10:00, and competition landings rose from sunset to a peak at sunrise. Be fishing the staging shallows from dusk onward, and stay for the sunrise peak.

Respect the graded cold floor while the water is still cold: intensive feeding fades below about 15 °C and pond tradition puts practical feeding cessation at about 5–8 °C, yet telemetry proves some foraging at 3.1 °C. Cold prespawn fish are a dimmer, not a switch — slow down, fish the warmest shallow water, and give a spot real time.

Use repeat visits deliberately: wild carp learned the location of a newly introduced food reward within four nights and returned to it nightly with precision, in turbid water and without visual landmarks. A staging spot that is quiet on the first evening is not a written-off spot for this species.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The spawn gate is the sharpest seasonal fact in this set: onset at 17–18 °C, the main batch spawning at 18–23 °C, declining by about 26 °C and stopping near 28 °C in the St. Lawrence tradition. The address is shallow, vegetated water — often freshly flooded margins, 25–50 cm deep on the Danube flood meadows in the record — with adhesive eggs laid on vegetation. In Manitoba the window runs late, May into June.

Fish the shallow vegetated margins themselves and the feeding water immediately beside them. Spawning is carried in the model as a location annotation with no feeding bonus — spawning carp are catchable by presence in the shallows, but spawning is not feeding, and this entry will not dress it up as a bite peak.

Wild running-water populations spawn on flooded terrestrial vegetation, and rising discharge is what moves fish sideways onto that flooded ground. When the water is up and the margins are flooded, fish the newly covered vegetation at the edges rather than the deep water the fish left.

Fish the night movement into the shallows: in the Pearl River spawning-season telemetry, tagged carp were detected more during the night than the day and moved into shallow shoreline habitat more frequently at night. Set up on the spawning margins before dark and fish through the first hours of night.

Keep the sunrise in the session: across 14 European competitions, landings built from sunset through the night and peaked at sunrise, then fell toward midday. A dawn finish on the margins is this species' own measured pattern, in the spawn window as in summer.

Do not read a quiet midday on the beds as a failed spot — the diel shape (dawn 0.85, day 0.55, dusk 0.90, night 1.0) says the middle of the day is the trough even at the peak of the season. Presence in the shallows is high all day; feeding is not.

spawningSources.citation: Seuil de frai 17–18 °C début / 18–23 °C principal / déclin ~26 °C (FAO; tradition du Saint-Laurent); migration printanière 5–10 °C (Banet 2016); rassemblement d'automne <10 °C (Bajer et al. 2011); le frai est une annotation — aucun bonus

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai de la carpe commune. Le registre de frai lunaire de la rivière Halda concerne les grandes carpes indiennes (catla/rohu/mrigal) dans une rivière tidale confondue par les crues — un résultat d'espèces différentes qui n'est pas transféré. Les calendriers de capture par phase lunaire de la carpe sont grade D. (Monographie de la carpe commune §4)

about: The freshwater drum — sheepshead across much of its range — is North America's only freshwater member of the croaker family, named for the booming sounds males make with their swim bladders. It's a traveller: Manitoba fish in the research averaged well over a hundred kilometres of movement in a season, migrations starting as the water passes about 5 °C, and its feeding plateaus in the warm low-to-mid twenties Celsius.

Drum spawn by broadcasting buoyant eggs over open water through early summer — no nest, no guarding — and feed along the bottom on molluscs, crayfish and insect larvae, grinding them with throat teeth. They pull far harder than their reputation suggests. Anglers meet them from docks, rivers and big lakes across the continent, and those who target them find a willing, strong fish that eats well from cold water.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the bottom menu this species actually eats in Manitoba water: caddisfly larvae were 79% of prey items and in over 80% of stomachs in the Lake Winnipeg study, with mayfly nymphs in 72% — a benthic insect-larvae diet, confirmed by isotopes. No lure is named for drum in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here: small, bottom-presented, larvae-sized is the supported shape for a fish that roots prey out of the bottom and processes it with pharyngeal teeth.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Time the day backwards from most species: drum are night-led — the model's shape is night 1.0, dusk 0.85, dawn 0.55, day 0.35 — and the prespawn movement and feeding follow that clock. Put the best hours at dusk and into the night on the staging water; a midday prespawn session is fishing this species' quiet shift.

Respect the cold floor underneath the season: growth stops below about 10 °C and juveniles were incapacitated at 1 °C and below in the laboratory record, so early prespawn fish in single-digit water are travelling on a slow metabolism. Slow everything down until the water is honestly into double digits.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the staging water is empty, the run may simply not have arrived — a May, pre-ice-off entry means the calendar lies about this season in both directions. Check the warmest staging water first, and check it at dusk, before concluding the fish are not there.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The spawning-season menu stays the benthic one — insect larvae rooted from the bottom — and the drumming you may hear is not part of it: male chorusing builds toward evening and peaks late in the evening in the Lake Champlain acoustic record, but chorusing is a spawning-aggregation signal, and the research files 'chorus equals feeding' as a misuse. No spawn lure is named in the drum literature; larvae-sized and on the bottom is the whole supported story.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the evening build, because two clocks agree on it: the diel shape puts dusk at 0.85 rising to a night maximum, and spawning-season calling builds from sporadic daytime calls to a full chorus by late afternoon and evening. The practical overlap — active, gathered fish in the evening — is real; just credit it to the diel pattern and the aggregation, not to feeding on the chorus.

Do not apply a guarding-fish rule to this species: drum broadcast buoyant eggs and leave them, so there is no nest defence, no guarding strike, and no measured spawn feeding bonus or penalty in either direction. The June-to-July strength in the rating rests on the measured movement and feeding season underneath the spawn, not on the spawn itself.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If spawning aggregations will not take, fish the fish that are not spawning: in a six-to-seven-week season, part of the population is always between bouts, feeding on the bottom in the same depth band. Drop off the aggregation's edge, fish after dark, and let the night-led pattern do the work.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: In Manitoba water, tie on the insect-larvae menu without apology: caddisfly and mayfly larvae dominate the stomachs and the isotopes, and growth was equal or better on that diet in the modern sample. The famous mussel story belongs to another basin's record — in the 2019 Lake Winnipeg stomachs, zebra mussels appeared in only 4 of 51 fish, and over 80% of those mussels were in a single fish — so mussel-based tactics are not written into this entry. Where a mayfly hatch is running, the diet-supported move is to match the hatch, because summer movement demonstrably keys onto hatches. No lure is named in the drum research itself; bottom-presented and larvae-sized is the supported form.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the night as the main event: adults and juveniles moved into the shallows at night to feed along the shoreline and retreated deep and offshore by day, night sampling and night angling produced the bulk of catches, and a second river's night electrofishing found this family's catch rates significantly higher after dark. Set up on the shoreline feeding ground before dark and fish it into the night; dawn, at 0.55, is the tail of the shift.

Use the warmth while it lasts, and note the top edge: swimming performance rose steadily from 10 to 30 °C in the factorial experiment, but field fish avoided about 30 °C and the standardised tolerance metrics sit near 30 to 32 °C. Inside the 22 to 26.5 °C plateau the fish are at their measured best; as the water pushes toward 30 °C, expect them in the deepest, coolest water available rather than on the night shallows.

Handle summer fish knowing the Red River angling record: about 31% of angled drum were deep-hooked in the oesophagus, and stress markers ran higher in summer than spring. A drum bound for release earns a quick, careful unhooking — and deep-hooked summer fish are the known cost of passive bottom presentations, so check baits promptly.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a summer day shift produces nothing, believe the diel data rather than changing baits: the day value is 0.35, a real but low floor on an all-hours-capable feeder, and the fix the research supports is the clock — come back at dusk and fish the shoreline movement as it starts.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The fall menu is the summer menu cooling down: benthic insect larvae on the bottom, with fish becoming a major food through late summer and fall in the one long Erie diet record — 52 to 94% fish, mostly young-of-year shad, from August to November. That is a different basin's stomach record, carried as such; in Manitoba water the larvae stay the proven base. No fall lure is named in the research.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The night-led clock still runs the fall day — dusk into night on the staging and feeding water — but the temperature floor is approaching: below about 10 °C growth has stopped and the fish are sliding toward the winter minimum. On cold fall days, fish the warmest part of the afternoon into dusk as one combined window and slow the presentation down.

Credit a warm fall honestly: the October shoulder in the season curve is this species' own telemetry, not a guess — a warm October produced a movement peak, so a mild autumn extends real fishing, and an early cold one ends it. Let the water temperature, not the calendar, call the season over.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall fish vanish from the shallows, they have started the winter slide, not left the system: drop to the deep, stable water and fish it at dusk. Below the high single digits, expect the near-winter pattern — present, deep, and barely feeding — and set expectations with it.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: On the rare winter day this is attempted, the offering is the smallest end of the bottom menu, delivered to a located fish: winter prey consumption is measured to be limited, so the presentation has to arrive at the fish, because the fish is not travelling to it. No winter presentation is named in the drum research, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Set the expectation the evidence sets: the winter section of the model runs on presence, depth and oxygen, not on a feeding pattern, because winter feeding was measured to be near-absent — the fish are not actively feeding in winter on the telemetry programme's own reading of the diet evidence. Any winter drum is an individual event, not a pattern to build a day around.

Fish the warmest deep water you can find if you fish at all: the winter selection of bottom water over 2 °C warmer than the surroundings is a survival behaviour at a northern range edge where ambient water sits at the species' cold threshold, and it is the only winter location rule the research actually measures.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A silent winter is the measured normal for this species, not a tactics failure: rarity of winter catches is behaviour — near-zero feeding plus deep aggregation — not absence, and the telemetry proves the fish are down there. The honest winter advice is to note the deep aggregation for spring and spend the feeding season's effort on a species that eats in winter.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The smallest bottom offering you would use in summer, set down to a located fish and left patient: there is no measured ice presentation for drum, and this entry claims none. With feeding near-absent, the offering's job is to be in front of the one fish in a hundred that takes — size and patience are the whole honest story.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish it as a low-expectation pattern from the first hole: winter oxygen depletion is a measured threat to this species' cold refuges — declining oxygen helped break up the warm backwater refuges and drive die-offs in the winter study — so the deepest, best-oxygenated aggregations are both the likeliest holding water and the only water worth the attempt. The night-led timing is the open-water diel shape carried under ice as a labelled transfer; the under-ice shape itself has never been measured.

Keep the attempt located rather than mobile: winter movement in the telemetry record fell to under 25 km a month, a fraction of the spring and summer travel, because the fish aggregate and stay. Drilling a long search line across a basin fishes water the fish crossed in October; sitting over one known deep aggregation fishes the winter behaviour that was actually measured.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Silence through the ice is the measured expectation for drum, and the entry will not dress it up as a solvable problem: the fish are present, aggregated and not feeding, and winter catches are extremely rare for behavioural reasons the telemetry established. If you need a winter bite, the honest move is a different species over the same deep water — the drum will be there, feeding, in May.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn drum are a movement season before they are a feeding season: seasonal migrations begin as the water passes about 5 °C, and Manitoba fish moved an average of about 161 km through the spring in the Red River telemetry programme. Fish the travel water and the staging depths on the way to the spawning reaches, not a single summer address.

The Manitoba chronology is the entry's spine: drum entered the rivers in May, before ice-off, on the earliest warming — the run starts while the season still looks like winter. Work the deep staging pools along the entry route from the first warming, weeks before the spawn itself.

Fish staging for the river runs hold in the basin water off the mouths through spring — summer telemetry later spreads lake fish across broad depths of about 6 to 16 m over fine substrate, and the prespawn concentration sits at the deep end of that range near the mouths.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The spawn is a broadcast over open water, not a nest season: it begins at 18 °C and runs six to seven weeks through June and July inside a band of 18 to just under 23 °C in the Manitoba telemetry intervals, with buoyant eggs released into the water and abandoned. Spawning fish gather over the open spawning water rather than holding any structure an angler can target nest by nest.

Post-spawn exit in the Manitoba record ran from mid-June through July, and spawning-site fidelity between years was near-total — the same reaches host the run every year. A reach that held spawning drum last June is the first place to look this June.

Basin fish spawn on the same 18 °C trigger after staging off the mouths; through the window they are spread across the broad 6 to 16 m summer depth band over fine substrate rather than crowded into the shallows.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer is the measured maximum: movement peaked through the warm months — about 219 km across summer and fall for Red River fish — on water inside the adult thermal plateau of 22 to 26.5 °C. By day the fish hold deep and offshore; the shallows are a night address, and the entry is organised around that split.

River summer fish range widely on the telemetry record, and part of that summer travel tracks episodic mayfly hatches — when a hatch is on, the fish move to it. A summer reach that was empty last week can hold travelling, hatch-focused fish this week.
Summer lake fish used broad depths of about 6 to 16 m over fine substrate by day. Start on that deep fine-bottom band, and treat the shallow shoreline as the night shift's water only.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall drum keep moving and feeding as the water cools through the teens — the telemetry shoulder is real, including a warm-October movement peak in the warm autumn of the study — then slide toward the deep, stable wintering water. In the Lake Erie record the same pattern reads as shallow warm water in summer giving way to deeper water in late fall.

River fish stage back toward the deep pools on their way out; post-spawn exit had already shown the pattern of long seasonal travel, and fall movement stays high until the cold arrives. Work the deep staging pools on the travel route rather than the summer shoreline.

Basin fish narrow their depth range as the season turns — from the broad summer band toward the tighter, deeper winter selection. Follow them down and out: the late-fall address is deep water over fine substrate, close to where they will spend the winter.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter drum are present, located, and barely feeding — all three are measured, and the entry holds them together: telemetry detected fish all winter, aggregated in deep water over clay and fine substrate at about 8 to 12 m, selecting the warmest, stillest bottom water available, which in the Manitoba record ran over 2 °C warmer than the flowing water nearby. They are not gone. They are sitting out the cold at the edge of a measured physiological floor — juveniles were incapacitated at 1 °C and below.

River fish in the telemetry record wintered out on the big water rather than in the channels — winter movement fell to about 44.5 km for the season against 161 km in spring, and the winter hotspots sat on the basin side of the system. Expect the channels to feel empty in winter because, measurably, the fish have left them.

The basin holds the winter fish, and detection probability for the tracked fish was actually highest in winter — about 0.57 — because the fish aggregate and stay put in the deep mid-basin and bay hotspots over fine substrate. Winter lake drum are findable; feeding them is the hard part.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: The ice set for freshwater drum is PROVISIONAL, and the entry carries that flag openly with its measured reason: drum are present under ice all winter in Manitoba telemetry — aggregated in deep, warm, still water at about 8 to 12 m over clay and fine substrate — but they are barely feeding, with winter prey consumption measured to be limited and the fish described by the telemetry programme as not actively feeding in winter. No under-ice diel or ice catch-rate study exists. Drill over the deep fine-bottom aggregations if you drill at all, and expect presence, not a bite.

The tracked basin fish were detected most reliably in winter — probability about 0.57 — holding mid-basin and bay hotspots in the warmest bottom water available, over 2 °C warmer than the nearby flowing water. The location is measurable; the feeding is the missing part.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 22–26.5 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for freshwater drum is an empty drawer, stated plainly: wind, fronts, barometric pressure, precipitation and moon have never been tested for this species' feeding or catchability in any source the research could find, in either direction — pressure and moon are zeroes by absence here, not measured nulls. There is no front trick for this fish to sell you: what is measured is temperature, darkness, season and oxygen, and those are what the other sections fish. A front matters here only as the temperature and light change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: After dark, drum move into the shallows to feed along the shoreline — adults and juveniles both, on the measured record — having spent the day deep and offshore. The night shoreline, especially where it borders the deep daytime water, is this species' primary feeding ground, and the model's night value of 1.0 against a day value of 0.35 is the widest diel split in this entry.

Build the session around the dark: arrive at the shoreline feeding ground before dusk, fish the dusk build at 0.85 as the fish arrive, and stay into the night peak rather than packing up at dark. Bottom presentations worked slowly along the shallow feeding ground match a rooting, benthic feeder that locates food by taste and touch as much as sight — drum still feed in the dark because darkness was never their obstacle.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Dusk is the hinge of the drum day: the shoreline movement starts as the light goes, spawning-season chorusing builds through the evening in season, and the model's dusk value of 0.85 is second only to full night. Be set up and quiet on the feeding ground before the transition; dawn runs the same movement in reverse, at a lower value, as fish slide back to deep water.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais testé pour le freshwater drum — aucun recensement de terrain, aucune expérience contrôlée pression-alimentation n'existe. Zéro par absence (pas un nul mesuré).

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai du drum. Les chœurs de saison de frai suivent la saison de reproduction, pas le cycle lunaire; aucun terme lunaire n'en est inféré (et le chœur est un signal de rassemblement de frai, pas un signal d'alimentation).

Aucune fonction alimentation-contre-débit n'existe. Les preuves de débit sont une corrélation de croissance avec les événements de grande magnitude (Jacquemin et al. 2015) et un mécanisme de perturbation des refuges hivernaux — histoire de vie, pas une fonction de morsure. Les eaux servies du drum dans le modèle sont des lacs; la réserve de la rivière Rouge est énoncée ici plutôt que notée.

L'alimentation au Manitoba se cale démontrablement sur les éclosions épisodiques d'éphémères et le mouvement estival les suit en partie (Hansen et al. 2020 via Glowa et al. 2024), mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure l'éclosion d'un lac; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.

La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour le drum; elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome (la construction de nuages du flathead est propre à l'espèce et n'est pas empruntée).

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn drum are a movement season before they are a feeding season: seasonal migrations begin as the water passes about 5 °C, and Manitoba fish moved an average of about 161 km through the spring in the Red River telemetry programme. Fish the travel water and the staging depths on the way to the spawning reaches, not a single summer address.

The Manitoba chronology is the entry's spine: drum entered the rivers in May, before ice-off, on the earliest warming — the run starts while the season still looks like winter. Work the deep staging pools along the entry route from the first warming, weeks before the spawn itself.

Fish staging for the river runs hold in the basin water off the mouths through spring — summer telemetry later spreads lake fish across broad depths of about 6 to 16 m over fine substrate, and the prespawn concentration sits at the deep end of that range near the mouths.

Time the day backwards from most species: drum are night-led — the model's shape is night 1.0, dusk 0.85, dawn 0.55, day 0.35 — and the prespawn movement and feeding follow that clock. Put the best hours at dusk and into the night on the staging water; a midday prespawn session is fishing this species' quiet shift.

Respect the cold floor underneath the season: growth stops below about 10 °C and juveniles were incapacitated at 1 °C and below in the laboratory record, so early prespawn fish in single-digit water are travelling on a slow metabolism. Slow everything down until the water is honestly into double digits.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The spawn is a broadcast over open water, not a nest season: it begins at 18 °C and runs six to seven weeks through June and July inside a band of 18 to just under 23 °C in the Manitoba telemetry intervals, with buoyant eggs released into the water and abandoned. Spawning fish gather over the open spawning water rather than holding any structure an angler can target nest by nest.

Post-spawn exit in the Manitoba record ran from mid-June through July, and spawning-site fidelity between years was near-total — the same reaches host the run every year. A reach that held spawning drum last June is the first place to look this June.

Basin fish spawn on the same 18 °C trigger after staging off the mouths; through the window they are spread across the broad 6 to 16 m summer depth band over fine substrate rather than crowded into the shallows.

Fish the evening build, because two clocks agree on it: the diel shape puts dusk at 0.85 rising to a night maximum, and spawning-season calling builds from sporadic daytime calls to a full chorus by late afternoon and evening. The practical overlap — active, gathered fish in the evening — is real; just credit it to the diel pattern and the aggregation, not to feeding on the chorus.

Do not apply a guarding-fish rule to this species: drum broadcast buoyant eggs and leave them, so there is no nest defence, no guarding strike, and no measured spawn feeding bonus or penalty in either direction. The June-to-July strength in the rating rests on the measured movement and feeding season underneath the spawn, not on the spawn itself.

spawningSources.citation: Chronologie de télémétrie du Manitoba — programmes de 5 ans, 80 poissons, ~50M de détections (Glowa et al. 2024; Rudolfsen et al. 2021) : entrée en rivière en mai avant la débâcle; frai 18–<23 °C juin–juill.; pics de mouvement printemps/été-automne contre minimum hivernal. Le frai est une annotation — aucun bonus, aucune règle de garde (frai en diffusion)

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai du drum. Les chœurs de saison de frai suivent la saison de reproduction, pas le cycle lunaire; aucun terme lunaire n'en est inféré (et le chœur est un signal de rassemblement de frai, pas un signal d'alimentation). (Monographie du freshwater drum §§3.2/4)

about: The lake sturgeon is a living fossil and the giant of the Great Lakes and northern rivers — a huge, shark-tailed, bottom-rooting fish that can outlive the angler who catches it, with females not maturing until they are decades old. It's a cold-water traveller: telemetry in the research shows fish refusing shallow rapids below about 7 °C, building their spring runs as the water warms toward a spawning band of roughly 12–18 °C.

Sturgeon spawn in spring over rock in current, in famous congregations below rapids and dams, and spend the rest of the year vacuuming insect larvae, snails and small fish from the bottom of big lakes and rivers. Because they grow so slowly and spawn so late, most waters protect them carefully — check the rules before targeting. Anglers who do fish for them, where it's open, chase the heaviest, oldest fish in fresh water.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No lure is named for lake sturgeon in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here: the supported menu is bottom food — chironomids, burrowing mayflies of the Hexagenia kind, amphipods, crayfish and molluscs — found by a fish that feeds without sight, using barbels, taste, touch and electrosense over mud, sand and silt-clay. Bottom presentations carrying natural scent and flavour are the diet applied to tackle; visual flash is a language this fish does not feed by.

Know the selectivity under the generalist label: in the Ft. Loudoun juvenile work, chironomids were 93–96% of prey by number and were taken selectively, even where other invertebrates were abundant. Small and chironomid-like on the bottom is a measured starting point, not a guess.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Let the thermometer pace the search: adult movement tracks water temperature closely — the Black Lake telemetry correlation was about 0.94 — so each degree of spring warming is literally more fish moving, farther. Cover the staging water more widely as the water rises; fish it as a few holding spots while it stays cold.

Do not build the prespawn day around a feeding window: the only adult telemetry found no daily rhythm at all, and the model's adult shape is near-flat with only a slight night lean. Fish the hours you can fish, thoroughly — the adult record does not support waiting for dark.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If prespawn fish will not take, leave the spawning run its room anyway: only about 10–20% of adults spawn in any given season, the rest are feeding fish somewhere else in the system, and the honest move is to look for the non-spawning majority in holding and feeding water rather than pressing the concentrated travellers.

In the coldest prespawn water — below the roughly 6.8 °C movement line — expect fish to be where winter left them, moving little. Fish the deep pools slowly and close; covering water is a warm-water tactic.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: There is no spawn bait story to tell honestly: whether spawning sturgeon fast has never been measured for this species — no stomach or ration study spans the migration — so no spawn offering and no spawn suppression are invented here. Keep the bottom menu of the prespawn entry — chironomids and other benthic invertebrates — for the feeding, non-spawning share of the population.
