The same honesty runs the other way: with only 10–20% of adults spawning in a season, most fish in spawn-season water are not spawners at all, and a bottom offering fished in staging and feeding water is fishing for those fish — not a technique aimed at fish on the beds.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Handle spawn-season fish as the conservation block directs, because these are the breeders: keep the fish in the water, support it horizontally, never lift it by the gills or tail alone, and release it immediately. A female you release this spring may not spawn again for 4–9 years — the release, done right, is the whole value of the encounter.

Fish the spawn as a migration to intercept, not a bed to work: fish move up to the reaches, spawn, and disperse to feeding areas, and the telemetry pattern is travel and staging. The resting pools and slower holding water beside the runs are where a bottom presentation meets a fish that is pausing, not performing.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the spawn water is crowded with fish that will not take, remember the designations before you press harder: the Manitoba-relevant units — Nelson River, Red–Assiniboine–Lake Winnipeg, and Winnipeg River–English River among them — are assessed Endangered, within a national picture of Endangered (DU1–5), Special Concern (DU6–7) and Threatened (DU8). Concentrated spawners that refuse are a population to admire and leave; the feeders are the dispersed fish.

If nothing is on the reaches yet, check the temperature against the band: onset is near 10 °C and the main band is roughly 12–18 °C, falling with latitude. Early is a staging pattern in deep water below; late is a postspawn pattern — the calendar alone does not open this season.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Feed the recovering fish the full benthic menu: the Black Lake adult summer diet by biomass ran to Hexagenia burrowing mayflies, leeches, chironomids, crayfish and caddis larvae — a rich bottom menu over the muck and soft bottoms the fish prefer. Bottom offerings with natural scent, sized to that menu, are the supported pattern; no specific lure is named in the research.

Keep the offering on the bottom and in contact with it: this fish finds food by barbel chemistry, touch and electrosense, including prey hidden beneath sandy substrate. A presentation travelling up in the column is fishing past the senses that do the feeding.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Cover water now: summer-bound adults ranged widely in the telemetry record — daily movements ran from tens of metres to nearly 6.9 km, rising with temperature. A postspawn search is a mobile search along soft-bottom feeding water, not a vigil over one pool.

Do not wait for clear water — this fish is built for the opposite: sturgeon feed by smell, touch and electrosense, and in the controlled contrast, young fish foraged more at about 22.5 NTU than in clear water at 0.1 NTU. Postspawn fish in stained water are not disadvantaged feeders; fish the bottom food where it lives, clear or not.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If postspawn fish are scattered and hard to pin, that is the dispersal working: use the diet to find them — where burrowing mayflies and chironomids are thick in soft bottom, feeding sturgeon are plausible; over hard, clean bottom with little benthos, they are not.

A postspawn fish in poor condition is a fish to release fastest of all — in the water, supported horizontally, no lift by gills or tail. The rating brought you to an encounter; the conservation frame decides how it ends, every time.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer bottom menu, again with its selectivity: benthic invertebrates dominate wherever stomachs were taken, chironomids first in most systems, with amphipods, Hexagenia, crayfish and molluscs varying by water. Bottom offerings carrying natural scent, matched to the local benthos, are the supported summer pattern — no specific lure is named in the research, and none is invented here.

This is also a gorger — daily consumption in the juvenile ration work varied up to 15-fold day to day on patchy prey — so a blank hour beside a good one is this species' normal variance, not necessarily a wrong bait. Stay on good bottom longer than catfish habits suggest before you change anything.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Read every summer number here as the entry reads its own rating: this is a DERIVED set, capped at Low confidence. No measured adult feeding response exists for this species at any factor — the temperature curve is telemetry movement (correlation about 0.94) and laboratory physiology wearing an activity label, and the prose says so rather than dressing distribution up as a feeding study.

Fish the day straight through if you like: adults in the only adult telemetry study showed no daily rhythm, and the near-flat shape (day 0.75, night 1.0) is a slight lean built from conflicted evidence — juveniles are night-active in the lab and in northern gillnets, adults were not rhythmic at all. Never let anyone sell you a best-at-night claim as an adult pattern; this entry does not.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer fish shut down in a heat wave, believe the physiology: above the 16–19 °C plateau the curve falls through the suppression zone, and by the low 30s the juvenile chronic record shows feeding down 20–35% past about 31.7 °C and near zero close to the thermal maximum. There is no lethal point to quote — the thermal maximum is a juvenile range of about 33–35 °C and no adult lethal has been measured — so the honest move is cooler, deeper water, not a bigger offering.

If you do connect in the heat, shorten the encounter: warm water is already a physiological cost to this fish, so keep it in the water, support it horizontally, skip any lift by gills or tail, and release it immediately. In summer especially, the release is part of the pattern, not an afterthought.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The fall bottom menu is the summer menu cooling: chironomids, burrowing mayflies, amphipods and crayfish over soft bottom, taken by a fish whose consumption swings widely day to day. Keep natural bottom offerings on the feeding flats while the fish are still dispersed, and on the staging pools as they gather.

As the water cools toward the winter floor, slow the bottom presentation down with it: fall activity is a movement-and-temperature construction in the model, and cooling fish in the telemetry record move less and hold tighter. The menu does not change in fall; the delivery does.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Track the temperature down as you tracked it up: movement rose with temperature all year (correlation about 0.94), so cooling water means shorter moves and tighter groups. Slow the search through fall — by late fall you are fishing addresses, not covering water.

Stained fall water is not a sturgeon problem: the turbidity response is the model's only inverted one — foraging measured higher in turbid water than clear in the juvenile contrast, on a non-visual feeding mechanism — and the model's turbidity anchors stay flat-to-positive far beyond any visual fish's range. Fish the bottom food in the murk with confidence; clarity is for the angler, not the fish.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If early-fall fish have left the summer flats, follow the consolidation rather than changing baits: the chronology says dispersed feeding gives way to gathering, and a flat that was right in August is honestly empty in November.

If a fall fish is bound for a closed system, the closure travels with the water, not the season — the Winnipeg River has been closed to sturgeon fishing entirely since 1994. Check the system before the tackle, in fall as in every season.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Winter food is stomach-verified, not presumed: February Winnebago stomachs held chironomid-dominated benthic invertebrates, and Black Lake winter stomachs ran to crayfish and Hexagenia by biomass. Small-to-moderate natural bottom offerings, matching that menu, are the winter tackle the evidence supports — no winter lure is named in the research.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish winter as presence at a low rate: fed young fish in the laboratory still held food in the gut at 1 °C, so feeding persists — inside a movement bottleneck, at a fish that has down-regulated its metabolism for the season. Slow, close, patient presentations over the aggregation are the whole winter technique the record supports.

Winter encounters carry the same rule as summer ones: catch-and-release only in Manitoba, zero limit, fish kept in the water, supported horizontally, released immediately — and some systems, the Winnipeg River since 1994, are closed to fishing for them at all, ice included.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the winter pool is silent, do not conclude the fish are gone: movement at 0.2 km/day means the population is present and barely moving, and winter feeding, while real, has never had its rate measured. A blank day on a located aggregation is inside this species' evidence.

Know what the winter pattern rests on: one full-winter telemetry bottleneck study, corroborating movement lines, and stomachs from two systems. That is a real pattern with thin numbers — fish it, and hold it at the Low confidence the set itself carries.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Through the ice, stay on the stomach record: chironomids first, with crayfish and Hexagenia in the winter diet by biomass — natural bottom offerings presented right on the soft bottom over the aggregation. No ice-specific lure or presentation has ever been measured for this species, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Do not wait for dark under the ice: the under-ice daily shape has never been measured, so the ice shape here is the open-water shape carried across and flattened — and the one direct winter-encounter record, the February spear fishery on Lake Winnebago, shows fish moving beneath the ice in daylight. That fishery proves presence and daytime movement, not appetite — its harvest tracks water clarity, because spearers must see the fish — and this entry uses it for presence only.

Fish the aggregation, not the open basin: at about 0.2 km/day of mid-winter movement, a sturgeon pattern through the ice is a located pool fished patiently, with presentations kept close to fish that are barely travelling.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the ice pool is silent, the honest first suspect is rate, not location: winter feeding is verified as present and unmeasured as to amount, inside a derived set capped at Low. Give a located aggregation time across days before moving — and never read a silent week as proof the winter pool is empty.

Any fish that does come through the ice gets the full conservation handling, in the coldest conditions of the year: kept in the water as far as the hole allows, supported horizontally, never lifted by the gills or tail alone, and released immediately. A winter female may be decades old and years from her next spawning; the release is the point of the encounter.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn sturgeon are travellers held back by cold: telemetry fish made no movement through shallow rapids and falls below about 6.8 °C, and the spring pattern builds as the water climbs toward the roughly 10 °C spawning onset. Fish the deep holding water below the spawning reaches and the travel routes between winter and spawning water.

Fish this season as an encounter, not a harvest: in Manitoba lake sturgeon are catch-and-release only, with a zero daily and possession limit province-wide — every prespawn fish you meet is a fish to release. A big prespawn female may be well over 24 years old — that is the usual age of first maturity — and she spawns only once every 4–9 years.

The spawning reaches they are travelling toward are specific water: the 48-site record puts peak suitability at a depth-averaged flow near 0.6 m/s over cobble of about 64–256 mm, in roughly 0.55–0.85 m of water in smaller systems and 0.75–5.25 m in larger ones. Prespawn effort belongs in the staging water below that kind of reach, not on the cobble itself.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs April–June, starting near 10 °C with the main band at roughly 12–18 °C depending on latitude — and the conservation frame is part of the location, prominently: Manitoba is zero-limit catch-and-release only for this fish, province-wide, and the Winnipeg River has been under a full conservation closure since 1994, with no fishing for sturgeon at all in that system. A high rating in the spawn window is an activity rating, never a harvest opportunity.

Spawning fish are concentrated in shallow, fast water — the species at its most encounterable and its most protected at the same moment. Encounterability at the spawn is aggregation, not feeding, and this entry scores it as a location fact with no feeding bonus — and treats the beds themselves as water to stay off.

On the spawning reaches, the measured address is cobble of about 64–256 mm at a peak-suitability flow near 0.6 m/s, within a suitable band of roughly 0.5–1.5 m/s, in water from under a metre deep in smaller systems to several metres in large ones. Fish the staging and resting water beside that cobble, where travelling and spent fish hold, rather than the active bed.

movementSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: Post-spawn fish disperse to feeding areas — that is the telemetry chronology — and non-spawners, the majority in any year, never left the feeding water at all. The postspawn pattern is a spreading one: start near the spawning reaches and work outward into the summer feeding water as the days pass.

The release rule does not relax after the spawn: Manitoba's zero limit is province-wide and year-round, and a spent female leaving the beds may not spawn again for 4–9 years. Every postspawn encounter is still catch-and-release, handled in the water and let go at once.

The temperature is now entering the model's plateau at roughly 16–19 °C — the top of the agency preference family (about 10–18 °C) and the top of the spring migration band (13–19 °C). Postspawn fish in this band are the most active sturgeon of the year so far.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer is the feeding plateau — the model's July and August values are 1.0 — and it is also where the conservation frame must be read plainly, in the entry's own words: this is an encounter-and-release fish. Manitoba allows no recreational harvest, zero limit, catch-and-release only province-wide; COSEWIC assesses the western and Manitoba units Endangered (DU1–5), others Special Concern (DU6–7) and Threatened (DU8); and a summer rating is not a harvest opportunity in any water the app serves.

Summer adults ranged widely over soft bottom, with a Black Lake depth preference around 10.3 m over muck, tracking crayfish and mayfly food; in Lake Champlain, juveniles and adults overlapped in shallow water under 10 m through summer and fall. There is no single summer depth — there is soft bottom with benthic food, at the depth your system keeps it.

The plateau ends early for a fish this size: Manitoba laboratory fish showed metabolic suppression of about 28% at 20 °C and 42% at 24 °C against 16 °C fish, the northern population's stress threshold sat at 20 °C, and sustained 24 °C acclimation killed fish in the lab. In a hot summer, the pattern moves to the coolest deep water available — and the rating falls with the temperature, honestly.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall brings consolidation: fish feed through the summer plateau's tail (September's season value is 0.90), make fall tributary movements in regulated systems as flows rise, and then gather toward overwintering water as the temperature falls. Early fall is feeding water; late fall is the road to the winter pool.

In river systems the fall move is measured, not guessed: Missouri tributary fish made fall migrations at rising and high discharge, and South Saskatchewan fish were still moving about 0.9 km/day in November before the mid-winter collapse. Fish the travel routes and the deep pools they lead to while the move is on.

The fall fish are next year's — and next decade's — population: females mature most often at 24–26 years and spawn every 4–9 years, so an adult you release this fall carries spawning seasons far into the future. Manitoba's catch-and-release-only rule, zero limit province-wide, applies in fall exactly as in spring.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter sturgeon are an aggregation, not a population spread out: South Saskatchewan telemetry fish compressed into a single deep pool — under 0.1% of 1,100 km of available habitat — moving about 0.2 km/day from mid-November to mid-March against 0.9 km/day at the season's shoulders, with neighbours about 313 m apart instead of 575 m. Find the deep, slow winter pool and you have found the fish.

Hold the pattern loosely by system: in Lake Champlain, juveniles ranged wider in winter — some into water over 25 m deep, moving 18–34 km — while adults stayed shallow near the spawning-river mouth. Sedentary is the measured adult pattern; young fish in lake systems may be somewhere else entirely.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: The ice set for lake sturgeon is PROVISIONAL, at the Low confidence cap of a derived set, and the entry carries both flags openly: winter movement collapse and single-pool aggregation are telemetry-measured, and winter feeding is stomach-verified in two systems — February stomachs with chironomid-dominated contents, and Black Lake winter stomachs with crayfish and burrowing mayflies — but no under-ice daily rhythm, feeding-rate or oxygen-risk measurement exists for this species. Fish the deep, slow pool where the population gathered in the fall.

Ice season changes nothing about the frame: Manitoba is catch-and-release only, zero limit, province-wide, and the Winnipeg River has been under a full conservation closure since 1994 — no fishing for sturgeon there, through the ice or otherwise. An ice rating is an activity estimate for an encounter-and-release fish, not a harvest opportunity.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at after dark; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 16–19 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: Fronts, barometric pressure, wind and moon have never been tested for lake sturgeon feeding, activity or catch in any source the research could find — and the one tempting borrowing — another sturgeon's pressure-cued migration — was refused: different species, different endpoint. There is no front pattern for this fish. A front matters here only as the temperature change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: The night overlay is a warning against itself: young sturgeon foraged more at night in the lab, but the only adult telemetry found no daily rhythm, so the adult shape stays near-flat (night 1.0 against a day of 0.75 — a lean, not a pattern). Fish after dark if the day gave out; do not plan a sturgeon trip around a night bite that adult evidence does not show.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Aucune courbe d'OD comportementale ou d'alimentation juvénile/adulte n'existe. Les seules données de dose sont un défi aigu larvaire (tous les poissons morts sous 3 mg/L; mortalité à 3–4 mg/L confondue par le régime, 11.7% contre 83.3%) et un coût chronique de condition des âges-0 à 80% de saturation. Tirer des ancrages adultes de données aiguës larvaires fabriquerait une courbe. Zéro par absence de type de preuve.

Aucune mesure hivernale d'OD d'aucune sorte n'existe pour cette espèce (aucun gradient de mortalité hivernale, aucune occupation d'OD sous la glace). Zéro par absence; les poids de glace se réallouent à phase/température.

Jamais testé pour l'esturgeon jaune — aucun recensement de terrain, aucune expérience contrôlée. Le résultat de migration par pression barométrique d'un autre esturgeon est une espèce différente et un critère de migration et n'est pas utilisé. Zéro par absence.
Jamais testé pour l'alimentation, l'activité, le mouvement ou le frai de l'esturgeon jaune. Zéro par absence.

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou l'activité de l'esturgeon jaune. Aucun poids d'indicateur de programme n'est porté : pour un mangeur benthique profond non visuel, la médiation lumière/turbidité derrière les indicateurs des crapets n'a aucun mécanisme (précédent dérivé du lake-whitefish). windAnchors : null. Zéro par absence.
Jamais testé pour l'esturgeon jaune. frontExposure : 0. Zéro par absence (pas un nul mesuré).

Le débit est mesuré pour le frai et la migration (adéquation de pointe 0.6 m·s⁻¹, 48 sites) — le débit de frai n'est pas une réponse d'alimentation, aucune fonction alimentation-contre-débit n'existe, et le moteur n'a aucune entrée de décharge pour les lacs servis. Zéro par catégorie + absence d'entrée (cet ensemble ne parque délibérément pas un poids de débit qu'il ne peut pas noter).

L'alimentation est démontrablement conditionnée par la disponibilité des invertébrés benthiques (alimentation sélective en chironomides; variation de régime site/mois), mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure le benthos d'un plan d'eau; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.
La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour l'esturgeon jaune; pour un mangeur non visuel, elle entre, si jamais, seulement par le facteur journalier. Aucun terme de nuages autonome.
Aucune réponse à l'eau de fonte n'a été mesurée ou décrite pour cette espèce. Zéro par absence (le terme générique d'eau de fonte n'est pas porté dans un ensemble dérivé sans aucun ancrage d'espèce).

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn sturgeon are travellers held back by cold: telemetry fish made no movement through shallow rapids and falls below about 6.8 °C, and the spring pattern builds as the water climbs toward the roughly 10 °C spawning onset. Fish the deep holding water below the spawning reaches and the travel routes between winter and spawning water.

Fish this season as an encounter, not a harvest: in Manitoba lake sturgeon are catch-and-release only, with a zero daily and possession limit province-wide — every prespawn fish you meet is a fish to release. A big prespawn female may be well over 24 years old — that is the usual age of first maturity — and she spawns only once every 4–9 years.

The spawning reaches they are travelling toward are specific water: the 48-site record puts peak suitability at a depth-averaged flow near 0.6 m/s over cobble of about 64–256 mm, in roughly 0.55–0.85 m of water in smaller systems and 0.75–5.25 m in larger ones. Prespawn effort belongs in the staging water below that kind of reach, not on the cobble itself.

Let the thermometer pace the search: adult movement tracks water temperature closely — the Black Lake telemetry correlation was about 0.94 — so each degree of spring warming is literally more fish moving, farther. Cover the staging water more widely as the water rises; fish it as a few holding spots while it stays cold.

Do not build the prespawn day around a feeding window: the only adult telemetry found no daily rhythm at all, and the model's adult shape is near-flat with only a slight night lean. Fish the hours you can fish, thoroughly — the adult record does not support waiting for dark.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs April–June, starting near 10 °C with the main band at roughly 12–18 °C depending on latitude — and the conservation frame is part of the location, prominently: Manitoba is zero-limit catch-and-release only for this fish, province-wide, and the Winnipeg River has been under a full conservation closure since 1994, with no fishing for sturgeon at all in that system. A high rating in the spawn window is an activity rating, never a harvest opportunity.

Spawning fish are concentrated in shallow, fast water — the species at its most encounterable and its most protected at the same moment. Encounterability at the spawn is aggregation, not feeding, and this entry scores it as a location fact with no feeding bonus — and treats the beds themselves as water to stay off.

On the spawning reaches, the measured address is cobble of about 64–256 mm at a peak-suitability flow near 0.6 m/s, within a suitable band of roughly 0.5–1.5 m/s, in water from under a metre deep in smaller systems to several metres in large ones. Fish the staging and resting water beside that cobble, where travelling and spent fish hold, rather than the active bed.

Handle spawn-season fish as the conservation block directs, because these are the breeders: keep the fish in the water, support it horizontally, never lift it by the gills or tail alone, and release it immediately. A female you release this spring may not spawn again for 4–9 years — the release, done right, is the whole value of the encounter.

Fish the spawn as a migration to intercept, not a bed to work: fish move up to the reaches, spawn, and disperse to feeding areas, and the telemetry pattern is travel and staging. The resting pools and slower holding water beside the runs are where a bottom presentation meets a fish that is pausing, not performing.

spawningSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: Post-spawn fish disperse to feeding areas — that is the telemetry chronology — and non-spawners, the majority in any year, never left the feeding water at all. The postspawn pattern is a spreading one: start near the spawning reaches and work outward into the summer feeding water as the days pass.

The release rule does not relax after the spawn: Manitoba's zero limit is province-wide and year-round, and a spent female leaving the beds may not spawn again for 4–9 years. Every postspawn encounter is still catch-and-release, handled in the water and let go at once.

The temperature is now entering the model's plateau at roughly 16–19 °C — the top of the agency preference family (about 10–18 °C) and the top of the spring migration band (13–19 °C). Postspawn fish in this band are the most active sturgeon of the year so far.

Cover water now: summer-bound adults ranged widely in the telemetry record — daily movements ran from tens of metres to nearly 6.9 km, rising with temperature. A postspawn search is a mobile search along soft-bottom feeding water, not a vigil over one pool.

Do not wait for clear water — this fish is built for the opposite: sturgeon feed by smell, touch and electrosense, and in the controlled contrast, young fish foraged more at about 22.5 NTU than in clear water at 0.1 NTU. Postspawn fish in stained water are not disadvantaged feeders; fish the bottom food where it lives, clear or not.

about: The lake trout — mackinaw, togue, grey trout — is the deep-water char of the big northern lakes, a slow-growing giant of genuinely cold water. In the rating model its feeding peaks at just 8–12 °C, the coldest plateau in this library, and its whole year is organised around finding that cold, oxygenated layer and staying in it.

In spring, before the surface warms, lakers cruise the shallows and can be caught on light gear; by summer they're down in the thermocline, and in fall they broadcast their eggs over the same rocky reefs year after year, building no nest at all. Because they grow so slowly, a big lake trout is an old fish. Anglers target them for the deep, heavy fight and for the chance at the largest fish most northern lakes hold.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The Shield standard is a white or silver tube jig, 3–4 in — it matches their forage: ciscoes, whitefish and suckers, all streamlined, thin, soft-scaled and silvery-white. Scented tubes are the same profile. Where the forage is tiny shiners instead, small flutter spoons match better — lure size follows the forage, always.
Vertical jigging spoons and lead-heads of ½–1 oz in white or chartreuse are the other standard.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the tube through the whole column — hopping it, popping it, swimming it, on a ¼- to ⅜-oz head and 8–10 lb line. And learn the chase trigger: when a trout appears on the sonar below your bait, reel rapidly. A fleeing bait makes a lake trout commit.
Snap-jigging works the same nerve: snap hard, pause, let it fall — the hits come on the drop. With a heavy 1-oz head you can pound bottom on humps — dig a hole in it, in the old phrase.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If shallow spring fish won't go, they may already be deeper than you think. Drop down the first big break and jig the column there — the spring window closes from the top down.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The trolling spread: a Spin-N-Glo behind a herring dodger, a rotating flasher, or a Fish Flash — attractors in use since the early 1950s. Dodger colours: chartreuse and brushed stainless ('trash can'). The No. 2 Spin-N-Glo is the most popular size; Nos. 4, 2 and 0 produce most of the fish. Attractor size follows depth and clarity: 4–6 in attractors in shallow or very clear water, 6–8 in deeper or off-colour.
Vertical jigging works all summer too: the white tube through the column, and jigging spoons of ½–1 oz.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Leader length is the mood dial. Behind a herring dodger: 12–24 in of 20-lb fluorocarbon — 12–18 in gives a violent snap for active fish, toward 24 in a soft, slow target for lethargic ones. Behind a Fish Flash, leaders run 36–72 in. Speeds are specific: the herring dodger fishes at 1.6–2.0 mph and is very speed-sensitive; a rotating flasher at 2.0–2.8; a Fish Flash at 1.6–2.8.

'Skipping bottom' — ball and dodger ticking bottom every few feet — works over silt, sand and gravel; over chunk rock, hold a few feet off. When you change the spread, change spoon colour and pattern first, then brand and size; and treat glow and UV as separate colours in the rotation, not finishes.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: In the afternoon the canon flips: spoons outproduce flashers and flies — except for bottom-oriented lake trout, which stay a dodger fish. If the flashers stop producing by midday, pull them and run clean spoons or plugs.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Keep it simple on the shoals: a jig with a twister tail, the white tube, and spoons. The forage-matching rule still holds — silvery-white profiles over the rock.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the shoals and their edges through the column. Spawn-season trout are concentrated and findable — the year's best chance to fish them shallow without electronics doing the finding.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shoals are quiet, the fish are staging off them — drop to the first deep edge beside the spawning rock and jig there. They use the deep edge as a hallway to the shoal.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: A white tube jig, 3½–5 in, on a ¼- to ⅜-oz head — corkscrew-plummeted down, or rigged swimbait-style with the head outside. Rod: 34–36 in inside a shelter, 36–42 in in the open; 10–12 lb braid with about a metre of 10–12 lb mono.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the tube through the column and use the chase trigger — a trout on the sonar gets a rapidly reeled, fleeing bait. And when your partner hooks one, drop down a nearby hole (or the same one) immediately: the pack is there and feeding.
A spoon trick with real scent: run the treble through the head of a freshly snipped sucker minnow. Rattling lipless cranks (Rippin' Rap class) call trout in when they're in a chasing mood.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: The western system is the backup plan: humps topping out at 30–50 ft are the pattern from around Christmas — if the food-following hasn't produced, set up on a deep hump and jig the column there.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The white tube still leads — but past 50 ft, the tube gives way to the deep spoon: a Williams Ice Spoon, 2.25 or 3.25 in, half-gold/half-silver, is the proven deep-water bait.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Jig the whole column over the flats and saddles, drop to the spoon when the fish are deeper than 50 ft, and drop a second line the moment anyone hooks up — packs of three or four are still the rule.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Colour note, honestly regional: the Shield school fishes white, silver and clear-flake; the western school fishes drab green, brown and olive over kokanee forage. Use the school your water belongs to — the books disagree because their lakes do.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: White tube on a ¼- to ⅜-oz head, the deep spoon if they're holding over the drop. Same tackle as mid-winter.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the shallow flat for cruisers and the edge for the pack. Late-ice trout roam more — check the flat first, then the drop, then back.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Slide shallower before you slide deeper — late-ice trout are travelling toward the shallows, and the flat next to the drop is the last stop.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: Spring is the shallow season — before the surface warms, lake trout can be caught shallow, and right after turnover the water is one temperature top to bottom (around 39 °F at turnover), so the fish may be anywhere. Enjoy it: by mid-to-late June on classic trout water they're already 70–140 ft down.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer lake trout live in the thermocline band — the cold layer that still holds oxygen. That's the whole location rule: find the cold, oxygenated water and you're in their world. Where the bottom reaches that layer, the Great Lakes canon fishes them right on or near bottom.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: Fall is the spawn: rocky reefs and shoals less than 40 ft deep — sometimes a foot deep — the same reefs every year (lake trout build no redd; they broadcast over the rock). And in canoe country, the autumn feeding frenzy around those shoals is famous: a simple jig and twister tail is the premier lure of the season there.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace précoce
lines: Follow the food, not a depth — that's the ice rule from the best lake-trout ice angler of his generation, whose best hour ever came over 19 ft of water, and who took a giant over 28 ft. Bottom where the gobies are; mid-column where smelt and ciscoes cruise. Trout hunt in packs of three or four — the fish are where their food is, in groups.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace de mi-hiver
lines: By mid-January the western pattern shifts from humps to flats and saddles — still in the 30–50 ft band. Food is still the rule; the structure type changes, not the depth.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace tardive
lines: Late ice moves trout shallow — but stay near deep water: a flat of 10–15 ft right beside a 50 ft-plus drop is the classic late-ice setup.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light; quietest at after dark.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at first light; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 8–12 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Calm and bright, or when the fish ride high, the trolling canon says pull the dodgers — run clean spoons or plugs instead. Heavy flash is a low-light and deep-water tool.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: First light is the heavy-flasher shift: big flashers and flies lead the spread early, before the sun is up and the fish settle.

about: The lake whitefish is the great cold-water staple of the northern lakes — a silvery, small-mouthed member of the salmon family that has fed people and predators in the Great Lakes and the north for centuries. It's a deep-cold fish: the rating model peaks its feeding in water of just 6–12 °C, and summer finds it down in the same cold, oxygenated depths as lake trout.

Whitefish feed mostly on the bottom — insect larvae, snails, tiny clams and crustaceans sucked up with their underslung mouths — and move shoreward in fall to spawn over rock and gravel as the water cools. They are a premier commercial and table fish, smoked whitefish being a northern institution. Anglers target them through the ice and in cold open water, for numbers, for the smoker, and for a delicate fight on light gear.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the measured diet, because it is the firmest tackle fact this species has: a benthic invertebrate menu — chironomids, Chaoborus, gastropods and sphaeriid clams — taken off and just above the bottom. The finest-scale study watched whitefish make foraging forays for exactly those chironomids and Chaoborus (Rodrigues et al. 2022). No lure or bait is named for lake whitefish anywhere in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here; small bottom presentations sized to that invertebrate menu are the whole supported statement.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the bottom thoroughly and let the distribution do the work: this is a benthopelagic fish whose finest study found activity tracking habitat, not the clock — vertical movement ran 502.5 m a day under high habitat constraint against 81.2 m a day under moderate constraint (Rodrigues et al. 2022) — so a spring whitefish's day is organised by where its cold, food-bearing bottom is, not by a feeding hour. Cover the shore-zone bottom in the occupied band before you worry about timing.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shore zone is quiet, the honest check is depth and bottom contact, not a new tactic: spring occupancy ran 10–25 m and bottom-oriented in the isothermal study lake, and a presentation that is not spending its time on or within a step of the bottom is not fishing the water these fish were measured in.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The benthic menu again — chironomids, Chaoborus, gastropods, sphaeriids — fished on the wash-zone bottom where the summer fish hold. Summer adds one distribution fact to the presentation: the Erie telemetry watched whitefish occupy a cool, well-oxygenated part of the deep layer in stratification (Kraus et al. 2023), so summer presentations belong in the cold water that still carries oxygen where the lake offers both — while the oxygen entry in the tough section below explains why that is a preference to fish by, never a threshold to quote.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the cold bottom persistently rather than by the clock, for the reason the spring entry gives: no stomach-based study of when adult whitefish feed exists at all, and the movement programmes that do exist disagree about the daily phase (see the light overlays). What summer telemetry does support is position discipline: stay on the thermocline–substrate intersection as it shifts, because the occupied band is only a few degrees wide at its core and the fish track it — late-July Huron fish sat at 25.1 m and 10.2 °C, in the layer, not at a fixed depth (Bergstedt et al. 2016). Find the layer on the sounder each trip; last month's depth is not this month's address.

That no-feeding-hour finding is worth its own line because it disciplines every summer hour, on any water: no stomach-based study of when adult whitefish feed exists at all, and the movement programmes that do exist disagree about the daily phase (see the light overlays) — so summer whitefish are fished by position, not by the clock. Keep the benthic presentation on the bottom in the coldest water available, cover it thoroughly, and let coverage do what timing cannot be shown to do.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the cold layer is not producing, check the oxygen story before you move lakes — and check it in this species' own terms, not a trout's: when the ELA lake forced a choice, whitefish chose cold over oxygen outright, with 51% of detections below 4 mg/L against only 4% warmer than 10 °C, and 51–87% of detections in water under 2 mg/L under severe constraint (Rodrigues et al. 2022). The rule that whitefish need 4 mg/L or better comes from another species' study — the source paper itself flags it — and this species' own fish routinely live below it. Erie fish leaned the other way, toward well-oxygenated water — the direction is population-dependent, kept unmerged in the study — so the practical rule is only this: do not abandon cold water merely because a borrowed oxygen threshold says the fish cannot be there. In an ELA-type lake, they demonstrably can.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The benthic invertebrate menu, unchanged — chironomids, Chaoborus, gastropods, sphaeriids, on bottom. Nothing fall-specific is measured in this species' diet, and this entry does not borrow a fall pattern from any other fish to fill the space.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the cooling as the schedule: the spawn is temperature-triggered (agency profiles put the trigger below 8 °C, the Maine work watched onset as the water fell through about 5–6 °C), so each cold step moves staging fish closer to the shallows. Work the shoal edges progressively shallower as the water falls through 10 °C toward 6 °C, and expect the feeding pattern to give way to the aggregation pattern described in the next entry once the window opens.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall fish are scattered, remember this population's measured width: occupancy envelopes in the studies run 6–32 m at the 50% level in summer (Challice et al. 2019) and 10–25 m through the isothermal season — staging whitefish use a broad shore band, not a single reef. Cover the band's bottom systematically before concluding the lake is between patterns.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Nothing spawn-specific is named in the whitefish literature — no egg presentation, no spawning lure — and none is invented here. On the shoal edges, the supported offering remains the benthic menu the diet studies measure. Presentations over the spawning rock itself are not a tactic this library can source for this species.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the aggregation's own rhythm, which is measured even though its feeding is not: site use builds over the 48 days to a week-long peak plateau rather than spiking for a night or two, so the season rewards returning to a known shoal across the window instead of chasing a single predicted peak day. Within the day, the spawning study is also the one place a daily movement pattern IS measured for this species: both sexes held shallower at night and deeper by day on the spawning grounds (Ryther et al. 2024) — a spawn-window result, stated as one, and not evidence about feeding hours in any other season.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shoals hold fish that will not respond, that is consistent with everything the study can and cannot say: an aggregation whose feeding has never been measured. Move off the rock to the first bottom at the shoal's edge and fish the benthic menu there — the staging and post-spawn fish around an aggregation are the defensible target, and the window is long enough (mid-October into December) that the edges fish for weeks.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The winter diet note in the record is a diet note and is used as one: the Champlain winter diet ran to gastropods and sphaeriid clams — the benthic menu at its hardest-shelled end. Small bottom presentations on the shore-zone bottom remain the whole supported tackle statement; no winter lure is named in the research.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish slowly and cover bottom: at half the open-water activity level, a winter whitefish is a fish to be found by position, not provoked by pace. The winter telemetry adds that the daily vertical pattern was at its weakest of the whole year in winter (Gorsky et al. 2012) — winter is the season where hour-of-day matters least for this fish on any evidence, so spend the effort on the bottom band instead of the clock.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A quiet winter shore zone is the species at its measured rate, not necessarily a wrong spot: half activity across a whole season means half the encounters, and the telemetry winters show individual fish settling into divergent winter strategies — some deep, some shallow (Rodrigues et al. 2022) — so a blank at one depth band is worth one move to the other band before it is worth leaving.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The benthic menu through the ice — chironomids, Chaoborus, gastropods, sphaeriids — presented on the bottom. The one positional fact in the angler record is consistent with the bottom-oriented telemetry: the Gull Lake, Alberta account has the fish holding 1–3 ft off bottom, with most action before noon (Grade C consensus, labelled as such). No ice lure or jig is named in the whitefish research, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the early-ice shoals at the morning end of the day, held loosely: the morning lean in this species' ice pattern comes from creel and angler consensus (the Simcoe dawn-to-noon emphasis, the Gull Lake before-noon account), not from any measurement, and the telemetry says the winter daily pattern is the weakest of the year. Morning is a lean, not a rule — a first-ice fishery rewards being on the proven shoal more than being there at a proven hour, because no proven hour exists.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shallow shoals are blank, go to the telemetry depth before you go home: Clear Lake fish held about 15 m (a 12–17 m band) at 2–3 °C for the December–April winter. Early-ice depth disagreement between the creel lake and the telemetry lake is real and unresolved in the study; fishing both bands is the honest response to it.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The benthic menu on bottom, unchanged — the ELA work watched these fish making foraging forays for chironomids and Chaoborus even into the low-oxygen deep water, which is the closest thing to a measured under-ice feeding fact this species has: the food is benthic invertebrates, the fish go to the bottom to get it, and the presentation belongs there with it.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Settle on a band and fish it thoroughly: at half activity with the year's weakest daily pattern, mid-winter whitefish are a position fishery. The morning lean from the creel consensus (dawn to noon on Simcoe) is the only timing guidance that exists and it is Grade C — worth fishing, not worth planning a day around to the exclusion of the depth work, which is where the telemetry says the variance actually lives.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If one depth band is dead, switch bands rather than presentations: the measured winter pattern is two coexisting strategies, deep and shallow, so a silent deep set genuinely does not clear the shallow shoals in the same lake on the same day — and the reverse is equally true. Cover both bands across a mid-winter session before calling the lake off.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The benthic menu, on bottom, at the deep band. No late-ice-specific presentation exists in the whitefish research — no meltwater or inflow response has ever been studied in this species, so this entry offers no late-ice inflow tactic rather than borrowing one from another fish, whose meltwater responses are their own measurements and not this fish's.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the deep band patiently through the morning lean and do not shorten the session on clock logic: winter's daily pattern is the year's weakest in the telemetry, activity is at half rate, and late-ice success in the creel record is a season-long accumulation on known deep structure. This is the season phase where the forty-year Simcoe series says the fishery itself peaks — the winter catch there vastly exceeds the summer catch, and whitefish are primarily an ice-fishery target in that system — so late ice is not this species' leftover season; on the creel evidence it is close to its main one.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the deep band is silent, work back up the winter bands in order — deep telemetry band, then the shallow winter strategy band — before changing lakes: the split-strategy winter (Rodrigues et al. 2022) means a late-ice population can be sitting a full band away from where the shape support points, in the same lake, for reasons no study explains. Band coverage is the whole late-ice adjustment this species' evidence supports.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: Start with what kind of entry this is, because it governs everything below: lake whitefish tactics rest on distribution — seven telemetry programmes, hydroacoustics and a forty-year winter creel — and there is no measured feeding response for this species at any factor, so these entries tell you where the fish demonstrably are and when they demonstrably move, and claim nothing finer. In spring the distribution is the isothermal one: in eastern Lake Ontario, fish used the shore water at 10–25 m, predominantly bottom-oriented, through the whole October–May isothermal season (Hlina et al. 2026), and the Michigan archival tags put spring occupancy anywhere in 0–20 °C water as the lake mixes. Spring whitefish are bottom fish spread through the cold shore zone — fish the bottom in that band, not a temperature hunt.

Activity is climbing out of the winter floor: winter activity ran at roughly half the spring, summer and fall level in the Clear Lake telemetry (Gorsky et al. 2012), so spring is a genuine recovery season — the fish are moving and feeding again at open-water rates after the ice, on the bottom structure of the shore zone.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer is the cold-water distribution season, and the convergence across five programmes is the strongest thing this species has: in the Experimental Lakes Area study (856,606 detections), stratified-period occupied water sat in an interquartile range of just 5.3–7.9 °C with a year-round mean of 5.8 °C and under 15% of detections warmer than 10 °C even when reaching cold water meant tolerating low oxygen (Rodrigues et al. 2022); Huron fish were rarely over 12 °C at any time of year, with July–September occupied means of 8.7–10.2 °C (Bergstedt et al. 2016); and the Algonquin occupancy model put summer probability over 75% at 7.7–13.6 °C and 10–29 m, with the fish holding at the thermocline–substrate wash zone where the cold layer meets bottom (Challice et al. 2019). Fish that wash zone — cold water ON bottom — and you are fishing the measured summer address in three independent systems.

State the width honestly alongside the core: Michigan summer occupancy ran 4–21.5 °C with a mean of 10.8 °C, and 58% of summer observations fell outside the textbook 10–14 °C optimal band (Reed et al. 2023). The core is cold and narrow; the tails are real. Fish the core first, but a warm-side blank does not prove the lake is empty — it may hold the wide part of this population's distribution. And do not let anyone anchor this fish warm on the laboratory number: the measured juvenile growth optimum is 18.5 °C (Edsall 1999), a different life stage sitting about 5 °C above where adults actually live, and it is ledgered in the study as do-not-use for adult fishing.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is the run-up to the spawn, and the staging distribution is the isothermal one returning: as stratification breaks down the Ontario fish came back to the shore zone at 10–25 m, bottom-oriented (Hlina et al. 2026), and Michigan fall occupancy ran 4–21 °C as the lake cooled through the band the fish prefer (Reed et al. 2023). Activity holds at full open-water level until the spawn window itself (Gorsky et al. 2012) — fall is a feeding season on the shore-zone bottom, fished like spring in reverse, with the spawning shallows about to matter.

Know the spawning address before you need it: spawning runs mid-October to early/mid-December at under 10 °C, typically as the water drops below 6 °C, in under 9 m over hard substrate on the agency profile, and in the Georgian Bay positioning study generally in under 5 m over rock and cobble (Ryther et al. 2024). The staging fish are on the bottom off that hard, shallow ground — fish the deep edge of the spawning shoals while the water is still above the trigger.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: The spawn is this species' best-documented event: a 48-day season in the Georgian Bay positioning study, with bell-shaped site occupancy, a plateau of about a week at its peak, males arriving first, and spawning generally in under 5 m over rock and cobble (Ryther et al. 2024); Clear Lake onset was watched on 5 November at 5 °C, with eggs still being collected under the ice on 11 December, and the full observed spawning range runs 0.5–10 °C. The honest framing matches the brown trout rule in this library: spawning feeding suppression has never been measured in whitefish — the season model's November dip is its softest number, flagged as such in the study — so this is an aggregation entry, not a feeding entry. The fish are findable, concentrated and shallow; whether the ones on the rock are feeding is a question the research does not answer, and the feeders are best sought on the bottom at the shoals' edges.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Open winter water is the floor of this fish's year: winter activity ran at roughly half the spring, summer and fall level (Gorsky et al. 2012) and the season values sit near 0.55 against the summer peak — reduced, not absent. The winter distribution on the measured lakes is the isothermal shore zone (10–25 m, bottom-oriented, October–May in the Ontario study), and the through-ice pattern is covered in the ice entry below; in open cold water, fish that same shore-zone bottom and expect a half-rate fishery.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace précoce
lines: PROVISIONAL — the whole ice set for this species is provisional, and this entry says so the way the study does: it rests on two full-winter telemetry datasets and a long winter creel, with no under-ice feeding or daily-feeding study anywhere behind it. First ice follows hard on the spawn — a minor through-ice fishery on Lake Winnipeg began soon after freeze-up, immediately post-spawn (Kennedy 1938) — and the shape support from the forty-year Simcoe winter fishery puts early-ice fish on humps and shoals at about 6 m. Treat those Simcoe depths as one shallow, productive lake's description, never as a species parameter: the telemetry lakes put winter fish deeper (about 15 m in Clear Lake). Fish the shallow structure near the spawning shoals first, at your own lake's early-ice depths.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace de mi-hiver
lines: Mid-winter is the telemetry season: Clear Lake fish held about 15 m at 2–3 °C under ice from December to April, at roughly half the open-water activity level (Gorsky et al. 2012), while the ELA winter showed the population splitting — two of five fish wintering deep (an 8.6–11.1 m band) while three held shallow (3.3–4.6 m) — divergent individual strategies in the same lake in the same winter (Rodrigues et al. 2022). The Simcoe shape support deepens fish toward about 30 m by late ice. There is no single mid-winter depth for this species on its own evidence; there are bands, and the fish are on bottom in one of them.

Oxygen belongs in a mid-winter where, stated in this species' measured terms: deep-water low oxygen persisted all winter in the ELA lake, and two of its five fish wintered for stretches in water averaging under 4 mg/L — some individuals in that study wintered routinely below 2 mg/L (Rodrigues et al. 2022). Do not cross deep winter structure off your map on a borrowed oxygen threshold; whitefish were measured living the winter in water another fish's rule would call empty.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace tardive
lines: Late ice carries the Simcoe shape to its deep end — fish deepening toward about 30 m later in the season, with that fishery's peak running late January to mid-February (Grade C shape support from the creel lake, stated as such) — against the telemetry lakes holding their winter bands (about 15 m in Clear Lake; the split deep/shallow strategies in the ELA). The defensible late-ice where is the deep end of YOUR lake's winter band, on bottom: the pattern the sources agree on is deepening and bottom orientation, while every absolute depth in the record belongs to one named lake and travels no further than this sentence.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at first light; quietest around midday and after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 6–12 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The morning lean, stated at exactly its strength: the model's clock for this species is near-flat and morning-leaning (dawn 0.9, day 0.65, dusk 0.8, night 0.75) because the evidence is genuinely split — one occupancy study found greater detection and activity in the morning than the afternoon with NO significant daily vertical movement at all (Challice et al. 2019), and the angler consensus (Simcoe's dawn-to-noon emphasis, the Gull Lake before-noon account) leans the same way. Fish dawn as the best-supported single window if you fish a window — and know that a window is all it is: no study has ever measured when adult whitefish feed, by stomach or otherwise, so anyone's dawn rule for this fish, including this one, is a lean on movement and catch records, not a feeding fact.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is where this entry is most careful, because the programmes conflict and the conflict is the finding: Lake Superior's trawl and hydroacoustic work found a diel BANK migration — deeper by day, shallower at night, staying near bottom, and explicitly NOT a vertical migration into open water (Gorman et al. 2012) — and Clear Lake fish rose in the column at night in spring and fall (Gorsky et al. 2012), while the Algonquin programme found no significant daily vertical movement at all. The supported night tactic is narrow: in systems where whitefish use a shallower night bank, they come to it along the bottom, so a night session fishes the shallow end of the day's bottom band — it does not suspend presentations in mid-water, and it does not reposition the whole day on a clock that two of the best programmes could not find.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Aucun test de vent pour le lake whitefish n'existe par aucune méthode — cherché exhaustivement 2026-11-06.
Aucun test de front n'existe. Les revendications génériques des guides sur la pression barométrique sont du folklore grade D et ne sont pas des sources.
Aucun test de pression n'existe par aucune méthode — aucun effet ajusté.
Aucune étude NTU/Secchi d'alimentation, de distance réactive ou de capture n'existe pour ce benthivore visuel — lacune honnête, pas un petit nombre.

Le seul résultat sur la lune est une étude au filet maillant de 1979 : les captures tombaient à la pleine lune dans les deux types de filets, attribué par les auteurs à la visibilité accrue du filet — un artefact d'engin, pas de l'alimentation. Mis en quarantaine comme tout autre effet lunaire d'artefact d'engin dans le programme.

Le régime est des invertébrés benthiques (chironomides, Chaoborus, gastéropodes, sphaériidés) mais le moteur n'a aucune entrée de proies benthiques et aucune fonction de réponse densité-de-proies n'existe. Aucun a priori de couche de proies d'une autre espèce n'a d'analogue chez le whitefish.
Réponse de transmission de lumière neige/glace non mesurée pour le whitefish (physique réelle, réponse du poisson inconnue) — non ajustée (cf. patron SPEC GAP G14).
Aucune étude de réponse aux apports/eau de fonte en fin de glace n'existe pour le whitefish.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: The spawn is this species' best-documented event: a 48-day season in the Georgian Bay positioning study, with bell-shaped site occupancy, a plateau of about a week at its peak, males arriving first, and spawning generally in under 5 m over rock and cobble (Ryther et al. 2024); Clear Lake onset was watched on 5 November at 5 °C, with eggs still being collected under the ice on 11 December, and the full observed spawning range runs 0.5–10 °C. The honest framing matches the brown trout rule in this library: spawning feeding suppression has never been measured in whitefish — the season model's November dip is its softest number, flagged as such in the study — so this is an aggregation entry, not a feeding entry. The fish are findable, concentrated and shallow; whether the ones on the rock are feeding is a question the research does not answer, and the feeders are best sought on the bottom at the shoals' edges.

Fish the aggregation's own rhythm, which is measured even though its feeding is not: site use builds over the 48 days to a week-long peak plateau rather than spiking for a night or two, so the season rewards returning to a known shoal across the window instead of chasing a single predicted peak day. Within the day, the spawning study is also the one place a daily movement pattern IS measured for this species: both sexes held shallower at night and deeper by day on the spawning grounds (Ryther et al. 2024) — a spawn-window result, stated as one, and not evidence about feeding hours in any other season.

spawningSources.citation: Gorsky et al. 2012 (activité hivernale ~la moitié des autres saisons); Ryther et al. 2024 (saison de frai de 48 jours dans la baie Georgienne, <5 m, roche/galets); agence du Maine 2021 (début 5 nov. à 5 °C); profil du MPO (frai sept.–déc., déclencheur <8 °C). Magnitude de novembre signalée molle : suppression d'alimentation au frai non mesurée.
Mécanique de l'étude sur la glace (durée du jour comme signal saisonnier sous la glace), appliquée à un benthivore d'eau froide qui fraie à l'automne.

about: The largemouth is the warm-water bass of the weeds and the shallows — the widest mouth, the deepest green, and a temperament that treats anything alive near cover as food. Of the black basses it wants the warmest water: the rating model puts its feeding peak in the high twenties Celsius, and it tolerates heat that shuts most other species down.

Largemouth live tight to things — lily pads, weed edges, docks, fallen trees and stump fields — in water often just a few feet deep, spawning on visible beds in protected flats each spring. They are ambush feeders that rarely chase far, which is why they're fished slowly and precisely. Anglers target them for the topwater explosion, the close-quarters fight in heavy cover, and because almost every farm pond and backwater in the south holds them.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: A suspending jerkbait is the favourite winter artificial of the power-fishing school — toward the upper end of the cold range, a crankbait joins it. With a jig: in clear lakes, a heavy 3/4- to 1-oz green pumpkin football jig; in murky water, a ½-oz black-and-blue flipping jig on steep channel banks.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Drag the football jig slowly on points, humps and rockpiles. Cold bass target small prey — if you're not getting bit, trim the jig's skirt and downsize the trailer before you change spots.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Go smaller and slower still, and fish the warmest bank you can find. In near-freezing water a bass may inspect a bait for a long time — the pause is the presentation.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Search with power first: a lipless crankbait combs the expanses, and in stained prespawn water a deep crawfish-pattern crankbait rooted along the bottom is the classic. For the staged fish, flip a ½-oz jig in a Texas craw colour to the outside corners of dock pilings.
Three jig colours cover 90% of everything for the jig school: black-and-blue, green pumpkin, Texas craw. Depth is the critical variable — get it right before you worry about anything else.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The general sequence: search fast to find them, then slow down on them. Watch how the fish are hooked — a bass hooked outside the mouth, or lost fish, is the signal to change colour, not location.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Slow down on the staging cover itself — isolated stumps and dock corners beside the coves, pitched at precisely, more than once. Prespawn fish on a spot are worth repeated exact casts.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: For bedding fish, a jig worked so the skirt writhes while the head stays pinned in place — the movement is in the tip of the rod, not the retrieve. Soft plastics that stay in front of a guarding fish do the same job.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: On a bed, patience and precision beat variety: put the bait in the bed and keep it there, shaking it in place. Off the beds, the prespawn pattern is still running a cast away in slightly deeper water.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If bed fish won't commit, leave them and fish the staging cover — you'll catch more and bother the spawn less. Come back to the stubborn ones with the light change at the end of the day.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Baits that stay in the strike zone instead of falling through it: walking topwaters, soft jerkbaits, stickworms, drop-shot rigs — presentations that hang high in the column where the resting fish are.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish high and slow around the vertical cover, shade side first. A postspawn bass near the surface will rise a few inches for a bait that hovers; it won't dive for one that sinks past.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the resting fish refuse everything, go back to prespawn water — the earliest spawners are already recovered and feeding there while the late spawners rest.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Pitch and punch: a 1-oz jig punched through the mats on braid, jigs and soft plastics along the outside edge. Crankbaits should run slightly deeper than the water you're fishing so they stay in contact and rip free through the weed tops.

Blades follow conditions: Colorado blades for vibration and thump in cold, stained water and low light; willow blades for flash in clear, warm, baitfish situations; a tandem for stained water in the in-between temperatures.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Flipping rules: most strikes come on the first fall, so the jig must fall vertically on slight slack — then shake it twice and feel. Heavy line is part of the technique: 25-lb fluorocarbon in cover, 60-lb braid in the extreme stuff.

For big bass specifically, the old masters' rule runs against the power game: big bass come on quiet, slow baits — worms, tubes, jigs, grubs — presented with more triggering quality than attraction: small, natural, with eyespots and a random bottom-contact action.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: When the weedline goes quiet at midday, the fish haven't left — they're in the thickest, shadiest part of it. Punch the mat itself, or wait for low light and fish the outside edge with topwater: dawn, dusk and overcast are topwater's hours.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Shallow and medium crankbaits matched to the local baitfish's size, square-bills bounced tentatively through riprap and stumps, and always a noisy chugger tied on in fall — the books insist on the chugger. Match the forage's belly and back colours to your lake's bluegill and shiners.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Keep lures off the bottom — fall baitfish suspend, and so do the bass. Pay more attention to where the baitfish are than to the surface temperature; the bait map is the bass map now.
A white 3/4-oz jig with a chunk trailer, counted down to the baitfish's depth and swum with a slow, constant retrieve, is the jig school's fall play.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Turnover — when the water's in the low 60s to upper 50s °F — is short and difficult fishing. It stabilizes in the low to mid 50s; if you're in the churn, fish the clearest, most stable water you can find and slow down.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Medium crankbaits at baitfish depth, the counted-down white jig swum slowly, and the chugger whenever the light is low or the surface is broken.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Swim baits at the bait's level, not on the bottom. As the water drops through the 50s °F, slow the whole programme down a step at a time.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Fronts in fall are not the enemy they are in spring — one veteran calls fall fronts a good thing for bass. If a front just passed, stay on the bait instead of retreating to deep water.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The winter kit arriving early: suspending jerkbaits, heavy football jigs dragged slowly, and crankbaits only on the warmer afternoons.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Drag slowly, pause long, and fish the warmest part of the day. The year's metabolism is winding down — match it.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Downsize the trailer and trim the skirt. Late-fall bass target smaller prey, and a smaller profile is often the whole fix.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The one book teaching there is: ice-bound bass can be tempted with a small jig or live bait. Small is the operative word — winter bass target small prey in everything the books describe.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish it small, slow and close to the bottom over the deep flats near spring structure — and give late ice a second look, when the season's second activity window opens.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If mid-winter bass won't go, that's the season, not your technique — the books describe this as their least active time of year. Save the effort for early and late ice.

movementSeasons.heading: Début de printemps
lines: The year's coldest bass live in the deepest water they'll use — on natural lakes, the deep flats and basins in about 15–30 ft. Structure is vertical and fast-sloping, close to a flat, and northern banks are warmest. Avoid water a cold north wind is hitting. This is the least active bass fishing of the year, and it's a patience game.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn bass travel: from the ends of winter bluffs along migration routes — ditches, contours, tapering points, fallen trees — toward the spawning flats. They stage on isolated cover beside sheltered coves: stumps in murky lakes, and the boat docks near cove entrances.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning bass are on flat, protected water — 10 ft or less on natural lakes — on beds you can often see. The biggest bass spawn first. Worth knowing: one of the great power fishermen personally skips the beds and stays with prespawn fish, which are more aggressive and heavier.

movementSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: Postspawn is a real tough time — the books say so plainly. The fish rest at vertical cover: dock pilings, submerged bushes, standing-tree trunks — and they suspend near the surface, sunning themselves, close to the bedding areas. The shady side of the rest stations — flooded bushes, stumps, laydowns, weed patches — fishes first.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: On northern natural lakes, summer largemouth are a weedline story — the whole game. The outside edge of the weeds, down to 20 ft and more, with the inside corners, dips and deeper cuts in the line as the prime ambush points. Weeds' irregularities — holes, pockets, points in the grass — are where the fish are.

movementSeasons.heading: Début d’automne
lines: Fall is the most baitfish-oriented season of the year, and our lakes have no shad — here, bass feed on bluegill and shiners, and both are grass-oriented. So fall largemouth are in the weedy areas with their food, not chasing open-water bait.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Cooling fall water keeps bass on the baitfish in the grass — weedy areas, weedline edges, and any shore the bait is using. It's still a baitfish season first and a temperature season second.

movementSeasons.heading: Fin d’automne
lines: Late-fall bass slide toward winter: the deepest structure near the remaining green weeds, steep banks and the basins they'll winter in — 15–30 ft on natural lakes. Northern banks still warm fastest on sunny days.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: Through the ice, bass winter in the deepest water of their year — deep flats and basins, 15–30 ft on natural lakes, near the cover they'll use in spring. They're most active in the first weeks after freeze-up and again at late ice; the middle of winter is their quietest time.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 26–30 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 37 °C, from the species' research file.
Wind: this species' feeding holds up best with wind 10–12 km/h — its own measured wind curve, not a generic one.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: Post-front on northern lakes, the pro pattern is cabbage-topped points and outside weedlines in 15–18 ft — locate them with a deep crankbait (DT16 class), then milk the spot with a jig or soft bait.

Here the books honestly disagree, and both camps catch fish — pick a style and commit. Camp one, 'slow and low': after a front the bass tuck tight to the thickest cover and the strike zone shrinks to inches, so fish the lightest weight that still penetrates the cover and make five or six precise casts to one spot before moving. Camp two, the dissent: burn a spinnerbait or lipless crankbait fast on a high trolling motor, hunting one fish willing to react, just to locate them — then slow down on whatever you find.

One researcher's caution is worth hearing: in his field log, no direct link between pressure itself and bass activity ever showed up — what changed behaviour was the weather that came with it. Fish the conditions, not the barometer.

weatherOverlays.heading: Avant l’arrivée d’un front
lines: Ahead of a front is the time the power game shines — search fast, cover the migration routes and staging cover, and pin down where the fish are before the change scatters your pattern.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Strong wind flips vegetation fish ON: work suspending jerkbaits slashed under the wave troughs and Colorado-blade spinnerbaits along the wind-beaten weedlines. Wind is a trigger for largemouth, not a problem.

weatherOverlays.heading: Couvert
lines: Overcast stretches everything — topwater and shallow baits that are dawn-only on bright days keep working. In one long-term field log, bass fed at notably higher rates under overcast than under clear skies; treat that as one man's careful observation, but the topwater extension is standard teaching.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Bright and calm in summer means the fish are deep in the weeds or under the mats at midday. Fish the shade — under mats, under docks, the shaded side of every piece of cover.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Early and late are topwater's shift — walking baits over the postspawn cover in clear water, and noisy baits along the weedlines. Have the topwater rod rigged before the light changes.

Aucun paramètre de turbidité d'achigan n'existe dans la base de preuves; rien n'est emprunté de la truite.
Aucun paramètre lunaire d'achigan ne survit à la cotation.

The general sequence: search fast to find them, then slow down on them. Watch how the fish are hooked — a bass hooked outside the mouth, or lost fish, is the signal to change colour, not location.
