The fish rest at vertical cover: dock pilings, submerged bushes, standing-tree trunks — and they suspend near the surface, sunning themselves, close to the bedding areas. The shady side of the rest stations — flooded bushes, stumps, laydowns, weed patches — fishes first.
Fish high and slow around the vertical cover, shade side first. A postspawn bass near the surface will rise a few inches for a bait that hovers; it won't dive for one that sinks past.

about: The mooneye is a silvery, herring-like fish of big northern rivers and lakes — the Red, the Assiniboine, the Winnipeg system — named for its large, bright eye, and a relative of the goldeye it so closely resembles. It's a measured fish in the research: stomachs were fullest in April and May in the Assiniboine programme, growth fastest June through August, and Manitoba's angling peak runs late summer into fall on the Winnipeg system.

Mooneye spawn by broadcasting eggs over shoals to drift into quiet water — no nest, no guarding — and feed at the surface and mid-depths on insects and small fish, often rising in the evening like trout. That surface feeding is their gift to anglers: mooneye take dry flies and small spinners, fight on light tackle like small salmon, and are targeted by fly fishers on prairie rivers as a homegrown rising fish.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The spring menu is the measured one: corixids dominate the Assiniboine stomach record, with adult beetles, adult and larval mayflies, midges and crustaceans behind them — small insect-profile offerings, fished at and near the surface where this surface feeder works, are the diet-supported pattern. No lure is named in the mooneye literature, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the light change at the end of the day hardest: the dusk-led timing in this entry is agency consensus backed by measured eye anatomy (a grouped, rod-rich retina with a reflective tapetum — hardware for low-light feeding), not a stomach-measured clock, and it is flagged that way wherever it appears. No diel feeding study exists for this species at any season.

Clarity is a location rule for this fish before it is anything else: mooneye are repeatedly described as intolerant of silt and turbid water, and their declines track siltation. In spring runoff, fish the clearest water you can find — a silted reach is the wrong address for this species even at the right temperature.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If prespawn schools are nowhere on the staging water, check the temperature against the spawn band: below about 8 °C the run has not started, and the feeding fish are still spread through the spring holding water rather than gathered below the shoals.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The insect menu continues through the spawn — corixids and the mayfly, midge and beetle items of the spring diet — presented at the surface and in the upper water over and below the shoals. Nothing spawn-specific is named in the literature; the diet is the tackle story, as it is all year for this fish.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the schools on the move: mooneye travel in schools, and a spawning-season school is a located fishery — work a found school thoroughly at the dusk peak rather than casting empty shoal water. The dusk timing remains consensus-grade (agency accounts plus eye anatomy), stated as such, not as a measured bite window.

Temperature is the spawn calendar: the run keys to the 8–15 °C band with its peak at 10–13 °C, latitude-shifted by weeks from south to north. If the water is in the band and the shoals are quiet, the local run is early or late — move along the migration route instead of changing presentations.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If shoal fish are present but not feeding at midday, that is this species' normal day value, not a refusal to solve: the model's daylight value is its lowest (0.55) on a dusk-led shape. Stay for the evening — the surface feeding this fish is built for happens at the light change.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Surface insects are the summer menu — this is a surface-feeding insectivore: corixids, mayflies, midges, beetles and other fallen and emerging insects, with crustaceans behind them in the Assiniboine record. Small insect-profile offerings fished at the surface in the evening are the whole supported pattern; the literature names no lure, and the entry invents none.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Dusk is the peak and night is a real second shift (the model runs dawn 0.70 / day 0.55 / dusk 1.0 / night 0.80): surface feeding in the evening and into the night is the agency account, the plausible mechanism being the evening insect fall and emergence — stated as interpretation, because the diel shape itself is consensus and anatomy, never stomach-measured. Plan the day around the last hour of light and fish into dark.

Guard the clarity rule in summer above all: this is the clear-water member of its family — its congener tolerates turbid water and mooneye is its opposite — and no dissolved-oxygen value of any kind has ever been measured for this species, so neither murk nor low-oxygen water comes with any sourced guidance except avoidance of the murk. After any silt event, the fish are in the clearest water in the system or they are not feeding.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer surface water pushes past the 27 °C avoidance, the shallows are the wrong address — avoidance is the measured response, so look for cooler water rather than new baits. And know the limit honestly: no lethal temperature has ever been measured for this species, so the curve's warm tail past avoidance is flagged interpolation, not a threshold to fish by.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Corixids are the fall menu, dominating the stomach record in the peak months — small insect-profile offerings sized and fished to that single dominant item are the most diet-specific pattern this species offers all year. Where corixids are not moving, fall back to the general insect ledger: mayflies, midges, beetles, crustaceans.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The dusk-led clock runs the fall day as it runs the summer one (consensus and anatomy, flagged as ever): surface feeding at the light change and into the night, tracking the evening insect movement — the corixid mechanism is interpretation offered by the research, not a measured parameter, and the practical consequence is simply to be on the feeding water at dusk while the migration runs.

Work schools, not water: fall feeding is concentrated where the prey concentrates, and a located school on the migration is worth an evening of thorough fishing. Cooling toward November shortens the season (the model's November value steps down and December falls to its floor), so late-fall effort belongs on the warmest, clearest afternoons sliding into dusk.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the fall water is silent, check clarity first and temperature second: silt shuts this species down by its best-evidenced response, and once the water falls toward the winter floor the feeding year is closing — the December value is a presence floor, not a feeding pattern.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No winter presentation is sourced for mooneye. If you fish open winter water at all, the year-round insect ledger at its smallest and slowest is the only diet the species offers — offered here as the honest minimum, not as a winter finding.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the deep holding pools slowly and give located fish time: the model's winter floor (0.25) is a presence floor built from documented overwintering, not a feeding rate, so expectations should be set by the floor, not by the spring and fall peaks.

Carry the open-water clock in only as a flag: the dusk-led shape is a consensus construction for the open-water seasons and has never been tested in winter. A winter dusk is a reasonable bet by that shape and nothing stronger — the entry says so rather than selling it as winter science.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A dead winter pool is the documented state of this species' knowledge, not necessarily a tactics failure: presence without measured feeding means silence proves nothing either way. The sourced mooneye seasons are the spring run, the summer growth season and the fall corixid peak — winter effort is honestly better spent there.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice presentation is sourced for mooneye. Nothing here is borrowed from another species to fill the space.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Treat ice-season mooneye as unstudied water: fish the winter holding pattern if you fish them at all, and know the library has no ice science to check your results against.

Open-water ratings resume at ice-off — that boundary is the ice chapter for this species. The spring feeding peak that follows, with stomachs at their fullest in April and May, is measured, and it is where this library's mooneye year actually begins.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: The sourced mooneye seasons are the spring run and spawn, the summer growth season and the fall corixid peak. The ice season is, on present evidence, a gap — the entry says so rather than papering over it.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Mooneye feed hard before they spawn, and it is measured: in the Assiniboine programme, stomachs were fullest in April and May — the spring peak of a two-peak feeding year — in the run-up to the mid-May spawn. Prespawn fish are travelling and feeding fish, staging toward the spawning shoals on the spring rise.
The staging address is the holding water below the spawning shoals: schools hold in the deep pools and slower margins and feed on the move, with the run to the shoals still ahead of them.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The spawn is a broadcast event with no nest and no guarding: eggs are shed over the shoals and drift, semibuoyant, into quiet water, and no parental care follows. Crucially for the fishing, May is independently a peak feeding month in the stomach record — spawning mooneye are not off their food the way a guarding species is, and the spawn renders in the rating as a location annotation only, with no feeding bonus and no suppression claimed.

The spawning address itself is clear, flowing water over rock and gravel shoals — measured at shared spawning shoals as about 0.8–2.0 m deep with surface flow around 0.4–1.0 m/s — reached on an upstream migration. In Manitoba the peak is mid-May at 10–13 °C; the range-wide band is 8–15 °C, late April in the south to mid-June in the north.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer is the growth season — growth was fastest June through August in the Assiniboine work, and Manitoba's angling peak runs August–September on the Winnipeg system — on a thermal centre that needs its provenance stated: the model's plateau (19–24 °C) follows a single field measurement, a preferendum of 22 °C with upper avoidance at 27 °C. A compiled preferendum family sitting near 27–29 °C exists in the Ontario metrics compilation; it is a database value with an untraced primary source, it is kept separate and not blended into the anchors, and the whole mooneye set is DERIVED, capped at Low confidence, for exactly this kind of thinness.

The summer pattern is split by design: schools hold in the deep pools and slower margins and feed mostly in the flowing water — occurrence record, not a measured feeding-versus-flow function. Fish the flowing feeding water at the light changes and the holding pools between feeds.

In big clear water the summer address is the nearshore zone: the Great Lakes record keeps mooneye within about a mile of shore and above 10 m deep, in the clear water this species requires. Fish the clear shallows and their first drop at dusk.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is the second measured feeding peak: Assiniboine stomachs were fullest again in October and November, riding the fall corixid migration — the autumn half of a bimodal feeding year whose growth peak, by contrast, sits in summer. Fall mooneye are feeding fish on a moving insect supply, and the cooling water is still well inside their season.

Fish the flowing feeding water below the holding pools as the corixid supply moves: the fall peak is a prey-migration pattern, so the schools set up where the drifting insects concentrate, and they feed there into the evening.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter mooneye are documented as present — overwintering in the deep holding pools — and that is nearly all that is documented: adult winter feeding and activity have never been measured for this species. The only winter diet record in its science is young-of-year fish eating stoneflies in their first winter, a first-year record this entry refuses to present as adult behaviour.

Manitoba's fishery agrees with the gap: the provincial mooneye record is an open-water, June-to-October fishery with its peak in late summer. Winter is this species' unmeasured season, and the entry treats it as one rather than dressing presence up as a pattern.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: No ice parameter set exists for this species, deliberately: no under-ice study of mooneye exists, no ice fishery targets it in its Manitoba range, and issuing an ice pattern would invent one. If your water is ice-covered, the honest guidance is the winter open-water pattern — deep holding pools — labelled as exactly that.

The winter record underneath that gap is one young-of-year diet note (stoneflies in the first winter) plus documented overwintering presence in deep pools. Adult winter feeding has never been measured, so there is no ice season in this fish's science to summarise — the coverage verdict is not-covered, and the entry carries it openly.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 19–24 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for mooneye is an absence across the board: wind, fronts, barometric pressure and moon have never been tested for this species' feeding or catch in any design, and dissolved oxygen has never been measured at all. The fish's name is not evidence either — it describes its eye, not its calendar, and no lunar test exists. There is no front trick for this fish to sell you: what exists is temperature, light, season and clarity, and a front matters only as the temperature, light and silt change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Low light is this species' home condition by construction: a grouped, rod-rich retina behind a reflective tapetum, agency accounts putting the most active feeding at dusk, and surface feeding through the evening. Be set up on the feeding water before the light goes — on the consensus shape the model carries (dusk 1.0), the last hour is the day, and travelling during it wastes the peak this fish actually has.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is a real shift for mooneye, not a tail of dusk: the model's night value is 0.80, built on surface feeding in the evening and during the night in the Ottawa account and the low-light eye the anatomy describes. Fish the surface slowly after dark where you found the schools at dusk — and hold the flag honestly: no stomach-based diel study exists, so this is consensus and anatomy, the best this species offers, labelled as such.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais mesuré pour le mooneye par aucune méthode — aucun seuil d'évitement, Pcrit, LOE ou courbe alimentation-contre-OD n'existe. Les données d'hémoglobine à effet Root (Regan & Brauner 2010) ne sont pas une valeur de tolérance. doAnchors : null plutôt qu'une courbe inventée (et aucune valeur d'OD d'un congénère n'est importée pour remplir le tiroir).

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou la capture du mooneye dans aucun protocole. Zéro par absence. (L'alternative d'indicateur de programme a été considérée et refusée dans l'ensemble : un ensemble dérivé plafonné à Faible ne parque pas 10 points sur une mécanique météo empruntée.)
Jamais testé pour le mooneye. Zéro par absence; frontExposure : 0.
Jamais testé pour le mooneye. Zéro par absence (pas un nul mesuré).
Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai du mooneye. Le nom commun de l'espèce et son tapetum ne sont pas des preuves lunaires — le nom décrit son œil, pas son calendrier. Zéro par absence.

Aucune fonction alimentation-contre-débit n'existe; les preuves sont l'occurrence d'habitat (se tient dans les fosses, s'alimente surtout en eau rapide; hauts-fonds de frai à 0.4–1.0 m/s). Aucun terme de débit n'est noté — le défaut de poids parqué du blue catfish n'est pas répété.

Les pics d'alimentation sont démontrablement conditionnés par la disponibilité des insectes/corixidés (Glenn 1975), mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure l'émergence d'insectes ou le flux de corixidés; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.
La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour le mooneye; elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome.

about: The muskellunge is the largest of the pike family and the most storied fish in North American fresh water — “the fish of ten thousand casts.” It's a cool-water apex predator, feeding best in the low twenties Celsius in the rating model, spawning in shallow bays at 9–15 °C after the pike have finished, and spending its life largely alone around weeds, wood and rock.

Muskies are ambush-and-roam hunters: after the spawn they range widely, covering edges and weedlines, before settling into the late-summer ambush game, following lures to the boat so often that the boatside figure-eight is part of the technique. Most muskies caught today are released, by law or by culture. Anglers target them for the follow, the boatside strike, and a fish that measures a life list in single entries.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: This is a searching-season fish in the making (the post-spawn mode below is the measured extreme of it). The monograph is movement and catch science, not a lure book — it names no baits, and these entries follow it: present forage-sized offerings along the travel lanes and let location do the work.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Keep the day's clock in view even now: dawn is this species' measured minimum, dusk its maximum, in every method that has timed it. A prespawn evening on a travel lane is worth two dawns.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the lanes are quiet, the move hasn't reached your bay — work back toward the deep edges. Spring muskies are distributed along a route, and the route is longer than one spot.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Nothing spawn-specific is sourced. Edge presentations at the dusk window are the season's honest play.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the bay mouths and first edges at dusk, when the species' clock peaks, rather than over the spawning shallows at midday — that advice is location plus diel, both measured, and it's as far as the evidence honestly goes in this window.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the bays are all spawners and no feeders, work the prespawn lanes again — late movers and early post-spawn fish travel them while the spawn peaks.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Forage-profile offerings fished on the move. One measured lever on size of encounter: hunger doubles catchability with no change in activity (fasted fish were caught over twice as often) — you can't set the lake's hunger, but it explains why the same water fishes dead one week and alive the next on identical weather.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Build the day toward dusk — dawn minimum, day intermediate, dusk maximum is consistent across creel, telemetry and burst-activity data, with June sharpening the crepuscular peaks. Save your best water for the last shift.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: When a searching-season fish won't show, resist downsizing the water: stay on routes and edges, and let the dusk window come to you on the best lane you have. Also note the vulnerability finding, because it tempers expectations honestly: the muskies that get caught were the larger but LESS explorative, less aggressive fish in the pond work — the bold fish you raise may be exactly the ones that don't eat.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Ambush-season presentations tight to the edge — the fish are holding, not roaming, so the bait has to arrive at the lie. Followers are this species' famous tease; the pond science says the caught fish are the shy ones, so a follow is information about location, and a slower, smaller second presentation to a known lie is the evidence-consistent next cast.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Dusk is still the peak; in June-style long days the crepuscular sharpening flattens by late summer, so spread effort through the day more evenly than in June — but never start with dawn, the measured minimum, on your best water.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: In a heat wave, the toughest and most honest advice in this entry: the fish are in refuges and stressed, catch-and-release itself kills a share of them, and the season will give you better, safer chances when the water drops back under the mid-20s.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Full-size forage profiles on the structure routes. Fall muskies are feeding up; the base rate that haunts summer improves, and standard presentations on good edges are the play the season's data supports.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Dusk maximum still rules the day. Cooling fronts that would be a pike story are not one here: pressure was a measured null for muskellunge (both success and catch rate), and precipitation likewise — fish the temperature transitions themselves, which are the measured fall trigger.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall water is quiet, check the warm side of the day — this species' activity rises with warmth through the teens and 20s, so a cold fall snap slows muskies more than it slows the pike beside them.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice presentation is sourced for muskellunge — and no other species' ice set was borrowed wholesale to fill this space, because a borrowed rating would look like knowledge it isn't.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Muskies are present and catchable under ice — the fishery exists; the science doesn't. If you fish them, you're ahead of the literature, and the app says so instead of pretending otherwise.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: The sourced muskie seasons are the spring routes, the searching early summer, the ambush late summer and the fall maximum. Through the ice, target the species this library's ice science actually covers.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Ahead of the spawn, muskies are on the move toward the shallow spawning bays — movement peaks ride the cold transitions of spring (the 4–12 °C band in the telemetry). Fish the routes: the edges and funnels between winter water and the bays, a step behind the pike, whose spawn runs first.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs at 9–15 °C, peaking near 12.8 °C, after the pike are done, in the shallow bays. One honesty rule the rating also follows: whether spawning muskies stop feeding has never been measured — no other fish's spawning fast is borrowed as a number — so the spawn renders here as a location note, not a predicted shutdown. The fish are in the bays; fish the edges and the fish travelling in and out, and leave the beds themselves alone.

movementSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: Post-spawn into midsummer is the searching mode: muskies range, covering water, before the late-summer shift to ambush. Fish like it — cover the edges, points and weedlines, and expect encounters anywhere along a route rather than on one pinned spot. Two-of-three stomachs in the big diet study were empty (34.3% fullness, the lowest feeding frequency among the programme's predators): this is a low-base-rate fish, and a quiet day is its normal, not your failure.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Late summer flips the mode to ambush: fish hold on weed edges, points and structure and wait. And the temperature story is this species' own, opposite to pike's — the plateau is warm, 19–24 °C, with the realised niche near 22 °C; but above about 24–26 °C the fish crowd into refuges (over 90% refuge occupancy at a 26 °C daily average in the river work), and warm-water catch-and-release mortality climbs toward 30% while it runs near zero below 25 °C. Fish the ambush edges near cool refuges in heat — and in real heat, weigh whether to fish at all, and handle any fish you catch for a fast, wet release.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is a maximum season — stomach fullness runs fall > summer > spring in the diet data, and movement peaks again on the cooling transitions. Fish the edges, points and weedlines as a feeding fish again, with the searching and ambush water both in play.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: Muskellunge under ice is a NOT COVERED state in this app, by decision: the entire under-ice evidence is one 1979 agency telemetry study — fish deeper (2.5–4.5 m) in moderately vegetated overwintering habitat, moving minimally, with one relocation away from low-oxygen water. No under-ice diel, light response or catchability data exists. A numeric ice rating would be invention, so there isn't one.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at first light.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at first light.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 19–24 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Wind: this species' feeding holds up best with wind 0–3.6 km/h — its own measured wind curve, not a generic one.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: Muskellunge pressure is a measured null — p = 0.249 for trip success, 0.722 for catch rate, read from the primary Escanaba table — and the front-as-package has never been measured in this species at all. The small front weight in the rating is shared machinery at Grade C, and this entry follows the data: there is no post-front muskie play to run. Fish the temperature and the dusk clock; the barometer has been tested and excused.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Reverse everything pike taught you: muskellunge catch rate was significantly HIGHER on calmer days in the Escanaba creel (the wind coefficient is negative; trip success showed no wind effect at all). A windy day is not a muskie trigger — spend windy hours on other species or other water, and save the calm days for this fish.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Calm is the win in this combination; the sun half is a small measured negative — solar radiation slightly lowered trip success, with no effect on catch rate. Net: a calm, bright day is good muskie weather, marginally better if a little cloud takes the edge off the sun. Fish the ambush edges without waiting for weather that this species never asked for.

weatherOverlays.heading: Couvert
lines: Grey is mildly favourable by the same solar finding — a very small effect, honestly sized. It is a tiebreaker for which day to choose, not a pattern.

weatherNotCounted.reason: NUL MESURÉ — la tendance de pression testée contre l'activité du maskinongé et trouvée nulle (p = 0.249 / 0.722 sur les tests). Zéro est la mesure.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Ahead of the spawn, muskies are on the move toward the shallow spawning bays — movement peaks ride the cold transitions of spring (the 4–12 °C band in the telemetry). Fish the routes: the edges and funnels between winter water and the bays, a step behind the pike, whose spawn runs first.
Keep the day's clock in view even now: dawn is this species' measured minimum, dusk its maximum, in every method that has timed it. A prespawn evening on a travel lane is worth two dawns.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Spawning runs at 9–15 °C, peaking near 12.8 °C, after the pike are done, in the shallow bays. One honesty rule the rating also follows: whether spawning muskies stop feeding has never been measured — no other fish's spawning fast is borrowed as a number — so the spawn renders here as a location note, not a predicted shutdown. The fish are in the bays; fish the edges and the fish travelling in and out, and leave the beds themselves alone.

Fish the bay mouths and first edges at dusk, when the species' clock peaks, rather than over the spawning shallows at midday — that advice is location plus diel, both measured, and it's as far as the evidence honestly goes in this window.

spawningSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: Post-spawn into midsummer is the searching mode: muskies range, covering water, before the late-summer shift to ambush. Fish like it — cover the edges, points and weedlines, and expect encounters anywhere along a route rather than on one pinned spot. Two-of-three stomachs in the big diet study were empty (34.3% fullness, the lowest feeding frequency among the programme's predators): this is a low-base-rate fish, and a quiet day is its normal, not your failure.

Build the day toward dusk — dawn minimum, day intermediate, dusk maximum is consistent across creel, telemetry and burst-activity data, with June sharpening the crepuscular peaks. Save your best water for the last shift.

about: The northern pike — jackfish or just “jack” across the prairies — is the north's ambush predator: long, green, toothy and built to explode out of cover. It is a genuinely cold-loving fish; in the rating model its feeding holds up best in water from near freezing through the mid-teens Celsius, and hot summer water stresses it more than almost any other fish in this library.

Pike live in and around vegetation — shallow bays, sloughs, cattails and weedlines — where they hang motionless until baitfish, perch or even ducklings drift within range, spawning in flooded shallows right at ice-out. Anglers love them because the strike is violent, the fight is close-quarters, and a big northern is a real trophy; they respect the teeth, the slime and a mouthful of hooks that demands pliers and care.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Early on, small and slender: a 3½-in soft swimbait on a light 1/8- to 1/4-oz jighead, a small slender spoon, or a 3¾-in minnow-profile crank. For a still presentation, the dead-bait float rig: a 25–30 cm smelt on a #6 treble with a short steel leader, set about 45 cm off the bottom in slack water.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Anchor up, let the spot settle for ten minutes, then fan-cast it before you move — and move only far enough to overlap your last casts. Pike in cold water punish run-and-gun fishing; a big early bay can fish for hours fished properly.
Cold water means a slow, steady retrieve — slow-roll a jig-and-swimbait just fast enough to keep the tail thumping, with the odd dart, and keep the reel turning the whole time.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: When a pike takes a dead bait, it runs, then stops to turn it — freespool until the bobber stops for a few seconds, then set. Rushing that pause is how early-season fish are lost.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small, slow and close: the early-season swimbait on a light jighead, small slender spoons, or a dead bait under a float at the bay mouths. This is not the season for big aggressive baits over the beds themselves.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the edges and the travel lanes, not the beds. Expect a short window of feeding fish around the spawn rather than a day of them, and give spawning fish themselves a pass — the feeders at the edges are the catchable ones.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shallows are all spawners, move out to the first real depth change and dead-bait it slowly. Post-spawn fish recovering at the edge will take a still bait they wouldn't chase.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: For the biggest post-spawn fish, go big and slow: a 1-oz tandem spinnerbait with big Colorado blades, or a straight-wire spinnerbait dressed with a 6-in grub, on heavy braid and a 35 cm, 100-lb fluorocarbon leader. Colour rules follow the water: grey-white and brown-gold in clear water, black-chartreuse and green-chartreuse in dirty water.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Slow-roll the big blades through the bay and along the channel edge — post-spawn pike are recovering, not chasing, and the big slow thump is what they answer. Cover the bay in a fan before you move, and overlap your casts.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Downshift to the dead-bait float rig in the slack corners of the bay. A recovering pike that ignores every moving bait will still pick up a still smelt sitting 45 cm off the bottom.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: A big shad-profile crankbait is the core open-water trolling bait. On the weedline: big spinnerbaits, weedless spoons and jerkbaits; for pressured fish, a ½- to ¾-oz single-blade spinnerbait, or go subtle — a weightless 7-in soft jerkbait rigged weedless. On deep flats, a heavy jig with a 7–8 in softbait; a 1½-oz jig head is the right weight to work that depth.
Leaders are not optional tackle, they're pike tackle: tieable wire around 20 lb covers most pike work (13 lb for the lightest presentations); heavy fluorocarbon for the big spinnerbaits.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: On deep flats, find the bait on sonar first — no bait, no pike — then snap-jig: rip the jig 6 ft up, drop the tip, and let it fall. Trolling depths matter: a big shad crank on 30-lb mono stays in the top 10 ft; on 40-lb braid the same bait runs 17 ft and deeper; in-line weights of ½–1 oz reach 12–25 ft — but never below the thermocline.

One caution from the books: don't let a lure surprise a pike. If you spot one, set a jig 4–5 ft behind it and barely lift it — a bait that lands on top of a pike spooks it; one that creeps up behind it gets eaten.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: When the pattern won't declare itself, fish the beaver lodges properly: work 75–100 ft out from them first, then move in. And when sucker spawn is on (around 10 °C), switch to wounded-sucker lures — a big slow wobbling bait or firetiger — around the spawning shallows.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Slowly reeled artificials or dead bait — the books are direct that in heat, those are the best odds. Troll the cool layer with a big shad crank (braid gets it to 17 ft+; in-line weights to 12–25 ft) and keep everything above the thermocline.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Slow down and fish deep. Short windows at dawn and dusk, when big pike slide up to feed, are worth more than a midday grind in the heat.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If you must fish midday, dead-bait the deepest cool water you can find and be patient — a hot-weather pike eats a still meal because it costs nothing to catch.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer baits still work — big spinnerbaits, jerkbaits, shad cranks — fished on the edges. Where bait is spawning (ciscoes and whitefish run the rock and reefs in fall), match it: pike intercept spawning baitfish on rock and reef edges, and that's a feed worth being on.

The summer baits still work — big spinnerbaits, jerkbaits, shad cranks — fished on the edges. Where bait is spawning (ciscoes and whitefish run the rock in fall), match it: pike intercept spawning baitfish on rock edges, and that's a feed worth being on.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Cover the edges with moving baits in the midday warmth. If the wind has blown the same direction for three days or more, fish where it's been pushing into shore — the food chain stacks up there.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Slow the edges down with a jig and big softbait, tight to the weedline's outside edge, and work the shaded sides of the thickest clumps — that's where the neutral fish sit.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Slow artificials and dead bait again — cold pike won't chase fast prey. The dead-bait float rig over the deep edge, or a jig-and-swimbait slow-rolled just off bottom, are the cold-water pair.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Everything slows down: the retrieve, the hops, and your expectations between bites. Stay on the best deep edge you have and fish it thoroughly instead of sampling five spots quickly.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Dead-bait it and wait. In the coldest water, patience isn't a virtue, it's the whole technique — a still smelt on the deep edge outfishes every moving bait on the days they won't move.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Dead bait on a quick-strike rig under a tip-up is the trophy method — every 25 lb pike in the old pro accounts came on it. Fresh dead ciscoes, suckers or smelt where they're legal. The rig: 14–18 in of 20–30 lb wire, two #4 trebles about 2½ in apart, hooks no more than 4 in apart even on the biggest bait, the front hook no farther forward than just above the bait's dorsal fin.
For the jigging rod: a live bait of 6–8 in on a single hook, 20-lb fluorocarbon leader (a #6 Kahle for a 6-in bait, #4 for an 8-in).

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Set the tip-ups on the structure tops and jig the edges, 20–40 ft of water within reach of the set lines. When a flag flies on the quick-strike rig, sweep-set immediately — the fish took the bait headfirst and the rig is built for a fast hookup.
An alternative to trebles: a barbless 5/0 circle hook (4/0 for smaller baits) on 18 in of 30-lb tieable wire — safer for the fish and the angler.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shallow weedbeds are quiet, believe the depth: the big fish may simply still be deep. Move a set line out to the deep edge of the bed before you move lakes.
If the shallow weedbeds are quiet, believe the depth: the big fish may simply still be deep. Move a set line out to the deep edge of the bed before you move.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Dead bait on quick-strike rigs stays the trophy play, jigging a live bait on the edges stays the active play — same rigs as first ice.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the travel lane: set lines along the deep edge pointing at the bays, and jig the edge while they soak. Mark what produces — staging routes repeat every year.
Work the travel lane: set lines along the deep edge pointing at the creek mouths and bays, and jig the edge while they soak. Mark what produces — staging routes repeat every year.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Slide shallower before you slide deeper. Late-season pike are moving one direction — toward the spawn — and the staging fish can be in 1–2 ft of water under the ice.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Big dead baits on quick-strike rigs for the trophies staging outside; jig the edges with live bait to find the active lane.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish it like the spring pattern arriving early — the lanes into the bays, the first edges, and check shallower water than feels right. These fish are feeding up ahead of the spawn.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the edges are quiet, the fish are all the way in — go shallow into the bay mouths themselves before you give up on the spot.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Before the spawn, pike gather where the food gathers: bays, connected sloughs and the funnel areas between them — channel edges, points, old weedlines and minor depth changes.

Before the spawn, pike gather where the food gathers: tributary mouths, bays, connected sloughs and the funnel areas between them — channel edges and minor depth changes. Work current areas first: inflows, necked-down spots and snowmelt runoff all concentrate early fish.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Pike are spawning now — in the flooded vegetation and shallow bays — and spawning pike fast more than they feed. The honest pattern is the fish at the edges: pre- and post-spawn fish along the channel edges and the first depth changes outside the spawning bays, where the north ends warm fastest.

movementSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: Right after the spawn, look in shallow mud-bottom bays full of cattails — the north end of the bay warms fastest and fishes first. Start in 1–4 ft. Channel edges with vegetation nearby hold the bigger recovering fish.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Three summer patterns, and the day tells you which: (A) open water — find the biggest bait schools; if bait is 15–30 ft down, troll it, if it's in the top 20 ft, cast it. (B) deep flats — packs of big pike hold on expansive flats 25–45 ft down by early summer (in young, deep, clear lakes, 25–60 ft), and the thermocline is a wall: the cold layer below it has no oxygen, so don't fish under it. (C) weedflats — on the deep weedline, active fish prowl the outside edge, neutral fish sit on cabbage points and inside turns, on the shaded side of the thickest clumps.
The biggest pike — 30 in and up — visit 40 ft and deeper on warm days, down in the cool layers. Summer is when the giants live deepest.

movementSeasons.heading: Mi-été
lines: The hottest water is a pike's worst season — above about 22 °C they feed best down in the cool layers, 25–65 ft, and in thermal extremes they will not chase fast prey at all. The deep flats and the cool side of the thermocline are the whole game now.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is the edges season — vegetation edges and rock edges are the most universal fall pike pattern there is. As it cools, pike also slide back toward the spring shallows, and the middle of the day, when the water is warmest, is when they're most aggressive.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne froid
lines: Below about 10 °C the fall shallows empty out — pike drop to the deep edges and the first drop-offs near where they'll winter, and some fish eat only every few days. A small fish digests in a day or two in warm water; at near-freezing it lasts for weeks. Fewer meals means fewer chances, but each chance is a real one.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace précoce
lines: First ice carries the fall locations — don't rush shallow. Work the weedbeds that held fish in fall: broad beds of cabbage or coontail around 6–18 ft, bordered by deeper water, and set up on the deep edges. Some of the biggest fish are still deep at first ice.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace de mi-hiver
lines: Mid-winter pike pattern like they stage for spring: from mid-February they follow the deep edges toward the spawning bays, shallower as the season runs — with the biggest fish in the bays at the season's edges and on main-lake structure in between.

Mid-winter pike pattern like they stage for spring: from mid-February they follow the deep edges toward the spawning creeks and bays — around 18 ft outside creek mouths late in February, shallower as the season runs — with the biggest fish in the bays at the season's edges and on structure in between.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace tardive
lines: Late ice is staging season: pike crowd the edges outside the spawning bays they'll enter at ice-out, shallower every week. Set up on those edges and in the mouths — this is the biggest-fish window of the ice season.

Late ice is staging season: pike crowd the edges outside the spawning creeks they'll enter at ice-out, shallower every week. Set up on those edges and in the mouths — this is the biggest-fish window of the ice season.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at after dark.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at midday; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 0–14.7 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 29.4 °C, from the species' research file.
Wind: this species' feeding holds up best with wind 25–35 km/h — its own measured wind curve, not a generic one.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: After a cold front, the pike that were on exposed bays simply vanish. The book answer is overhead cover: isolated stands of dead reeds and rushes in shallow bays, the cover that doesn't move with the weather. Fish over the top of it.

After a cold front, the pike that were on creek mouths simply vanish. The book answer is overhead cover: isolated stands of dead reeds and rushes in shallow bays, the cover that doesn't move with the weather. Fish over the top of it.

Downsize and go weedless — this is muskie-tackle fishing: 50–65 lb braid, a small weedless spoon with a twin-tail grub (silver or gold spoon, chartreuse, white or black-brown grub). A slow-sinking bait they can reach without leaving cover.
Fish slowly over the top of the dead cover and let the bait sink into the pockets. Post-front pike aren't travelling to a bait — it has to come to them, practically on top of them.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Wind flips summer pike shallow: on windy, cloudy days the deep-flat fish rise to shallow reefs and rocky points in 5–10 ft where the waves roll in. Fish where the wind has blown into the same shore for days, if it has — everything they eat stacks up there.

Wind flips summer pike shallow: on windy, cloudy days the deep-flat fish rise to shallow water in 5–10 ft where the waves roll in. Fish where the wind has blown into the same shore for days, if it has — everything they eat stacks up there.
Big suspending baits are the windy-shore tool — they hang in the wave wash where the pike are looking.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Sun and calm send summer pike back to the deep flats — don't waste the flat calm on the shallows in summer; go deep and fish the cool layer above the thermocline.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Sunset into twilight is a shallow-water window: pike slide into the water they spent the day near — on pressured lakes they may be in 2 ft or less around the panfish areas at last light.
Sunset into twilight is a shallow-water window: pike slide into the water they spent the day near — they may be in 2 ft or less around the panfish areas at last light.
Spinnerbaits are the low-light search bait around that shallow evening water.

weatherOverlays.heading: Couvert
lines: Cloud does for pike what wind does — it brings the deep fish up. Grey days are for checking the shallow reefs and points you'd fish in wind, even at midday.
Cloud does for pike what wind does — it brings the deep fish up. Grey days are for checking the shallow water you'd fish in wind, even at midday.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Nul mesuré — « la pression barométrique n'avait aucun effet sur les taux de capture du brochet » dans l'expérience à l'échelle du lac.

Before the spawn, pike gather where the food gathers: tributary mouths, bays, connected sloughs and the funnel areas between them — channel edges and minor depth changes. Work current areas first: inflows, necked-down spots and snowmelt runoff all concentrate early fish.

Anchor up, let the spot settle for ten minutes, then fan-cast it before you move — and move only far enough to overlap your last casts. Pike in cold water punish run-and-gun fishing; a big early bay can fish for hours fished properly.
Cold water means a slow, steady retrieve — slow-roll a jig-and-swimbait just fast enough to keep the tail thumping, with the odd dart, and keep the reel turning the whole time.

The honest pattern is the fish at the edges: pre- and post-spawn fish along the channel edges and the first depth changes outside the spawning bays, where the north ends warm fastest.

Fish the edges and the travel lanes, not the beds. Expect a short window of feeding fish around the spawn rather than a day of them, and give spawning fish themselves a pass — the feeders at the edges are the catchable ones.

about: The pumpkinseed is the jewel of the panfish — a small sunfish painted in orange, turquoise and gold, with a red crescent on its ear that no other sunfish matches. It is the cooler cousin among the Lepomis: its measured temperature preference sits below the bluegill's, peaking in the low-to-mid twenties Celsius in the rating model, and it owns the shallow, vegetated littoral of northern lakes and ponds.

Pumpkinseed spawn in colonies of small nests on sand and gravel in water sometimes only inches deep, males fanning and guarding through the season, and they feed all summer on snails, insects and small crustaceans among the weeds. They are bold, curious biters. Anglers — and especially kids and fly fishers — target them for non-stop action, for the colours, and for sweet fillets when a mess of big ones comes together.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small offerings matched to the measured diet at this size and season: the young and smaller fish feed in the vegetation on insect larvae and other vegetation-dwelling invertebrates, and chironomids run through the diet all year. No lure is named in the pumpkinseed literature, and none is invented here — small, natural, and presented in the vegetation at close range is the whole supported tackle story for a visual, encounter-driven littoral feeder.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Time the day by this species' own clock, not bluegill's: pumpkinseed feeding peaks at dawn and dusk on a solid daylight base — the stomach studies agree on the twin peaks. Be set up on the shallows at the light changes, and fish the warming middle of the day as a real second shift, not a wait for evening.

Below about 8 °C, expect the measured floor: spontaneous activity collapses toward a minimum at 7.9 °C and feeding drops markedly below it. Cold prespawn fish are a patience pattern — slow, close presentations in the warmest shallow water you can find.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shallows are empty, the temperature has not arrived — nest-building is temperature-gated from ~13–15 °C, so drop to the first edge off the nesting flats and wait for the water rather than changing baits.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Offerings sized to the littoral menu — insect larvae and the small benthic invertebrates of the nesting shallows — worked in and around the beds. The adult specialisation on snails (below) is a feeding-ground pattern; on the colonies themselves, size to the small invertebrate food the shallows hold. No spawn-specific lure is named in the literature.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the light changes hardest: guarding males feed measurably less than females, and what feeding they do is concentrated at dawn and dusk near the nest — the twin peaks are the spawn clock as much as the summer one. And the guard-state rule, stated as the rating states it: a male that charges a bait on the nest is defending, not feeding — strikes on nests are aggression, and the entry says so rather than dressing them up as a bite pattern.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Between bouts the colonies thin — parental males sit out their 10–11-day bout feeding little, then the next wave builds. Check the edges just off the colony and the neighbouring bluegill beds before you conclude the spawn is done; with bouts running May to August, it pulses rather than ends.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the measured adult diet, because it is this species' defining science: large pumpkinseed are mollusc specialists — adult diets averaged 63–73% snails by mass — crushing them with a specialised pharyngeal mill, alongside chironomids, other insect larvae and crustaceans; small fish stay on vegetation invertebrates. Bottom-and-vegetation presentations sized to snails and larvae are the supported pattern. One lake-to-lake warning the research is explicit about: feeding performance is gated by the individual lake's snail fauna and the fish's crushing morphology — a snail-rich lake's fish feed on snails at roughly twice the rate of a snail-poor lake's. No lure is named in the pumpkinseed literature, and none is invented here.

A seasonal surprise worth a cast: in late spring and summer, several Ontario pond populations fed extensively on small fish (brook stickleback) where bass were absent. Where small forage fish crowd the shallows, a small fish-profile offering is diet-supported, not a guess.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Dawn and dusk are the peaks — three independent stomach studies put fullness highest at the light changes — with a solid daylight base between them (the model's day value is 0.85, not a lull). Work the vegetation edges thoroughly at the transitions; the prey here does not migrate up and down the column the way bluegill's zooplankton does, so the fish stay on the littoral food rather than chasing it into open water.

Clarity is a location rule with a direction but no dose–response: adults select the less turbid water. In stained conditions, fish the clearest shallows you can find and put the bait closer and slower — the study measures the preference, not a distance, and the entry invents none.

Oxygen is this fish's quiet advantage: head-to-head, pumpkinseed tolerated significantly lower dissolved oxygen than bluegill, and nests function at bottom oxygen down to about 2.4 mg/L. In a hot, still basin where other panfish have vacated the bottom, pumpkinseed may still be there — check the low-oxygen shallows other entries tell you to abandon.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer fish look but won't take, shrink and slow in place — a visual feeder refusing a bait it can see is giving a size-and-speed verdict. And if the water has pushed past the low 30s °C, you are above the preference plateau and into the avoidance zone: find cooler water before you change a single bait.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer menu, a step smaller and slower: larvae and benthic invertebrates in the vegetation, snail-sized bottom offerings where the snail beds are. Cooling shortens the effective feeding day for a dawn/dusk fish — concentrate the best presentations at the light changes.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The twin peaks still run the day in fall, and the floor is coming: activity holds until the water nears about 8 °C, then collapses toward the 7.9 °C minimum. Fish the warmest part of the shallows on cold days and give located pockets real time — cooling fish move little.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the fall shallows are silent, check the temperature before the tackle: below the 7.9 °C floor this species is measured to be minimally active, and the fix is the warmest water in the system, not a new presentation.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small and slow, delivered close in the still, oxygenated pockets. Winter consumption is a fraction of summer's, so the presentation has to arrive at the fish — this is not a searching season, and no winter-specific lure is named in the literature.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the dawn and dusk edges of the short day first, per the species' year-round twin peaks, and give each located pocket real time — winter fish move little, so finding them is most of the catch. The oxygen gate is the location rule with this species' own numbers: winterkill risk binds at very low oxygen (the reported lethal band is about 0.4–2.0 mg/L, and live pumpkinseed were observed congregating at ice holes after a week below 1.0 mg/L) — they outlast bluegill down that gradient, so the last fishable pockets in a depleting basin are likelier to hold pumpkinseed than anything else.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a winter pocket is dead, it is usually the oxygen, not the bait — move toward better-oxygenated water. And know the limit honestly: a severe winterkill removed 85% of one studied population, so in a basin with a winterkill history, absence is a population fact, not a tactics failure.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small, natural offerings fished close and still in the located pockets — the open-water diet (larvae and small benthic invertebrates) at its smallest. No ice-specific presentation is measured for this species; small and slow is the winter evidence applied honestly, not an ice finding.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the light changes first, on the transferred twin-peak pattern, and treat oxygen as the address: pumpkinseed tolerate lower oxygen than bluegill head-to-head, with a winter lethal band around 0.4–2.0 mg/L, so as a basin depletes through the winter they persist in pockets other panfish have left — fish deeper into the low-oxygen shallows than bluegill habits suggest, and check the inflow and ice-hole water in a stressed lake.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Mid-winter silence is usually the oxygen gate or a winterkill history, not presentation: this species survives low oxygen better than its cousins but is not immune (one winterkill removed 85% of a population). Move toward better-oxygenated water before you change baits — and if the whole basin is depleted, that is the honest end of the pattern.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: As the water climbs through the low teens toward the ~15 °C nest-building onset, pumpkinseed move into the shallow, vegetated littoral they will nest in — colonies form on sand and gravel in water from about 15 cm deep to a few feet. Fish the vegetated shallows near that nesting ground; this species stages in its feeding habitat, close to where it will spawn.

In streams the habitat record is specific: adults hold near the bank in the clearer, slower water, with plant cover and woody structure over sand — and avoid riffles, deep water and high velocity. Fish the quiet, covered bank water, not the runs.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The spawn is a colony season: nests in colonies of about 3–15, on sand and gravel in water from about 15 cm to a few feet deep, each nest roughly twice the fish's length (about 10–38 cm across), often in or beside bluegill colonies. Onset is around 15 °C with the main band at 17–25 °C, and the colonies pulse in repeated bouts of about 10–11 days from May into August — there is almost always a fresh wave of nesting fish somewhere in the window.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer pumpkinseed are littoral, vegetation-oriented fish working the shallows for a benthic menu — and they are the cooler cousin, measurably: their modern measured temperature preference sits at about 22–25 °C with the model's plateau at 22–27 °C, roughly 5 °C cooler than bluegill's, and avoidance begins above about 31 °C. In hot weather, fish the shaded, vegetated shallows and the cooler bays rather than assuming a sunfish wants the warmest water in the lake.
River fish hold the same address as spring: near-bank, clearer, slower water with plant cover and wood over sand, out of the riffles and the fast water.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall pumpkinseed keep feeding in the littoral as it cools — the October river record shows feeding continuing, spread across the day — sliding toward the deeper, stiller water as the temperature falls toward the winter pattern. Fish the deep edges off the summer vegetation while the water is still above the floor, and the warmest still shallows as it drops.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter pumpkinseed keep feeding — that is measured, not folklore: 88% of juvenile pond fish sampled mid-winter contained prey, and February field fish in Ontario ponds were trappable and feeding. The pattern is reduced and oxygen-gated, not dormant: fish hold at low activity below the 7.9 °C floor, in the still water that still carries oxygen. Canadian, long-winter populations benefited most from winter feeding in the trials — at the northern edge of the range, this is a genuinely winter-active panfish.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: The ice set for pumpkinseed is issued, capped at Moderate confidence, and the entry carries that flag openly — the same ruling bluegill received, on stronger winter evidence: winter feeding is measured (88% of mid-winter pond juveniles contained prey), the 7.9 °C activity floor is measured, and the oxygen-risk gradient below is this species' own. What has never been measured is the under-ice diel curve, so the timing below is the open-water dawn/dusk shape carried under the ice as a labelled within-species transfer. Fish the still, vegetated shallows and their deep edges, in the water that still holds oxygen.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light and dusk; quietest at after dark.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at first light and dusk; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 22–27 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for pumpkinseed is stronger than a null — it is an absence: wind, fronts, barometric pressure and moon have never been tested for this species' feeding or catchability in any source the research could find, in either direction. Some fish at least have a historical field null; pumpkinseed has nothing, and this entry will not borrow one. There is no front trick for this fish to sell you: what is measured is temperature, light, season and oxygen, and those are what the other sections fish. A front matters here only as the temperature and light change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The light changes are this species' measured peaks — stomach fullness peaked at dawn and at dusk across the replicated studies, for feeding females and nest-guarding males alike. Be set up on the vegetation edges before the transition, not travelling during it; chironomid emergence at the transitions is the plausible mechanism the study offers, stated as interpretation, and the practical consequence is the same either way: the shallows feed first and last.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is low for pumpkinseed, but it is not the zero that panfish folklore assumes: the model's night value is 0.25 — midnight stomachs were non-empty in the diel work, trap-net catch bottomed out overnight rather than vanishing, and one river study in October found feeding peaking overnight (a single riverine, autumn result, kept flagged in the research and not allowed to flip the shape). After dark, fish slowly in the same littoral cover you fished at dusk — and know dawn is the better bet.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais testé pour le pumpkinseed — aucun recensement de terrain, aucune expérience contrôlée pression-alimentation n'existe. Zéro par ABSENCE (pas un nul mesuré; cette formulation appartient à une espèce à nul mesuré seulement).
Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai du pumpkinseed. Le cycle d'épisodes de frai de 10–11 jours garantit des coïncidences lunaires occasionnelles; la coïncidence n'est pas un signal.

Aucune fonction alimentation-contre-débit n'existe; la seule donnée de débit est l'occurrence d'habitat (les adultes évitent la haute vélocité dans les ruisseaux). Les lacs servis du pumpkinseed sont de l'habitat littoral de lac/étang; aucun terme de débit n'est noté.

L'alimentation adulte est démontrablement conditionnée par la faune d'escargots de chaque lac (morphologie + disponibilité), mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure la faune d'escargots d'un lac; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.

La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour le pumpkinseed; elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome (la construction de nuages du flathead est propre à l'espèce et n'est pas empruntée).

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: As the water climbs through the low teens toward the ~15 °C nest-building onset, pumpkinseed move into the shallow, vegetated littoral they will nest in — colonies form on sand and gravel in water from about 15 cm deep to a few feet. Fish the vegetated shallows near that nesting ground; this species stages in its feeding habitat, close to where it will spawn.

In streams the habitat record is specific: adults hold near the bank in the clearer, slower water, with plant cover and woody structure over sand — and avoid riffles, deep water and high velocity. Fish the quiet, covered bank water, not the runs.

Time the day by this species' own clock, not bluegill's: pumpkinseed feeding peaks at dawn and dusk on a solid daylight base — the stomach studies agree on the twin peaks. Be set up on the shallows at the light changes, and fish the warming middle of the day as a real second shift, not a wait for evening.

Below about 8 °C, expect the measured floor: spontaneous activity collapses toward a minimum at 7.9 °C and feeding drops markedly below it. Cold prespawn fish are a patience pattern — slow, close presentations in the warmest shallow water you can find.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The spawn is a colony season: nests in colonies of about 3–15, on sand and gravel in water from about 15 cm to a few feet deep, each nest roughly twice the fish's length (about 10–38 cm across), often in or beside bluegill colonies. Onset is around 15 °C with the main band at 17–25 °C, and the colonies pulse in repeated bouts of about 10–11 days from May into August — there is almost always a fresh wave of nesting fish somewhere in the window.

Fish the light changes hardest: guarding males feed measurably less than females, and what feeding they do is concentrated at dawn and dusk near the nest — the twin peaks are the spawn clock as much as the summer one. And the guard-state rule, stated as the rating states it: a male that charges a bait on the nest is defending, not feeding — strikes on nests are aggression, and the entry says so rather than dressing them up as a bite pattern.

spawningSources.citation: Chronologie saisonnière (colonies de frai ~15–25 °C, épisodes répétés de 10–11 jours mai–août; la fenêtre de garde est une annotation — les mâles qui gardent s'alimentent MOINS, aucun bonus); alimentation hivernale mesurée (prévalence d'étang de mi-hiver 88%)

about: The rainbow trout is the Pacific salmon family's most travelled member — native to the Pacific slope, now stocked and naturalised across the continent, with its sea-run form called steelhead. Rainbows are cool-water fish that live where temperature and oxygen suit them, roughly the 10–18 °C band, and in the rating model their feeding peaks in the high teens Celsius.

In lakes they organise into zones — the littoral shoals, the open-water layer and the depths — tracking insects, zooplankton and forage fish as the seasons turn, and spawning in spring in flowing water over gravel. They are aerial, acrobatic fighters and eager takers of flies and lures alike. Anglers target them everywhere from mountain streams to prairie pothole lakes, for the jump, the colours, and the table.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Chironomids are the year-round stillwater staple — the pupa patterns (basic black-and-red is the type) fished as they ascend. Leeches are the searching pattern when there's no hatch, and the low-light pattern always. One disagreement we keep honest: a famous stillwater authority holds that trout feed only at shoreline edges and in the top foot of the surface, with deep fish merely resting — while the Kamloops school demonstrably catches feeding fish deep, on chironomid pupae ascending from as much as 40 ft. Both are in the books; if the edges are dead, the deep chironomid game is real and proven.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The Kamloops trio of presentations: (1) Indicator fishing — the fly rides about 2 ft off bottom; deep work takes leaders of 17–24 ft, with the pupae suspended at the depth the sounder shows, and a slight breeze supplies the movement. (2) 'Naked' — floating line, long leader, no indicator, a very slow retrieve. (3) 'Dangling' — a sinking line lowered to about 2 ft off bottom; strikes are violent and the trout hook themselves.
Retrieves in this canon are specified to the second — check your wristwatch. Slow means measured, not approximate.

In rivers, read the water first: currents, rocks, pools, riffles, runs, bends. During a hatch, fish the emerger early; the exact-imitation school (Swisher & Richards) found their flat-floating patterns roughly twice as effective as hackled flies on selective fish — match the insect, not the catalogue. The 'pounds of meat' rule settles fly choice: fish take the food that gives the most food value for the least effort.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: No hatch? The Balanced Leech is not just an indicator fly — cast and retrieved, it hops and pitches, and it's the proven no-hatch searcher.
In rivers on the toughest days, remember where the biggest trout are: resting, in daylight, in the deep lies — they have to be provoked, not fed.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Chironomid pupae at the sounder's depth, leeches for searching and for the summer doldrums, and the big subaquatic food patterns when they're hunting meat. Match lure and fly size to the food you can see — 'look over the side of the boat' is the whole selection method.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Deep indicator work is the summer skill: leaders of 17–24 ft (a 25-ft leader in the master's own account), pupae hung at the depth the fish are showing, a slight breeze doing the moving. Or dangle a sinking line to 2 ft off bottom and wait for the rod to be nearly taken from you.
Time the zones: rainbows travel between deep and shallow at dawn and dusk — the drop-offs at the light changes are the summer addresses for moving fish.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: In the doldrums, leeches at first and last light, fished slow.

And if the lake gives you nothing, a river will: tight-line nymphing through the pools and runs produces in the heat, and the biggest river fish can be provoked from their resting lies with a streamer worked with a jerk-strip — animate it by jerking the rod tip, not by pulling line.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Leeches move to the front in fall — the non-hatch searching choice and the low-light pattern in one. Chironomids still produce on the warm afternoons.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the shoal edges and drop-offs with the long-leader presentations, slow. Fall rainbows feed deliberately — the retrieves timed to the second matter more, not less, as the water cools.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: When the lake is quiet, go to moving water: fall rivers fish well with nymphs and swung wet flies — the classic down-and-across swing with a hand-twist retrieve is a century old and still catches these fish.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Deep presentations only: chironomid pupae hung at the sounder's depth on very long leaders, or dangled lines at 2 ft off bottom in the comfort layer. Surface and shoal patterns are for cooler days.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: If you can't reach the comfort layer with your tackle, the honest answer is to fish the coldest part of the day — dawn — in the deepest part of the shoal zone, or switch water. Warm, oxygen-thin water stresses these fish; handle any you catch with extra care and release them quickly.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Springs and inflows are the warm-season refuges — where cold water enters, rainbows gather. Fish the inflow edges at first light.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Being straight about the sources: rainbow-specific ice tactics were the thinnest ice coverage in tonight's library work. The one ice-fishing book in the canon covers trout — location, strategy, jigging and set lines, with sonar — but its rainbow-specific depths and baits weren't something we could verify, so we won't invent them.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: What carries over with confidence from the open-water canon: these are insect-eaters that feed by sight in the top of their world — small, natural presentations, fished slowly in the shoal zone, are the consistent-with-canon approach. For the rest, treat ice rainbows as the experiment they honestly are in the literature.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the ice rainbows won't go, that's a genuinely under-documented fishery — the books leave it nearly blank. The proven cold-season rainbow fishing is the open water: late fall and early spring on the shoals.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: Find the comfort water first: rainbows live where temperature and oxygen suit them — roughly the 10–18 °C band — and in a lake that's organised in three zones: the littoral shoals, the drop-offs, and the deep water. Spring puts them on the shoals and along the shoreline edges, where the food is.
The stillwater master's first move costs nothing: look over the side of the boat. The food tells you where the fish are — rainbow trout feed mostly on aquatic insects, and the hatch is the map.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer rainbows track the comfort band — temperature plus oxygen, around 10–18 °C — and the thermocline is an oxygen barrier as much as a temperature layer; don't fish under it expecting life. The big summer chironomid emergences rise out of deep water: in the classic worked example, trout were feeding 3–5 ft off the bottom over 29 ft of water, on pupae coming up from as deep as 40 ft.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall cools the shoals back into the comfort band and the fish return to the littoral zone and the drop-offs — the spring map, reversed. Lake fish concentrate where the food is as the insect year winds down: leeches, scuds and the last emergences along the shoals.

movementSeasons.heading: Eau chaude
lines: The water is above the comfort band — the fish have left for the cool, oxygenated layer, and the thermocline is a hard ceiling on their world: below it, oxygen fails. Fish the layer itself and the drop-offs that reach it, or don't fish rainbows at all today.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: Under the ice, rainbows stay in their comfort water — the same temperature-and-oxygen thinking that runs their whole year. Shallower than the deep species, along the shoal and drop-off water they used in the fall.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light and dusk; quietest at after dark.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at midday; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 17–19 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 25.5 °C, from the species' research file.
