Aucun mesuré pour cette espèce.
Quigley et al. 2023 ont trouvé les effets solunaires/lunaires nuls pour les pêches à la truite en général (la température de l'air était le seul prédicteur significatif) — cohérent avec le zéro ici.

about: The rock bass — redeye, goggle-eye — is the shade-loving panfish of rocky lakes and streams, a deep-bodied, red-eyed member of the sunfish family that lives where its name says: in the shadow of boulders, rootwads and woody cover. It's a measured fish of moderate temperatures, feeding best around the low twenties Celsius, and so sedentary that a good rock in July may hold the same fish for weeks.

Rock bass share the smallmouth's coarse spawning ground in northern lakes, fanning circular nests in sand and gravel near cover at about 15–21 °C, and they feed on crayfish, insects and small fish, striking short and holding tight to home. Anglers meet them while fishing for everything else — and keep meeting them, because rock bass are abundant, willing, and underrated on the table and on light tackle.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Offerings matched to the measured benthic diet: crayfish, large aquatic insect larvae (dragonfly nymphs and hellgrammites in the stream diet work) and small invertebrates, presented down at the rock and wood. Rock bass look down — the retinal study shows a high-acuity zone aimed at the benthos in front and below — so the bait belongs on the bottom in front of the cover, not over it. No lure is named in the rock bass literature, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Start with this species' clock, because it is the opposite of its cousins': rock bass feed most actively from dusk through the night, with dawn elevated and midday the floor. Prespawn effort spent at the light changes and after dark is fishing the measured peak; a midday prespawn trip is fishing the daily minimum. Below about 8.5 °C, expect the floor itself — the Ontario winter work puts the feeding onset near 8.5 °C, and cold prespawn fish barely move for food.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the rocky shallows are empty, the water has not reached the prospecting band — drop to the deeper cover off the spawning ground and wait for the temperature, not a different bait. This spawn is temperature-gated, in May–June and late June at northern latitudes.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small benthic offerings pitched to the nest edges and the cover beside them — crayfish and large-insect profiles from the diet ledger. Nothing spawn-specific beyond the nests themselves is rock-bass-measured, and no lure is named in the literature.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Know what a nest strike is: guarding males do not eat while they guard — they fast on reserves, darken, fan and circle the nest, and their strikes are territorial defence, not feeding. Fish the nest fish if you choose, but read the entry honestly: the catchable feeders are the females and the males between cycles (males can complete more than one nesting cycle in a season), at the dusk-to-night feeding peak, on the cover around the nesting ground. Eggs hatch in about 3–4 days and fry leave the nest around 9–10 days after hatching, so a guarded nest is a short tenancy — note the spot and come back for the postspawn feed.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A nest male that swats everything and eats nothing is the guard state working exactly as documented — about a third of nests fail to predation despite the guard, which is why the defence is relentless. Move to the feeding fish on the adjacent cover rather than pestering the nest.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the diet, and know it splits by water: in streams, crayfish lead by calories, then small fish, then insects. In lakes, the big Lake Ontario stomach study (218 fish) is amphipod-and-insect-led — more caddis larvae than midges — with snails and crayfish significant and fish becoming important only in fish over about 200 mm. So the lake pattern is small benthic invertebrate and crayfish offerings at the rock; the river pattern leads with crayfish. Juveniles of both waters eat amphipods, copepods and aquatic insects — small fish want small offerings. No lure is named in the rock bass literature, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The day is upside down versus the other basses, and it is measured three ways — retinal anatomy built for dim-light benthic feeding, a river diel study peaking from 20:00 to 04:00, and the agency synthesis (most active late evening and early morning): dusk is the peak, night runs near it, dawn is elevated, and midday is the floor — but not a zero, because the study fish fed at low levels throughout the day and summer rock bass are famously catchable on structure at noon. Fish the cover all day if you must; fish it at dusk and after dark if you can.

Clarity is a hard address for this fish: rock bass responded physiologically to silt at just 10 NTU, they are on record as preferring clear water and intolerant of turbidity and siltation — and the lake fish in the experiment showed no clear ability to compensate, while river fish adjusted within about an hour. After a silting rain, lake rock bass are the first fish to write off and the last to recover; give the lake a clearing window, and in a river, wait out the first hour of dirty water before judging the spot.

A temperature honesty note the entry keeps visible: a laboratory preferendum of 29–31 °C exists for this species and was rejected as the activity anchor in the research — it came from mostly juvenile fish seined beside a power-plant thermal discharge that had run for 56 years, and the authors themselves flagged the bias. The 21 °C field figure above is the wild fish's number; do not let anyone sell you a rock bass pattern built on the lab fish.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If bright midday fish on the cover won't take, you are fishing the measured daily floor — shrink the offering, put it tight to the shaded side of the structure, and slow down; or bank the spot for dusk, when the same fish are the most catchable rock bass of the day. And check the oxygen in hot, still weather: the agency record calls this species intolerant of low dissolved oxygen (direction only — no threshold was ever measured), so in a stagnant basin the fish are in the oxygenated layer, not on the deep rock.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer benthic menu, slower and tighter to the cover: crayfish and large-insect offerings in the river pattern, amphipod-and-insect-sized offerings in lakes. Cooling compresses the feeding toward the dusk peak — save the best presentations for the light change.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the transitions and the early night hardest as the days shorten. As the water approaches about 8.5 °C the feeding floor arrives — the Ontario collections found rock bass abstaining from feeding for weeks at 6.5–8.5 °C — so late-fall effort belongs on the warmest afternoons in the deepest cover, in short, located-fish sessions.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall fish have gone silent, check the temperature before the tackle: below the 8.5 °C floor this species is measured to fast for weeks, and no presentation fixes a fasting fish. The deep wintering cover is the address that remains.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small, slow, bottom offerings over located fish on the hard-bottom flats. Winter consumption is minimal, so the bait has to arrive at a sedentary fish — no winter-specific lure is named in the rock bass literature.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the day's edges — early morning, late afternoon, and sometimes at night, per the ice literature, consistent with this species' open-water dusk-to-night signature — and give a located school real time. Rock bass are caught through the ice in Manitoba; the occurrence is documented, the catch rates are not, and the entry invents no numbers for them.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A dead mid-winter flat is usually the fast itself, compounded by low oxygen — the ice literature notes rock bass rarely feed during low-oxygen periods. Move toward better-oxygenated water and shallower late-season ground before you conclude the lake has none.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small, slow, bottom offerings over the hard-bottom flats — the open-water benthic diet at winter size. No ice presentation is rock-bass-measured; this is the winter evidence applied honestly, not an ice finding.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the day's edges and into the early night on the transferred pattern (early morning, late afternoon, sometimes night, per the ice literature), set up on located schools on the mid-depth flats, and treat oxygen as a gate: rock bass are recorded as intolerant of low dissolved oxygen and the ice literature has them rarely feeding in low-oxygen periods, so a depleting basin's flats go quiet from the bottom up — move toward oxygenated water as the winter deepens, and toward the vegetated shallows as it ends.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Mid-winter silence on the flats is the documented fast more often than it is your presentation. The sourced moves are oxygen and timing, in that order — and if neither produces, the honest verdict is that this species' ice science runs out here: it has never been measured under ice well enough to promise more.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: As the water climbs through the low teens, rock bass move onto the coarse spawning ground they share with smallmouth in northern lakes — sand and gravel with wood or rock cover nearby. Fish the rocky shallows and the cover beside them; prospecting begins around 13–15 °C, ahead of spawning proper.

In rivers, prespawn fish hold the low-velocity cover they prefer all year — rootwads and woody structure in the slower water, more rootwad-oriented and slower than the smallmouth beside them. Locations are highly cover-correlated for this species; fish the cover, not the open pool.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Northern rock bass spawn at about 15–21 °C, on circular nests about 20–30 cm across that the male fans in sand and gravel near cover — wood or rock, the same coarse-substrate-plus-cover habitat smallmouth choose in the same lakes, with the two species' nesting overlapping in time. Larger, older males nest earliest. (The literature also carries wider, warmer southern bands, to 27 °C; the monograph keeps them separate and this entry fishes the northern band.)

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer rock bass are cover-bound and sedentary: rocky structure, rootwads and woody cover in clear water, holding in the shadow of the structure by day. Temperature frames the season — the field-measured preference is about 21 °C (20.7–21.3 °C across the two field studies), with the model's plateau running to about 24 °C; the growth-optimum compilation sits higher, at 27.7 °C, on the declining limb. Fish the rock and wood in the low-20s °C water first.
River fish hold lower-velocity woody cover than smallmouth — rootwads over log complexes — and barely travel. A found river rock bass is a resident, not a traveller; work its cover thoroughly.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall feeding is directly documented, not assumed: the river diel study's fish were feeding in mid-October, on the same dusk-through-night pattern, so the season holds up through September and October and falls with temperature toward the winter floor rather than ending at Labour Day. Fish the summer rock and wood cover, sliding deeper and slower as the water cools.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter rock bass are a trough, honestly stated: Ontario through-ice collections at 6.5–8.5 °C found fish that appeared not to have eaten for several weeks, and the centrarchid winter synthesis generalises that — greatly reduced feeding that does not universally cease. Fish school in winter. What feeding remains concentrates where the season's own notes put it: first in the shallows early, then mid-depth hard-bottom flats and drop-offs, reactivating toward the vegetated shallows late — that progression is the ice literature's description (expert consensus), not a measurement, and the entry labels it as such.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: PROVISIONAL — and the entry carries the flag the research requires: this ice set is a flagged provisional, not a validated one. What is species-own: rock bass are present and caught through the ice (including in Manitoba), Ontario collections show them winter-fasting at 6.5–8.5 °C, they school in winter, and the ice literature describes first-ice shallows, mid-winter mid-depth hard-bottom flats and drop-offs, and a late-ice reactivation toward vegetated shallows. What does not exist: any under-ice diel, light, oxygen-response or catch-rate study of this species — the shapes below are the programme ice scaffold, and the timing is the measured open-water dusk-to-night shape carried under ice, dampened and labelled a transfer.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 20.7–24 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 31.8 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for rock bass is a documented absence: no front, barometric-pressure, wind, precipitation or moon effect has ever been measured for this species, in any study design the research could find — no creel model, no telemetry term, no controlled trial. Pressure and moon are therefore zero in the rating as decisions, not oversights, and this entry borrows no other species' coefficient to fill the space. There is no front trick for this fish to sell you: what is measured is temperature, light, season and turbidity, and those are what the other sections fish. A front matters here only as the temperature, light and silt change it actually delivers — and the silt change, at least, is real (see the summer entry).

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: Dusk is the measured peak of this species' day — the start of the 20:00–04:00 feeding window the river study recorded. Be set up on your best rock and wood cover before the light goes, not travelling while it changes; the first hour of darkness is prime rock bass time, not the tail of the day shift.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is a main shift for rock bass, not a leftover: the model's night value is 0.90, just under the dusk peak — the anatomy (a retina specialised for crepuscular benthic feeding), the measured overnight feeding peak, and the crayfish diet all point the same way, because crayfish are nocturnally active benthic prey. Fish crayfish and large-insect offerings slowly along the rock and wood after dark. This is the entry the bass habits will talk you out of; the rock bass evidence says the opposite of the smallmouth's near-rest night.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Bright midday is this species' measured daily floor (day value 0.55, not zero): the fish hold in the shadow of their structure — the angling consensus to fish the shady side of the cover agrees with the anatomy and the diel data. Fish tight, shaded and slow at noon, and treat a midday fish as a located, provoked fish rather than a feeding-pattern fish.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais mesuré pour le rock bass dans aucun protocole. Aucun coefficient n'est emprunté : les revendications de pression ailleurs dans le programme sont testées nulles ou non mesurées, et le mécanisme de vessie natatoire est une trivialité d'équivalent de profondeur. Zéro est une décision, pas une omission.

Jamais mesuré pour le rock bass — aucune analyse d'alimentation lunaire et aucune étude de signal de frai lunaire n'existe pour cette espèce. Rien n'est emprunté à la littérature lunaire d'aucune autre espèce.

Le rock bass choisit des abris à faible vélocité (position d'habitat, Probst et al. 1984), mais aucun coefficient débit-contre-taux-d'alimentation n'existe et le modèle de lac n'a aucune entrée de débit pour cet ensemble.

Le régime est chargé en écrevisses/benthique (Probst et al. 1984; Elrod et al. 1981), mais la composition du régime n'est pas un coefficient d'heure d'alimentation. La voie de proies benthique-nocturne est déjà comptée dans le facteur lumière/journalier; un poids de proies séparé la compterait deux fois.

NOTE DE PORTÉE (pas un zéro) : le rock bass riverain compense au limon en ~60 min (Bunt et al. 2004); la courbe notée est la forme lacustre (non compensante) parce que le moteur sert les lacs. Enregistré ici pour que le choix soit visible.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: As the water climbs through the low teens, rock bass move onto the coarse spawning ground they share with smallmouth in northern lakes — sand and gravel with wood or rock cover nearby. Fish the rocky shallows and the cover beside them; prospecting begins around 13–15 °C, ahead of spawning proper.

In rivers, prespawn fish hold the low-velocity cover they prefer all year — rootwads and woody structure in the slower water, more rootwad-oriented and slower than the smallmouth beside them. Locations are highly cover-correlated for this species; fish the cover, not the open pool.

Start with this species' clock, because it is the opposite of its cousins': rock bass feed most actively from dusk through the night, with dawn elevated and midday the floor. Prespawn effort spent at the light changes and after dark is fishing the measured peak; a midday prespawn trip is fishing the daily minimum. Below about 8.5 °C, expect the floor itself — the Ontario winter work puts the feeding onset near 8.5 °C, and cold prespawn fish barely move for food.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Northern rock bass spawn at about 15–21 °C, on circular nests about 20–30 cm across that the male fans in sand and gravel near cover — wood or rock, the same coarse-substrate-plus-cover habitat smallmouth choose in the same lakes, with the two species' nesting overlapping in time. Larger, older males nest earliest. (The literature also carries wider, warmer southern bands, to 27 °C; the monograph keeps them separate and this entry fishes the northern band.)

Know what a nest strike is: guarding males do not eat while they guard — they fast on reserves, darken, fan and circle the nest, and their strikes are territorial defence, not feeding. Fish the nest fish if you choose, but read the entry honestly: the catchable feeders are the females and the males between cycles (males can complete more than one nesting cycle in a season), at the dusk-to-night feeding peak, on the cover around the nesting ground. Eggs hatch in about 3–4 days and fry leave the nest around 9–10 days after hatching, so a guarded nest is a short tenancy — note the spot and come back for the postspawn feed.

spawningSources.citation: Frai 15.6–21.1 °C (Scott & Crossman 1973), chronologie nid/alevins + jeûne du mâle qui garde (Gross & Nowell 1980 — annotation seulement, aucun coefficient), habitat de frai de lac nord-tempéré (Musch 2007); alimentation d'octobre mesurée (Johnson & Dropkin 1993) et tient la valeur d'automne élevée délibérément

about: The sauger is the walleye's river brother — smaller, slimmer, camouflaged in saddle blotches, and built for current and dim water in a way that lets it hunt where walleye won't. It's a fish of big rivers and turbid lakes, with a measured thermal preference near 19–20 °C inside a plateau of 18–24 °C, and a lower heat ceiling than its cousin — the research puts its upper lethal point around 26–27 °C.

Sauger spawn at night in shallow flowing water, broadcasting eggs over gravel and cobble, and spend the year along channel edges and current breaks, often deeper and further into the current than walleye. Anglers who fish big rivers — the Red, the Missouri, the Mississippi — target them alongside walleye, value them as the better fighter of the two by many accounts, and rank the eating just as high.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Match the demersal menu the stomach work measured: bottom-oriented prey fish — emerald shiner was over 75% of the food in one studied feeding bay, with yellow perch and young sauger also taken roughly in proportion to what was available, because sauger are not highly selective feeders. No lure or technique is named for sauger in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here — bottom-presented, prey-fish-sized and unhurried is the supported shape of it.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the dark half of the day hardest: two-thirds of the tracked sauger in one movement study moved into the feeding areas between sunset and midnight, and most of the rest arrived before 03:00. Be set up on the staging pools before sunset rather than travelling after it.

Credit the cold-water physiology honestly: meals were still being digested at 5 °C — about 90% of a meal in 54 hours — and feeding continued every one to three days through the cold months in the southern reservoir record, even though growth in length stops at about 12 °C and below. Cold prespawn fish do feed; they just feed on a slow clock, so give a located pool real time.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If staging fish will not move for a bait, shrink the travel, not the spot: this is a demersal feeder whose prey sits on the bottom, so a presentation that leaves the bottom leaves the menu. Stay on the deepest slow water you have found and wait for the sunset movement instead of searching.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: There is no spawn tackle story in the sauger research, and this entry will not dress one up: no lure is named, and the honest offering is the year-round one — prey-fish-sized, on the bottom, in the gravel shallows the aggregation is using. What changes at spawn is the address and the hour, not the menu.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish it after dark: spawning is nocturnal, and the movement record peaks between sunset and midnight. And read the catch rate honestly — spawning aggregations concentrate fish, and high catch rates on an aggregation are a density effect the research flags explicitly, not proof of a feeding peak. Sauger broadcast their eggs and give no parental care, so there is no nest-guarding strike pattern to fish for either.

Expect the window to be population-variable, not a single weekend: some fish migrate hundreds of kilometres to spawn, while roughly a quarter to a third in one tracked reservoir population stayed resident and spawned locally. If one reach is empty, the next gravel reach may simply hold a different contingent.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the gravel is crowded with fish that will not take, you are watching the density effect from the wrong side — spawning fish are spawning, not feeding. Drop to the deep slow water just off the spawning ground and fish the fish that are staging and recovering there, at dusk and into the night.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The summer menu is the demersal one: prey fish taken off the bottom — emerald shiner in the northern bay record, shad in the southern reservoirs, perch and young sauger elsewhere — with benthic invertebrates, including crayfish and insects, a real secondary food when prey fish are scarce. No lure is named in the sauger literature, and none is invented here: size to the bottom prey fish, keep it down, and let the fish's own low-light feeding do the rest.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Use the diel shape the model is built on — dusk 1.0, night 0.85, dawn 0.80, day 0.65 — because it is measured, not borrowed: the sauger's tapetum is well developed and spread across the whole retina, demersal prey were eaten throughout the full 24 hours, and the daytime score is a real shift, not a lull, in the turbid water this fish lives in. In clear, bright conditions the balance tips to night; in murk, the day stays open.

Watch the top of the temperature band as carefully as the bottom: the measured juvenile upper lethal family runs 26.6 to 30.4 °C, and the model's ceiling uses 26.6 °C, the family's low end — sauger's own number, not a walleye hand-me-down. As water pushes past the mid-20s, expect the fish deeper and slower, and past the plateau the honest move is to the coolest deep water available.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a bright summer day is dead, do not conclude the fish have left — in clearer water this species feeds at night, and the same deep pools reopen after dark. Either wait for the light to go or find the most turbid water in the system, where the daytime feeding window stays open longest.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Upsize only to the menu: the autumn ration peak is a prey-fish ration — the same demersal shiner, shad and perch diet, eaten at the year's highest daily rate of up to roughly 3.5% of body weight on the top days in the Lake of the Woods record. No fall-specific lure is named in the research; prey-fish-sized, on the bottom, in the deep pools is the supported pattern at the season when the fish are most willing to use it.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the whole dark window, not just the edges of it: dusk is the peak, night holds at 0.85, and in the low-light months the Ohio record showed feeding running essentially continuously. October's combination — peak ration, falling light, cooling water moving into the plateau — is the best set-up this species offers all year.

Let cooling work for you down to a point: ration stays high while the water falls through the teens, and gonadal growth through the coming winter is built on this autumn feeding. As the water drops toward 5 °C the digestion clock stretches — about 54 hours for a meal — so slow the presentation as the season deepens without abandoning the deep pools.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall fish are marked but refusing, the variable to change is light, not tackle: come back at dusk or after dark on the same pool. And if the water has already fallen out of the teens, treat the day as an early-winter day — fewer, slower feeds on the deepest slow water — rather than fishing it like October.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small end of the prey-fish menu, presented on the bottom of the deep pools and given time: at 5 °C a meal takes roughly 54 hours to digest, so a winter fish that fed yesterday is not hunting today. No winter-specific tackle is named in the sauger research — the winter difference is patience and address, not gear.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish slow windows on the deepest slow water, and handle deep-caught winter fish with the measured caution from the Pool 4 winter fishery: release mortality ran about 2.4% for fish from shallower than 9 m against 21 to 38% from 9.1 m and deeper. A deep winter sauger you intend to release is a fish to bring up and return quickly, or to leave alone.

Time the day on the carried-over shape with its flag showing: the under-ice and winter diel pattern has never been measured for sauger, so dusk-first timing here is the open-water sunset-to-midnight movement applied to winter as a labelled transfer, not a winter finding.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A dead winter pool is usually a fed pool or an empty one, and the test is time: with digestion running to days, one good feeding window can silence a pool for the next two. Move to the next deep pool rather than changing baits in the one that just fed.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The winter end of the demersal menu — prey-fish-sized, on the bottom of the deep pools. No ice-specific presentation has ever been measured for sauger, and none is claimed here; the winter evidence supports the address and the patience, and the tackle follows the open-water diet honestly.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Give each pool time on the measured winter clock: this species digests a meal in about 54 hours at 5 °C and fed every one to three days through a measured winter, so a pool's fish feed in windows days apart, not hours. The dusk-first timing is the open-water diel shape carried under ice as a labelled transfer — the under-ice shape itself is unmeasured, and the provisional flag above is exactly about that gap.

Handle deep fish as the winter mortality data directs: in the Pool 4 winter fishery, release mortality was about 2.4% from shallower than 9 m and 21 to 38% from 9.1 m and deeper. Through the ice, a deep sauger bound for release should come up once, quickly, or the deep pools should be fished for the table only.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the ice pools are silent for days, that is consistent with the measured winter clock rather than proof of absence — but check the geography before the tackle: if you are on open basin water, the measured winter concentration is toward the mouth and the pools, and moving water, not baits, is the fix the data supports.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Before the spawn, sauger stage toward flowing-water spawning ground while the ration is still in its measured low half of the year — the field ration programme put the low from March through July, so prespawn fish are present and catchable but are not feeding at the autumn rate. Expect staging fish to hold deep and move little through the cold part of the day.

The staging address is the deep, low-velocity pool: across the big-water studies, adults select high turbidity, low slope and deep, slow pools, and spawning aggregations form downstream of warm, turbid inflows. Work the deep slow water below those inflows first.

On big turbid water, stage on the deep basin water nearest the inflow mouths — sauger were recorded from about 3 to 35 m deep in one northern system, routinely working darker, deeper water than walleye use. Start deep and check shallower only at the light changes.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: The spawn itself is a shallow, flowing-water event at night: a broadcast over gravel, cobble and rubble — also sand, boulders and bedrock — in about 0.6 to 3.6 m of water, with males arriving first. Range-wide the published temperature family runs about 2.0 to 15.6 °C, and in Manitoba the run is mid-to-late May, weeks after the walleye run ends in the same system.

Look for the aggregation below warm, turbid inflows: in study after study the spawning fish concentrated downstream of tributaries carrying warm, turbid water, on clean gravel in flowing water — on the home system, tributary mouths and gravel reaches are where the May fish gather.

Where a turbid inflow enters big water, the delta and its secondary channels drew the spawning fish in the Missouri record — warmer water and high physical turbidity over gravel, chosen over the open main channel. Fish the inflow's gravel fan and its side channels first.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer is this species' own thermal country: the measured preferendum sits near 19.6 °C inside a physiological optimum plateau of 18 to 24 °C, with a May-to-August field preference of about 15 to 21 °C. Fish the deep, dark water inside that band — as summer flows and turbidity fall, the fish shift deeper, and the deep water is the summer address.

The summer river address is the deep, low-velocity pool in the main channel: high turbidity, low slope, slow water over depth. When the water clears and drops, expect the fish to be in the deepest pools rather than spread through the shallows.

On the big turbid basin, summer fish use the deep open water — the Ottawa record ran to 35 m, well below where walleye were typically found. Do not assume a shallow summer pattern on a fish whose eye is built for darker water than its cousin's.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is sauger's measured peak, and the entry is built around it: the Ohio River ration programme — 550 stomachs over fourteen months — found daily ration high from August through January with its maximum in October, and the low from March through July, the reverse of the walleye shape. Fish the deep pools and deep basin edges with the confidence that this, not summer, is the feeding season.

Cooling river fish settle into the large, deep, low-velocity pools and move short distances between neighbouring pools — the fall-to-early-spring telemetry pattern. Once you find one occupied pool, its neighbours are worth the same careful work.

On the big basin, fall fish stay on the deep water they used in summer and slide toward the inflow mouths as the year turns — the winter geography of the home system concentrates sauger toward the river mouth while the open basin's winter catch is overwhelmingly walleye.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Open-water winter sauger hold the fall pattern at its slowest: sedentary in large, deep, low-velocity pools, moving short distances between nearby pools, on the telemetry record. The physiology underneath is measured and unusual — this fish keeps feeding and digesting at temperatures where many species stop, with meals processed every one to three days across the 5 to 15 °C band in the reservoir record.

The winter river fishery on the home system is this species' own: in the winter 2024 creel between Lockport and the mouth, sauger were 33,985 of 49,425 fish caught — 69% of the catch. Winter river sauger are not a rumour; they are the main event, concentrated in the deep pools.

The basin splits the species in winter, and the entry says so rather than averaging it: sauger were 43% of the studied winter commercial catch in 1950–51, yet only about 2.6% of the south-basin winter angling catch in 2018–19, when walleye made up 95%. On open basin water expect sauger to be scarce in winter; toward the inflow mouths, expect them concentrated.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: The ice set for sauger is PROVISIONAL, and the entry carries that flag openly: winter feeding physiology, winter deep-pool habitat and a dominant ice fishery are all measured for this species, but its behaviour under ice — the diel shape, activity against snow, light and oxygen — has never been studied, and its Manitoba winter ration is unknown. Fish the large, deep, low-velocity pools and the deep basin water near the inflow mouths, where the winter fish are measured to hold.
The home-system ice geography is explicit: the winter 2024 creel from Lockport to the mouth recorded sauger at 69% of all fish caught. On the river in winter, sauger are the fishery.

On the open basin the same winter tells the opposite story — about 2.6% sauger in the 2018–19 south-basin winter angling catch against 95% walleye. Basin ice is walleye water that holds some sauger; the mouth water is where sauger concentrate.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 18–24 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 26.6 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for sauger is a documented null plus an absence, and they are different things. Barometric pressure was tested in the Lake Winnipeg catch models and was never statistically significant for sauger — that is a measured zero. Frontal passage itself has never been isolated in any sauger study, and moon has never been tested at all, so there is no front trick or moon phase to sell you for this fish: what is measured is temperature, light, turbidity and season, and those are what the other sections fish. A front matters here only as the cloud, temperature and flow change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Couvert
lines: Grey skies are a measured sauger positive, through the light pathway: in the Lake Winnipeg catch models, sauger catch rose with high cloud opacity — an indicator of decreased light — along with high temperature. Under a solid overcast, stretch the shallow and daytime fishing you would otherwise save for dusk; the cloud is doing part of the darkness work for a fish whose eye is the most light-sensitive in its genus.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The light changes run this species' day: two-thirds of tracked sauger moved into the feeding areas between sunset and midnight, and the model's dusk value is its maximum. Be set up on the deep pools and their edges before the transition, and work the first hours of darkness as the main shift — dawn, at 0.80, is the second window, not an afterthought.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: After dark the fish that held the deep pools by day work their edges and the nearby feeding flats — the sunset-to-midnight movement is the map. Start where the deep water meets the feeding ground, not in the middle of either.

Night is a primary sauger window, not a tail: the model's night value is 0.85 against walleye's 0.60, because the night feeding is sauger's own measurement — demersal prey used through the full 24 hours, movement into feeding areas running to 03:00, and night spawning in season. Fish the deep pools and their shallow edges slowly after dark, on the bottom, and expect the bite to hold for hours rather than spike and die.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Wind has a real sauger pathway and no measured size, and the entry keeps those separate: daily food consumption was influenced by wave activity in the Lake of the Woods programme — the plausible route is wind stirring turbidity and cutting light — but no study measured how much wind helps or hurts, so no wind speed is promised here. What you can use is the mechanism: a chop that muddies and darkens the shallows extends the conditions this fish feeds in; a blow that does neither is just weather.

weatherNotCounted.reason: La pression barométrique a été incluse comme covariable dans les GLM capture/effort du lac Winnipeg et aucun effet de pression du sauger n'est rapporté parmi les corrélats significatifs (le sauger suivait la température, l'opacité nuageuse, la décharge); le texte complet de la thèse dit que la relation pression–CPUE « n'a jamais été statistiquement significative » (vérifié 2026-11-06). Zéro par testé, aucun effet rapporté — formulation explicitement plus faible qu'un nul publié : le nul publié appartient à une autre espèce et n'est pas emprunté.
Jamais testé pour l'alimentation, la capture ou le frai du sauger dans aucune source localisée. Zéro par absence. Le nul lunaire publié d'une autre espèce est refusé comme nul du sauger.

Un vrai signal du sauger existe (captures culminant à la décharge moyenne de la rivière Rouge [B]; vélocités de frai bornées par Delphi 9.1–61.0 cm/s [C]), mais le moteur n'a aucune entrée de décharge/débit pour les lacs servis — aucun poids n'est parqué sur un facteur qui ne peut jamais noter (la leçon du blue catfish). Rouvrir si une entrée de débit de rivière est livrée.

La ration du sauger est démontrablement liée aux proies (activité des vagues + densité de proies [A]) et son champ de proies démersal explique sa large fenêtre journalière, mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure la densité de proies démersales; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.

L'opacité nuageuse est un corrélat positif significatif du sauger — comme indicateur d'intensité lumineuse dans le GLM. Elle entre par la voie du facteur lumière; aucun terme de nuages autonome (la construction de nuages du flathead est propre à l'espèce et n'est pas empruntée).

spawningSources.citation: Direction mesurée à l'échelle de l'habitat (les adultes choisissent la haute turbidité; frai sous les apports troubles — synthèse MICRA 2007; Jaeger et al. 2005; Graeb 2006); le seul test de terrain capture-contre-turbidité est un nul (Speers 2007); dose–réponse jamais mesurée — les ancrages sont de l'ingénierie †. PAS le type distance-de-réaction : la relation du sauger définit l'habitat, pas une pénalité visuelle

Ration de terrain : haute août–janv., maximum en octobre, basse mars–juill. Aucun ancrage; le facteur est NO_DATA (neutre §1.3)

about: The smallmouth — bronzeback to its fans — is the bass of rock, current and clear water, and pound for pound one of the hardest-fighting fish in fresh water. It's a cool-water bass: the rating model peaks its feeding in the low twenties Celsius, distinctly cooler than its largemouth cousin, and it thrives exactly where the water is cleanest and the bottom hardest.

Smallmouth hold on sand-and-gravel spawning flats in spring, then spend the summer around boulders, reefs and rocky points, feeding on crayfish, minnows and insects and roaming in loose wolfpacks. They jump, they bulldog, and they punish light tackle. Anglers target them for sport pure and simple — a river smallmouth on a light rod is many people's favourite fight in fishing.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Tubes are the all-season staple — jigheads up to 1/4 oz. In the coldest trophy windows (water in the high 40s to low 50s °F) it's small tubes and hair jigs fished painfully slow. A jig-and-grub swum slowly and horizontally covers the 40–58 °F window. After a jerkbait finds a pack, a 1/16-oz green pumpkin Ned rig is the clean-up follow-up.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the warmest pocket you can find — on the big lakes the trophy water is usually right where a light wind blows directly into shore. Slow is the whole prespawn technique: painfully slow tubes, then slower.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: When they won't move in cold water, repeat-cast rule: five, six or more presentations to the same spot before you give up on it. Cold prespawn smallmouth often eat the cast that looks exactly like the four they ignored.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The sight-fishing kit: a 3-in hair jig — black is the best colour day in and day out — pitched to visible fish, and tubes. In June, pods of big bass feed in 1–3 ft on young baitfish where you can see them work.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the sun at your back and your shadow off the water. A 1/16-oz black marabou hair jig pitched to standing cabbage clumps is the Shield-country sight-fishing standard.
During the spawn itself, poppers fished slow and quiet — the opposite of summer topwater style — are a season-specific play.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Guarding males that ignore everything are guarding, not feeding — note the spot and come back after the spawn, when those same fish bunch on the postspawn rock pattern, hungry.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Tubes, hair jigs and drop-shot rigs for the funk; then the rock baits — football jigs and craws on the breaks. For the suspended chalk-line fish, baits that hang in the column: jerkbaits and drop-shots fished high.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Slow down through the funk — deeper and slower than the spawn. When it breaks, hunt rock systematically: boulders first, then reef edges, then the break lines.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Deadstick a soft plastic in place for one to three full minutes. In the postspawn funk, a bait that does nothing, for longer than feels sane, is a legitimate and proven presentation.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Tubes everywhere; lipless crankbaits and blade baits ripped over rock humps in 15–35 ft when they're chasing; suspending jerkbaits as the search bait on Shield lakes. Topwater over the early-summer cabbage flats.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Cover water in the scatter season — the pods are small and spread. When a jerkbait finds a pack, drop the Ned rig or a tube on them immediately; packs feed competitively for a minute and then it's over.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Finesse is the late-summer answer: smaller tubes, drop-shots held still, deadsticked plastics. When bait is everywhere, your bait has to be the one that acts hurt, not the one that acts loud.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The depth ladder does the searching: square-bill crankbaits across the rocks in 4–8 ft, fast; then mid-divers on the 12-ft contour; then deeper divers touching bottom on the 16-ft break — moving deeper in 4-ft steps until you find the pod's level. Lipless baits and blade baits rip over the humps.

Fall livebait is its own system: a lively minnow or chub dragged tight to bottom on a 1- to 1½-oz no-snagg sinker, the bait a foot off bottom, hooks #4 to 2/0 for 3–8 in baits — on low-stretch mono, not braid; the fish feel braid's resistance and drop the bait.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Pods feed hard — when you find them, work fast and stay on them. Deep-diving suspending jerkbaits with long pauses are deadly in near-white-cap fall weather.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the ladder finds nothing shallow, the pod is one step deeper — keep stepping down in 4-ft increments rather than changing lakes. Fall pods are somewhere on the break; the ladder is how you prove where.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The crankbait depth ladder, blade baits over the humps, and the dragged live-minnow system on mono. Hair jigs and tubes for when they want it slow.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the pods you've found thoroughly before searching for new ones — a fall pod is worth an hour. Slow down as the water falls through the 40s °F: tubes and jig-and-pigs are the cold formula (a 3½-in tube on a 1/4-oz head; 1/8 oz in lower, clearer water).

Slow down as the water falls through the 40s °F: tubes and jig-and-pigs are the cold formula (a 3½-in tube on a 1/4-oz head; 1/8 oz in lower, clearer water), and above about 42 °F, slow-rolled spinnerbaits and 3½-in jerkbaits in the deep pools join in.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Hunt the warmest water — a creek mouth or bay 2 °F warmer than the main lake is a magnet in the cold months. Cold smallmouth gather where the water is least cold.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The cold-water formula: tubes and jig-and-pigs — a 3½-in tube on a 1/4-oz head (1/8 oz in lower, clearer water). Everything else is a warm-day bonus.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Slow, deep and patient. Fish the warmest pocket of the wintering area and give a spot many presentations — cold smallmouth do not move far for food.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A 2 °F difference is the whole game now — hunt the slightly warmer water (an inflow, a protected bay) before you change a single bait.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Here we have to be straight with you: none of the smallmouth books behind this app covers fishing for them through the ice. There's no book-taught ice lure or rig for smallmouth to pass on, and we'd rather tell you that than make one up.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: What the books do cover is their cold open water, right up to freeze-up and right after ice-out: tubes and jig-and-pigs fished painfully slowly in the deep pools (a 3½-in tube on a 1/4-oz head) — that's the sourced winter pattern, for open water.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If smallmouth are the goal in the cold months, the honest advice from this library is to fish them in open water — river mouths, below dams, the last open pools — with the cold-water tube formula, and hunt your ice fish among the species the ice books actually cover.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: South-facing bays warm quickest, and in stable weather prespawn smallmouth feed in 2–6 ft. The biggest females stage a step away, on secondary points and 'stickouts' beside the spawning areas at the backs of bays and coves, in little packs — that's the trophy pattern. On the Great Lakes they're shallow until the water reaches the mid-60s °F; in the cold 40s °F they're confined to harbours and wind-protected bays.
If cold pushes in — an offshore wind, heavy waves rolling in — they retreat to 15–25 ft.
In rivers in the 50s °F they're bunched in the deeper bank eddies and pools; keep moving until you find the bunch.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai
lines: Smallmouth spawn on sand mixed with pea gravel, nests built beside a log or boulder, in 2–5 ft. The males guard; the biggest bass hold the tallest, fastest-growing new cabbage nearby once the spawn ends.
River bass nest entirely out of the current, on sand mixed with pea gravel, nests built beside a log or boulder, in 2–5 ft. The males guard.

movementSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: The postspawn funk lasts about a week — slow retrieves, deeper water than the spawn. Then the rock hunt begins: the biggest boulders, reefs and rocky points, and the 'elevator' — the sharp breaks the fish ride between deep and shallow. On the big lakes there's also the chalk line: fish suspended high over 40–50 ft of water, halfway between the spawning bay and the summer islands.
On sunny days, postspawn fish suspend in the new cabbage — and the biggest bass dominate the tallest, fastest-growing cabbage in the area.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer smallmouth feed on top of reefs and humps in 2–10 ft. Wind blowing into a spot pulls them into 2–3 ft and keeps them there until the water clears. Late summer is the scatter season — the forage glut spreads them out, and the answer is to search faster and finesse more.

movementSeasons.heading: Début d’automne
lines: As the water drops below about 60 °F, smallmouth gather on steep-breaking shorelines, main-lake points and rock humps, packed in pods — and they stay active shallow until the water cools into the 40s °F. Steep and rocky is the fall address.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Steep breaks, main-lake points and rock humps, in pods, active shallow on the warmest part of the day. Fall smallmouth bunch tighter than at any other open-water time — find one and you've found the group.

movementSeasons.heading: Fin d’automne
lines: Wintering water: on the Great Lakes, the ends of large points, deep reefs and rockpiles over 40–45 ft flats, around 40 ft down.

Wintering water: in northern rivers, deep, slow water around clay, rock and boulders. (In the biggest northern rivers these fish migrate — 70 miles and more has been tracked — while in smaller Ozark-style water they barely travel at all; know which kind of river you're on.)

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: Where smallmouth winter is well taught: deep water — around 40 ft on the Great Lakes, off the ends of big points and over deep reefs and rockpiles.
Where smallmouth winter is well taught: in northern rivers, the deep, slow pools around clay, rock and boulders.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 20–24 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 32 °C, from the species' research file.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: After a summer cold front, smallmouth drop off the tops of the reefs and humps and tuck where the rock meets the sand at the base — usually 12–25 ft (10–14 ft in shallow lakes; 15–40 ft ledges in deep ones). And the deeper the bass, the less the front bothers them: from about 25 ft down they score bigger and more consistently after fronts than the shallow fish do.

Craws are kings after a front — the fish refuse to rise. The #1 post-front bait is a 1/4-oz football head with a 4-in craw, crawled along the rock-to-sand transition with long pauses. Second is the drop-shot, fished dead still — held in place, your own pulse makes a dangling plastic dance; dead-sticking is a close second to it.
Go dark: a real dark melon tube is the post-front colour rule. Scent makes a genuine difference on these days.
The strike zone collapses to inches. Everything is bottom, slow, and full of pauses — if your bait is rising off the bottom, it's out of the game.

The counter-move: rivers. After a front, river smallmouth odds actually improve for larger fish. Slow down — swum grubs, crawled hair jigs, drop-shots — and fish tight behind current breaks, from the centre of the pool to its tail. Topwaters and cranks can still work in the river when the lake is dead.

weatherOverlays.heading: Automne — le lendemain d’un front
lines: Forget the usual post-front advice — in fall, cold fronts turn smallmouth ON. The nastiest days around turnover are the best days of the season. Get out in it, fish the steep breaks and humps with the depth ladder and blade baits, and expect the pods to be feeding, not hiding.

weatherOverlays.heading: Début d’automne — le lendemain d’un front
lines: Forget the usual post-front advice — in fall, cold fronts turn smallmouth ON. The nastiest days are often the best days of the season. Get out in it, fish the steep breaks and humps with the depth ladder and blade baits, and expect the pods to be feeding, not hiding.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Heavy onshore wind in early summer condenses the whole food chain — work the points, reefs and windward shorelines FAST with spinnerbaits, lipless cranks and shallow-to-medium crankbaits. Wind into the spot is a feeding trigger for smallmouth.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Post-front bluebird days — bright, cold and still — are the dark-bait days: dark tubes, scent, and presentations dead-slow on the bottom. That's the known cure; there isn't a better one in the books.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The day's edges are worth being set up for — the trophy survey lore points to the windows around sunrise and sunset again and again. Be on your best rock when the light changes.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Aucun effet mesuré de la tendance de pression n'existe pour les achigans. Le terme est 0 sur la force des nuls au niveau de la famille tirés des tests de pression directs du programme — amendement, décision de Dave 2026-10-23 après l'audit de Manns.
ÉCART DE SPÉC G5 : aucune étude contrôlée d'alimentation en oxygène dissous n'existe pour l'achigan à petite bouche. Rien n'est estimé à sa place.
Aucune donnée pour cette espèce; rien d'emprunté.
Aucun paramètre lunaire ne survit à la cotation.

Fish the sun at your back and your shadow off the water. A 1/16-oz black marabou hair jig pitched to standing cabbage clumps is the Shield-country sight-fishing standard.
During the spawn itself, poppers fished slow and quiet — the opposite of summer topwater style — are a season-specific play.

Then the rock hunt begins: the biggest boulders, reefs and rocky points, and the 'elevator' — the sharp breaks the fish ride between deep and shallow. On the big lakes there's also the chalk line: fish suspended high over 40–50 ft of water, halfway between the spawning bay and the summer islands.
On sunny days, postspawn fish suspend in the new cabbage — and the biggest bass dominate the tallest, fastest-growing cabbage in the area.
Slow down through the funk — deeper and slower than the spawn. When it breaks, hunt rock systematically: boulders first, then reef edges, then the break lines.

about: The splake is a hatchery-made cross — lake trout × brook trout, Salvelinus namaycush × fontinalis — bred to combine the brook trout's fast early growth with the lake trout's size, and stocked in cold lakes across the north. It fishes like its parents: a cold-water char whose summer life is a temperature story, sliding deep as the surface warms and feeding shallow in spring on a littoral menu of insects, mayfly nymphs above all in the spring stomach records.

Splake approach the spawning shoals from mid-October, though as a hybrid they rarely establish self-sustaining populations — most splake fisheries exist because hatcheries maintain them. They look the part of both parents: forked tail from the laker, worm-patterned back and coloured spots from the brookie. Anglers target them as a beautiful, catchable char of the stocked-lake country, on spoons, jigs and flies.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The spring menu is measured at both ends of the size range: insects (mayfly nymphs first) for the shallow feeders, with the ontogenetic switch behind them — invertebrates in year one, then fish forage, crayfish and perch-type prey for larger splake in the Shield-lake diet work. Insect-profile offerings for the littoral fish and small fish-profile offerings for the larger ones are the supported patterns; no lure is named in the splake literature, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the temperature band, not the calendar: splake growth efficiency is already at its plateau from about 10.6 °C in the hatchery work, inside a habitat optimum of 10–16 °C — once the shallows reach the low teens, spring fish are at full activity in their band, and the pattern is strong until the surface pushes them deep.

Work a found school thoroughly: strong schooling behaviour is part of this fish's record (gill-net catches gave further evidence of it), so a located school is a located fishery — the catch is in the finding, and thorough fishing of the find beats searching new shallows.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the spring shallows are empty in warming water, the fish have already made the summer move — drop to the first cool water off the littoral rather than waiting for a shallow pattern the temperature has ended.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Summer splake are piscivores in the cool layer: rainbow smelt was the primary diet in all seasons and years in the Lake Superior programme with coregonines second, smelt, sticklebacks and alewives for the Huron fish, and crayfish plus yellow perch for larger Shield-lake fish. Fish-profile offerings matched to the local forage are the supported pattern; where no pelagic forage exists, the crayfish-and-perch menu is the Shield-lake alternative the diet work describes.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the band, not a depth: locate water in the 10–14 °C plateau that still holds oxygen above the 5 mg/L knee, wherever in the water column that band sits in your water, and present inside it exactly. A bait running above the band is in water the field record says is empty; one below the oxygen wall is under the fish.

Hold the timing honestly: no diel feeding rhythm has ever been measured for splake — none, by any method — and the model's day shape is carried flat and neutral for exactly that reason. Do not plan a splake day around a splake-proven clock; the splake-measured levers are temperature, depth and season, and those are what this entry fishes.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a shallow, unstratified lake goes dead in a heat wave, believe it: in years when one Maine pond stayed mixed with bottom temperatures above 21 °C, stocked splake were not recovered at all — they survived in stratified years and emigrated in the hot ones. Thermal absence is a population fact in that water, not a presentation problem.

One identity caveat the set carries everywhere: this entry describes F1 hatchery splake as stocked. Second-generation fish and backcrosses are measurably different fish on the temperature and depth axes — the lake-trout backcross ran broader in summer than lake trout themselves — so a water holding mostly backcross fish will not sit where this entry puts F1 fish.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The fall menu is the year's fullest: minnows and other small fish, crayfish, and the littoral insects of the shallows — fish-profile offerings first for the cooling-water piscivores, crayfish profiles in the Shield-lake pattern. Nothing fall-specific beyond the diet is measured; the seasonal change is in the fish's address, not its menu.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the cooling as a return to the band: as surface water drops back through the mid-teens into the 10–14 °C plateau, splake leave the summer layer and the whole littoral reopens — cover the shallowing water thoroughly, and expect schools, worked thoroughly when found, to carry the day.

Late in the season, separate the feeders from the spawners by address: feeding fish work the littoral and the shoal approaches, while fish crowding the rocky shoals themselves from mid-October are arriving on spawning business. The fallspawn entry takes over on the shoals; this entry fishes the feeders around them.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall littoral fish are scarce at good temperatures, check the calendar against the shoals: the approach begins in mid-October, and a population sliding onto the spawning grounds can empty the feeding shallows before the spawn itself starts — move toward the shoal approaches rather than changing baits.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No spawn-specific offering is measured for splake, and no feeding bonus is issued for this window: shoal fish are there to spawn, not to feed, and their catchability is presence and aggression. Offerings fished at the shoal edges — where staging and post-spawn fish hold — are the honest pattern; baits worked over the redds are fishing the aggression, and the entry says so.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the edges and the staging water, not the redds: the programme-wide rule applies here on splake's own observed behaviour — a fish that charges on the shoal is defending a site, not feeding. Whether spawning splake also feed less has never been measured for this species, and no suppression coefficient is claimed; the location is the whole sourced pattern.

Time the window by the observed calendar: approach from mid-October, peak spawning late October into early November, done by mid-November. Outside that bracket the shoals are just rocky shallows again, and the fall and winter entries are the better guides.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If shoal fish will not eat, they are working as observed — spawning fish on redds are not a feeding pattern to crack. Move off the shoals to the deeper staging water nearby, where pre- and post-spawn fish are the catchable ones.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The winter menu is the measured one: minnows and crayfish from the winter stomachs — small fish-profile and crayfish-profile offerings, fished slowly in the shallow feeding water. No winter-specific presentation is measured for splake; the diet is the supported pattern.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish winter as a located-fish season: schools and shallow feeding flats, worked thoroughly. The honest limit rides along — splake winterkill tolerance has never been measured, and these are disproportionately small stocked lakes, so late-winter oxygen is the standing question in this fish's winter (see the ice entry for the same point under ice).

Spread winter effort through the day on located fish: the under-ice and open-water day shapes alike are carried neutral (flagged in the ice entry), never splake measurements — there is no splake clock to fish, so fish the located fish.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a small stocked lake dies late in winter, suspect oxygen before presentation: the risk level in the model is derived from the small-lake class splake are planted into, not from a splake winterkill measurement (none exists) — move toward the best-oxygenated water you can find, or to a deeper water, before changing baits.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The winter diet is the tackle story: minnows and crayfish from the winter stomachs — small fish-profile and crayfish-profile offerings fished slowly over the shallow flats. No ice-specific presentation has ever been measured for splake; small and slow is the winter diet applied honestly, not an ice finding.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Treat oxygen as the address in small stocked lakes: splake are planted into exactly the small, sometimes aerated parkland and Shield lakes where late-winter oxygen fails first, and the model's risk level (15, between its parents' 5 and 20, argued toward the small-lake parent by lake class) prices that. As the winter depletes a small lake, fish toward its best-oxygenated water — and know the level is derived, not a splake winterkill measurement: none exists.

Timing under ice is carried neutral, and the entry says so: no under-ice day shape has ever been measured for splake, by any method. Spread effort through the day on located schools rather than betting the trip on a splake dawn that no study has ever timed.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Mid-winter silence in a small stocked lake is oxygen until proven otherwise: move toward better-oxygenated water before changing a single bait — and if the whole lake is depleted, absence can be a population fact (winterkill tolerance is unmeasured, so no lake's survival is promised), not a tactics failure.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: Spring splake feed in the shallows: in the Jack Lake record, spring stomachs were full of littoral insects with mayfly nymphs dominant — a shallow, insect-feeding season before the summer depth pattern sets in. Fish the littoral feeding water while the surface is still cold and the fish are on it.

As the surface warms through the teens, the season turns: splake leave the shallows for the cool layer, and by full summer no fish are found where the temperature exceeds about 15.6 °C. Fish spring as a closing shallow window — the warming itself is the movement cue.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Splake's summer is a temperature story, and its evidence tier is stated plainly: this is a DERIVED set capped at Low confidence — but the temperature factor is the anchored part, built on splake's own growth experiments and field bounds rather than on its parents. The model's plateau is 10–14 °C (the overlap of the 10–16 °C habitat optimum, the growth-efficiency plateau from 10.6 °C and the lower half of the agency preferendum bracket of about 12–16 °C), with 16 °C held high rather than perfect: growth is real there in the hatchery, occupancy is not in the field.

The summer address is the thermocline and the water just under it: Great Lakes hybrids concentrated in the thermocline in summer, Maine gillnetting took most fish in the thermocline and hypolimnion, and at Parvin Lake no splake was caught where the temperature exceeded 15.6 °C. Find the cool layer; the fish are in it, not at a fixed depth.

Oxygen draws the floor of that layer: optimal habitat carries dissolved oxygen above 5 mg/L, tolerable to about 4, and in the Pallette Lake record the summer feeding zone was cut off at depth by inadequate oxygen while food persisted below it. Summer splake are squeezed between warm surface water and the oxygen wall — fish the band between.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall cooling reopens the shallows and builds toward the spawn: splake approach the spawning shoals from mid-October, and September fish are feeding fish on the move back up — fall stomachs in the Jack Lake record held mayfly nymphs, minnows and crayfish. Fish the cooling littoral and the routes toward the rocky shoals while the water falls back through the plateau.

This is one of the two best seasons in the fish's own record: Manitoba's park guidance puts splake angling success best in fall and winter in its stocked Duck Mountain lakes, and the season curve peaks in October. Fall is not a wind-down for splake; it is the front half of its best window.

movementSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: The spawn is directly observed, over ten seasons at Jack Lake: splake spawn on rocky shoals from late October to early November, approaching from mid-October, females selecting redd sites and dominant males turning aggressive, first eggs from about October 22–30 across years and last activity by mid-November. It is an intermediate ritual — redd-site selection from one parent's heritage on the other parent's lake-shoal ground — and it happens on the shoals, every year.

The aggregation is a population event because of the hybrid's own clock: splake mature on the brook parent's schedule, not the lake parent's — a third of males and some females mature at age two, all fish by age four, against the lake parent's six to seven years. A stocked population runs a spawning aggregation every fall from its second year, in lakes where the lake parent would barely have begun.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter is a feeding season for splake, not a shutdown: the small wild winter stomach sample at Jack Lake held minnows and crayfish — wild fish with food in them in winter — and the season floor in the model is held at 0.60 on that evidence. In open winter water, fish the shallower feeding ground the stocked-lake pattern uses; winter distribution runs shallower than the summer layer.

The fishery record agrees at scale: Maine's management plan caps a winter harvest rate explicitly (no more than 0.40 splake per acre) because the winter take is large enough to need one, and Manitoba's guidance names fall and winter as the best splake seasons in its stocked lakes. Winter splake are a target, not an accident.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: The ice set for splake is issued as part of a DERIVED set, capped at Low confidence, and the entry carries that flag openly: winter feeding and a substantial winter fishery are documented for splake itself — wild winter stomachs with food in them, a record-class fish taken through a complete creel in December, agency winter-harvest management in Maine, and Manitoba guidance naming fall and winter as its best splake seasons, with the provincial record (25.75 in, Laurie Lake, February 2025) an ice fish. What has never been measured is under-ice activity structure, so the timing below is carried neutral and no oxygen level is scored — Low is exactly where that evidence sits.

Fish the shallow end of the winter pattern: the northern stocked-trout canon (expert consensus, graded as such) puts winter splake over shallow, food-rich flats under about 10 ft, light-sensitive and easily spooked — consistent with the parents' under-ice shallowing. Step lightly, keep the hole shaded, and work the flats and their first edge.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 10–14 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for splake is an absence: front, pressure, wind and moon have never been tested for splake. The one pressure text in the splake record is a spearfishing anecdote, filed as do-not-use. There is no front trick for this fish: what is measured is temperature and season, and a front matters only as the temperature and light change it actually delivers.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais mesuré pour le splake — aucun terme de vent n'existe pour cet hybride dans aucune étude. Zéro par absence.
Jamais mesuré pour le splake. frontExposure 0 — zéro par absence.

Jamais testé pour le splake — aucun recensement de terrain, aucune expérience contrôlée pression-alimentation n'existe. Le seul texte de pression au registre est une anecdote de chasse sous-marine grade D. Zéro par absence (pas un nul mesuré).

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation ou le frai du splake, ni pour aucun des deux parents. La fenêtre de frai d'automne (fin oct.–début nov.) garantit des coïncidences lunaires occasionnelles sur une montaison de ~3 semaines; la coïncidence n'est pas un signal.

Les pêches servies du splake sont des lacs ensemencés; aucune fonction alimentation-contre-débit n'existe pour le splake, et l'ensemble de lac d'aucun des deux parents ne note le débit. L'usage de ruisseau est temporaire/de saison fraîche seulement (Obrey 2002). Non noté.

Le régime du splake est démontrablement conditionné par le lac et plastique (insectes → écrevisses → poissons; piscivorie d'éperlans/corégonines là où disponible), mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure la base de proies d'un lac; un terme de proies noté serait inventé. Un modérateur connu non modélisé, énoncé pas caché.
La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour le splake; elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome.

spawningSeasons.heading: Frai d’automne
lines: The spawn is directly observed, over ten seasons at Jack Lake: splake spawn on rocky shoals from late October to early November, approaching from mid-October, females selecting redd sites and dominant males turning aggressive, first eggs from about October 22–30 across years and last activity by mid-November. It is an intermediate ritual — redd-site selection from one parent's heritage on the other parent's lake-shoal ground — and it happens on the shoals, every year.

The aggregation is a population event because of the hybrid's own clock: splake mature on the brook parent's schedule, not the lake parent's — a third of males and some females mature at age two, all fish by age four, against the lake parent's six to seven years. A stocked population runs a spawning aggregation every fall from its second year, in lakes where the lake parent would barely have begun.

Fish the edges and the staging water, not the redds: the programme-wide rule applies here on splake's own observed behaviour — a fish that charges on the shoal is defending a site, not feeding. Whether spawning splake also feed less has never been measured for this species, and no suppression coefficient is claimed; the location is the whole sourced pattern.

Time the window by the observed calendar: approach from mid-October, peak spawning late October into early November, done by mid-November. Outside that bracket the shoals are just rocky shallows again, and the fall and winter entries are the better guides.

spawningSources.citation: Le propre registre saisonnier de régime du splake : %IRI saisonnier par classe de proies (Maine CFWRU Cooperative Unit Report 2000-1); pic d'alimentation en œufs de novembre sur les corégonidés qui fraient et estomacs de janvier/mars portant de la nourriture au lac Pallette (Christie, dans Berst & Spangler 1973; Martin & Baldwin 1960); régime saisonnier du lac Supérieur (Conner et al. 1993). Rassemblement de frai d'automne observé fin oct.–début nov. (Berst et al. 1981) — annotation d'emplacement, aucun bonus d'alimentation
