about: The tiger trout is a hatchery cross between a brown trout and a brook trout — Salmo trutta × Salvelinus fontinalis — named for the bold, maze-like vermiculations that stripe its flanks like a tiger's. It's an honest entry in this library: no activity, temperature, or time-of-day response has ever been measured for this hybrid, so its rating is a derived set that borrows nothing from any other fish — its factors rest on neutral terms until a tiger-specific study exists.

Tiger trout are sterile, so every one in the water was stocked, and managers use them as a beautiful, catchable, controllable trout for lakes where brook trout stunt or need a check. They are aggressive for a trout, often taking streamers and spoons meant for bigger fish. Anglers target them as a bucket-list novelty — a fish you may fish a season to see once, and never forget when you do.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the diet tiers the tiger record actually measures: juveniles and smaller fish take zooplankton and aquatic invertebrates, and adults shift toward fish prey where small-bodied forage fish are available, with crayfish and insects in the agency diet accounts. Small invertebrate presentations for ordinary fish and a fish-profile option for large adults are the diet-supported tiers — and that is the whole supported statement, because no lure, fly pattern or size is named for tiger trout in the research behind this entry, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Time the day by a deliberately flattened clock, and know why it is flat: the parents conflict — brook is the day-led trout, brown the dusk- and night-led one — so the derived diel is a midpoint blend (dawn 0.80, day 0.80, dusk 0.85, night 0.70) that claims no real peak. That blend is flagged in the study as the set's largest structural risk. Fish across the day with a slight lean to dusk, and do not fish this hybrid as either parent's clock.

Expect lake-to-lake results to vary for a stocked-fish reason that is measured: in seven Colorado subalpine lakes, age-1 tiger size ran from 115 to 229 mm and the strongest predictor was the cohort's own stocking density, mediated by system productivity (Hansen et al. 2022). A lake whose tigers grow slowly is often a stocking-density story, not a presentation story.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If spring shallows are silent, check the temperature against the cold limb before changing baits: the blended curve sits at 0.55 at 7 °C and 0.40 at 4 °C, so a cold spring lake is a slow lake on this evidence — fish the warmest water that is climbing toward the plateau and give it real time.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Lead with the piscivore tier for adult fish in forage-rich water — a fish-profile presentation is diet-supported for this hybrid in a way it is not for most trout, on the Scofield record above — and keep small invertebrate presentations for smaller fish on the juvenile menu. No lure is named in the tiger literature; the menu tiers are the supported tackle story.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the flat clock as flat: dawn, day and dusk sit within 0.05 of each other on the blend, with night lower at 0.70. A summer plan built on coverage of plateau-temperature water will out-fish a plan built on waiting for a peak hour this hybrid has never been shown to have.

Do not fish the famous aggression claim, because the one controlled test contradicts it: in laboratory trials, rainbow trout initiated 10.2 times more aggressive interactions than tiger trout, and tigers initiated only 1.9 times more than cutthroat (Hafen & Budy 2015) — and tiger aggression against its own two parents has never been tested at all. What anglers read as aggression is most parsimoniously piscivory plus stocked, naïve fish; there is no aggression bonus anywhere in this entry or its rating.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If plateau water is quiet, check the warm limb before the tackle: the blended curve falls to 0.75 at 19 °C and 0.50 at 21 °C. Warming past the plateau is a measured-direction problem on the parent curves — move toward cooler water rather than cycling presentations in water the curve is already leaving.

On clarity, the honest limit: no tiger turbidity measurement exists, and the rating carries no turbidity term for this fish at all. This entry offers no tiger clarity rule of its own, because there is none to offer.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The menu does not change in warm water — invertebrates for smaller fish, fish prey for adults — and the presentation question is honestly secondary to the address. No warm-water lure or tactic is named for this hybrid, and none is invented here to fill the space.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Compress effort toward dusk, the blend's one slight lead at 0.85 — and do not import the brown parent's night pattern to rescue a warm day: on the tiger blend, night at 0.70 is the lowest quarter of the clock, because the other parent is a day fish. Warm tiger water is a temperature problem with a small dusk lean, not a night fishery anyone has measured.

Once you find a cool band that still carries oxygen, work it thoroughly instead of searching the warm surface between spots: the fishable warm-season water in a shallow stocked lake can be a thin layer — a found layer fished carefully is worth more than a lake searched quickly.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the whole lake sits at 23 °C or warmer with no cooler band reachable, there is no presentation fix on this evidence — and do not let anyone quote you a tiger lethal temperature to decide by: none has been measured, the parents' incipient lethals are different measurements on different fish (brook 25.3 °C, brown 24.7 °C), and the study refused to average them into a fabricated 25.0 °C. Travel to cooler water or wait for the fall cooling, which is this set's next strong season.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The adult piscivore tier stays first in fall: the Scofield diet record was seasonal, with chub share varying by season but piscivory present across them (Winters et al. 2017), so a fish-profile presentation for large adults remains diet-supported as the water cools, alongside the invertebrate menu for smaller fish. Nothing fall-specific beyond that diet record is measured, and no spawn pattern is borrowed from either parent to fill this section.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the temperature decline as the schedule: as long as the water holds in or near the 13–17 °C plateau the season value stays high, and the fall-off after that is the cold limb, not a behavioural switch. There is also no flow trigger to wait for — the only flow responses evidenced in either parent are spawning-migration triggers, a sterile fish has no spawning migration, and the rating carries flow at zero for exactly that hybrid-specific reason.

Keep fall hours spread across the day on the flattened blend (dawn 0.80, day 0.80, dusk 0.85, night 0.70): because the spawning structure was removed from this season, there is no special fall hour hiding in the parents' spawning behaviour either — the honest fall pattern is ordinary feeding hours on cooling water, with dusk holding only the blend's small lean.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall fish go quiet, do not wait for a spawning peak that will never come and do not read the quiet as a spawn fast — this fish does not spawn. Check the temperature against the cold limb (0.55 at 7 °C on the blend) and fish the warmest holding water; late-fall quiet in a sterile hybrid is a temperature story, told at a feeding rate that declines toward the winter floor.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Small and slow on the winter menu: the invertebrate tier at its smallest, delivered close to holding fish that are not travelling far to a bait on a floor-rate season. No winter-specific lure is named for this hybrid, and the fish-profile tier belongs to active adult feeding in warmer water, not to a winter claim.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Use the same flattened clock, carried into winter without embellishment: dawn 0.80, day 0.80, dusk 0.85, night 0.70 is a blend of two conflicting parent shapes, and no winter diel measurement of any kind exists for the hybrid to sharpen it. Spend winter effort on position — the right stocked lake, the right holding water — rather than on hour-picking a curve that was built to claim as little as possible.

Fish a winter lake like its fish may have been educated, because catchability is learned in the parent record this set leans on: in the brown parent's work, anglers took 11–23% of a heavily fished population per trip series against up to 47% of a naïve one (Young & Hayes 2004), a caution the study carries over to stocked tigers in kind. A winter lake that fished easily at stocking and harder since is showing that learning curve, not a vanished population.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A quiet winter session is the arithmetic of this set, not necessarily a wrong lake: a derived floor built from two parents' low winter rates promises few chances. Shorten the session, fish the warmest holding water perfectly, and save the long efforts for the spring climb back toward the plateau.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice lure, jig or bait is named for tiger trout in any source behind this entry, and none is invented here. The diet-supported shape carried under ice, labelled as a transfer from the open-water record, is the two tiers at their smallest and slowest: invertebrate presentations for ordinary fish, and a fish-profile option for the largest adults on the measured adult piscivory — a diet fact, not an ice finding.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the flattened blend, because that is literally what the ice clock is: the open-water diel (dawn 0.80, day 0.80, dusk 0.85, night 0.70) carried under ice as a labelled within-set transfer, never measured beneath it. No hour is a proven tiger hour under ice; dusk holds the blend's small lean, the day is its equal within a few points, and a located school of stocked fish matters more than the clock on every piece of evidence available.

Set expectations by the winter arithmetic and the stocking reality together: the season floor is low, and a given lake's tiger size and density are outputs of its stocking programme and productivity (Hansen et al. 2022) as much as of the fish — a slow lake through the ice may simply be a lightly stocked or crowded one.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If a provisional ice pattern is silent, treat it as an open question rather than a failed one — the evidence under this entry is fishery records plus neutral terms, and your lake is allowed to disagree with both. Move first toward better-oxygenated water in the shallow stocked lake before changing presentations; and if the whole basin is quiet, the honest reading is the floor rate of a derived set, not a tactic you have not tried yet.

movementSeasons.heading: Printemps
lines: Start with what kind of entry this is, because it governs everything below: tiger trout's rating is a DERIVED set, confidence capped at Low, and 0 of its 100 open-water points rest on a tiger-measured response function — no activity, diel, thermal or weather study of this hybrid exists at all. No other fish's curve is used for it: temperature, time of day and season are carried flat and neutral, and oxygen and turbidity are not scored — the rating rests on the generic terms, and the prose says so wherever a number is used.

Spring is a temperature climb toward a blended plateau: the derived curve reaches 0.80 at 10 °C on its way to a 13–17 °C plateau built point by point between brook's 13–16 °C and brown's 14–18 °C plateaus, and the season values rise with it — 0.50 in March, 0.70 in April, 0.85 in May. Fish the stocked-lake water that is warming into that band first; the coldest water in the system is the last water this curve rewards.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer water inside the blended 13–17 °C plateau is this set's prime band — a construction between the parents' plateaus, not a measured tiger preference, and the entry never quotes it as one. The season values hold near the year's top through the band (June and July at 0.90, August at 0.85), so the summer search is for water holding in the teens rather than for a special hour or a special shore.

In stocked lakes, the adult address follows the forage fish: at Scofield Reservoir, stocked adult tigers ate Utah chub at up to 80% of diet depending on season, and the population's consumption exceeded the chub's annual production (Winters et al. 2017). Where a stocked lake holds dense small-bodied forage fish, adult tigers are piscivores working that forage — fish the water the forage schools use, at the depths they hold.

movementSeasons.heading: Eau chaude
lines: Above the plateau this is a relocation problem on borrowed numbers, stated as such: the blended curve falls through 0.75 at 19 °C, 0.50 at 21 °C, 0.25 at 23 °C and 0.05 at 25 °C. Find water back inside 13–17 °C — the coolest, deepest holding water a shallow stocked lake offers, and any inflow-cooled corner — before spending effort anywhere else.

On oxygen, the honest limit: no tiger oxygen response has ever been measured, so the rating scores no oxygen term for this fish. Tiger occupancy of stocked lakes with large low-oxygen portions of the water column (Hansen et al. 2022) is an occurrence fact, not a response curve, and it does not make warm, low-oxygen water a feeding address.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is a feeding season that simply continues, and that continuity is the one place tiger-specific evidence changes a number in this whole set: the season values hold at 0.85 through September and October and ease to 0.75 in November, declining with temperature only. Fish the cooling stocked lakes as a long feeding shoulder, on the same forage and invertebrate addresses as summer, as the water falls back through the plateau.

What fall is not, for this fish: a spawning season. Tiger trout are a sterile hatchery hybrid — survivors are not reproductively viable, and modern production induces triploidy to guarantee it. There is no spawning migration, no redd, no guarding and no pre-spawn aggregation to stage below, and both parents' October–November spawning shapes were deliberately removed from the derived season curve rather than inherited.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter is the derived floor: season values sit at 0.50 in December and 0.40 through January and February, between the parents' measured winters — brook feeding in the littoral all winter on its own telemetry, and the brown parent's under-ice consumption running at roughly a tenth to a sixth of its summer peak in its one lake study. Those are parent numbers, labelled as the blend's ingredients; no tiger winter feeding rate exists. In open winter water, fish the holding water the fish already occupy and expect a low rate, not a shutdown.

Cold water itself is not the barrier the floor might suggest: the blended cold limb holds 0.40 at 4 °C and 0.30 at 1 °C, so a winter tiger in near-freezing water is a slow fish on this curve, not an absent one — the through-ice pattern for stocked lakes is covered in the ice entry below.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: PROVISIONAL — flagged in the entry the way the study flags the set: tiger trout are demonstrably caught through the ice, and that fishery record is all the ice evidence there is. Manitoba's Parkland stocked lakes produce Master Angler tigers through the ice (Twin Lakes fish of 26.5 in on 25 Jan 2025 and 26.35 in on 6 Apr 2025), and a North Dakota state-record tiger was taken through the ice on 4 Jan 2026 — but no under-ice feeding, diel or oxygen study of this hybrid exists in any system, so this whole entry is provisional and capped at the set's Low confidence.

The signature water shows the class to fish: Twin Lakes is a small, shallow stocked lake (43.2 ha, maximum depth 6.4 m, aerated, catch-and-release) in the Duck Mountain Parkland. Shallow stocked lakes of that class are the winter address — with the oxygen caution that belongs to shallow water under ice: no tiger oxygen measurement exists, so the rating scores none, and better-oxygenated water is the prudent search — stated as prudence, not as a tiger curve.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 0–40 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: The honest weather note for tiger trout is an absence, stated in full: wind, fronts, barometric pressure and moon have never been tested for this hybrid's feeding or catchability in any source the research could find, in either direction — and both parents carry those factors at zero as well, brown's pressure and moon results being nulls and brook's being unmeasured. There is no tiger front trick to sell you. A front matters here only as the temperature and light change it actually delivers, which the other sections already fish.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Jamais testé pour la tiger trout — aucun recensement de terrain, aucune étude contrôlée. Zéro par absence.
Jamais mesuré pour cet hybride (frontExposure 0). Zéro par absence.

Jamais testé pour l'alimentation de la tiger trout. La voie lunaire connue dans sa famille rythme la migration de frai — un comportement qu'un hybride stérile n'accomplit pas. Zéro par absence + inapplicabilité structurale de la voie de migration.

Un hybride stérile n'a aucune migration de frai, et ses eaux servies sont des lacs; aucune réponse de débit n'a été mesurée pour la tiger trout. Zéro par raisonnement propre à l'hybride, énoncé — pas par silence.

La piscivorie adulte est mesurée pour la tiger et forte (Utah chub jusqu'à 80% du régime; consommation de population dépassant la production de proies — Winters et al. 2017), et la croissance précoce est conditionnée par la compétition/la densité (Hansen et al. 2022) — mais aucune entrée du moteur ne mesure la base de proies d'un lac ou la densité d'ensemencement d'une population de tiger, alors aucun terme de proies n'est noté. Des modérateurs connus non modélisés, énoncés.

La couverture nuageuse n'a jamais été isolée pour la tiger trout (ni pour aucun des deux parents comme terme autonome); elle entre seulement par la voie du facteur lumière. Aucun terme de nuages autonome.

spawningSources.citation: Aucun taux d'alimentation mensuel n'existe pour la tiger trout — la seule preuve saisonnière est une étude de régime de trois saisons avec l'hiver non échantillonné (Winters & Budy 2015). Le facteur est porté PLAT au neutre 0.60. (L'hybride est stérile — USGS NAS; Scheerer et al. 1987 — alors aucune structure de frai n'est modélisée non plus.)

about: The walleye is a cool-water member of the perch family, and across much of Canada it's the fish the whole season is planned around — known as pickerel in Canadian kitchens and “dore” in French. Its namesake eyes are built for low light, with a reflective layer that lets it feed comfortably in dim, deep or stained water where other predators struggle. In this app's rating model its feeding peaks in water in the high teens to low twenties Celsius, and it fades fast as water pushes toward the upper twenties.

Walleye live where structure meets food: rocky shoals, gravel bars, points, humps and reefs, sliding deeper as the water warms and gathering near their spawning shoals each spring. They hunt minnows and perch, feed hardest at dawn, dusk and after dark, and school up enough that one caught fish usually means more below. Anglers target them because they are equal parts puzzle and table fish — light-sensitive, weather-sensitive, and some of the finest eating in fresh water.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: A jig and minnow is the spring standard — 1/16- or 1/8-oz in the shallows. Keep the jig on the bottom: when in doubt about the weight, go heavier rather than lighter, because a jig that isn't touching bottom isn't fishing.

A jig and minnow is the spring standard — 1/4- to 3/8-oz in river current. Keep the jig on the bottom: when in doubt about the weight, go heavier rather than lighter, because a jig that isn't touching bottom isn't fishing.
In rivers, lean to oranges, yellows and chartreuses — but in unusually clear river water, dull browns, blacks and whites do better.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Work the jig slowly along the bottom — lift it a few inches to a foot, let it fall back, and rest it. Cold water means cold fish: short lifts, long pauses.
Time your best shallow spots for morning, evening, dark or a windy day — that's when the females visit. The males are there all day.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the shallows are dead, drop to the first deeper water beside the spawning area and slow right down. A minnow on a plain hook under a slip bobber, set just off the bottom, gives a wary prespawn fish something it doesn't have to chase.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Jigs and minnows still lead, but this is when rigging and crankbaits come back into play — the books call the warming stretch ahead great for jigging, rigging and cranking alike. A live-bait rig (walking sinker, a leader of a foot to a metre, a size 2–4 hook) with a minnow is the slow search tool.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Cover water slowly and don't expect violence — these are recovering fish. Work a spot thoroughly before you move; a resting fish often eats on the third or fourth good pass, not the first.
The bait rotation turns with the season: minnows in spring, leeches as late spring arrives, crawlers into summer.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Anchor over the best-looking flat edge and slip-bobber a leech or minnow just off the bottom. Postspawn fish that won't chase will still rise a few inches for something hanging in front of them.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The full menu works now: jigs, live-bait rigs and crankbaits. For rigging, match the walking sinker to the depth (1/16-oz in the shallows up to 1½ oz deep), a leader of about 30–90 cm — longer, up to several metres, on clear, pressured water, shorter in dark water — and a size 2–4 hook.
Bait follows the calendar: minnows give way to leeches, and crawlers come on as the water warms.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Jig the breaks, rig the flats, and troll cranks when you need to find them. When you mark fish, run a trolled crankbait 2–5 ft above them, never below — walleyes rise to a bait; they rarely dive for one.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Slow down and go to live bait on the spot-on-the-spot — the inside turn, the tip of the point, the one patch of rock. A slip bobber with a leech, set a foot above the rocks, soaks the exact spot a trolled bait just passes over.

Slow down and go to live bait on the spot-on-the-spot — the inside turn, the one patch of rock. A slip bobber with a leech, set a foot above the rocks, soaks the exact spot a trolled bait just passes over.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Trolling is the summer search engine. Use dive curves to put crankbaits exactly where you want them — the prime trolling band is 15–25 ft — or add a snap weight: an ounce clipped on 20 ft ahead of the bait, with 100 ft of line out, runs the bait about 30% deeper than it would on its own (that method was tested at 2.0 mph).

Colours follow the water: chrome, purple and naturals in clear water; clown, firetiger, chartreuse and wonderbread in stained water; UV and glow when it's overcast or the light is low; gold is the staple in tea-stained water. A black bait run high in the column silhouettes against the sky and gets noticed.
Bottom bouncers with spinners or crawlers cover the breaks: an ounce of bouncer for every 10 ft of water, the line at about 45°, at 1.0–1.5 mph.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Summer trolling speeds run 1.8–2.2 mph. Run baits 2–5 ft above the fish you mark, never below. With leadcore, one to two colours back with a stickbait reaches 15–22 ft at a slow 1.2–1.6 mph — a good way to comb a basin edge.
Summer trolling speeds run 1.8–2.2 mph. Run baits 2–5 ft above the fish you mark, never below. With leadcore, one to two colours back with a stickbait reaches 15–22 ft at a slow 1.2–1.6 mph.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: In the dog days the feed happens in short, intense windows, mostly in low light — be on deep structure at dawn and dusk instead of grinding at noon. At midday, the shaded side of the thickest cover and the deepest edge you can fish are the percentage plays.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Crankbaits still cover water — this is snap-weight season (an ounce 20 ft ahead of the bait, 100 ft out, for roughly 30% more depth) — but the jig and minnow starts taking its share back as the water cools.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Ease the trolling speed down toward the cold-water range, 1.2–1.6 mph, and keep baits 2–5 ft above marked fish. Toward evening, check the tops of the points — fall fish slide up to feed as the light goes.
Ease the trolling speed down toward the cold-water range, 1.2–1.6 mph, and keep baits 2–5 ft above marked fish. Toward evening, fall fish slide up to feed as the light goes.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If they won't chase, go vertical: a jig and minnow worked in place over the deep edge, lifted a few inches to a foot, dropped on a free fall and rested. Cold-shoulder fish eat a bait that isn't going anywhere.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: A jig and a small fathead or shiner is the fall staple — 1/8-oz is the working size — and to cover water, troll a crankbait slowly, 1.2–1.6 mph in cold water, running it 2–5 ft above the fish you mark, never below.
Jighead colour follows the water: blue in clear water, gold if it's tea-stained.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Drag the jig, let it sit, drag it again, with a slight hop now and then. Keep it on the bottom and keep the pauses long — fall fish in cold water don't chase.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: A small leech under a slip bobber, or on a dropshot shaken in place, is the old reliable — no matter the conditions, a walleye will eventually eat a small leech. And be on the shallow side of your best spot at dusk: the short feeding spree as the light goes is the best window of a fall day.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Jig and minnow, heavier as the depth demands. A stinger hook earns its keep now: cold fish nip tails.

Jig and minnow, heavier as the depth and current demand — in rivers, 1/4- to 3/8-oz in the holes, breaks and eddies is the classic cold-water rig. A stinger hook earns its keep now: cold fish nip tails.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Vertical and slow. Lift the jig a few inches to a foot, let it fall freely, rest it on the bottom. Long pauses aren't a mistake in near-freezing water — they're the presentation.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Put a minnow under a slip bobber just off the bottom on the best spot you have and give it time. Late-fall walleye feed in brief windows; being set up and still when a window opens beats running around looking for a better one.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Five presentations cover first ice: a jigging spoon (Buck-Shot or Swedish Pimple class) with the treble tipped with a minnow head, a jig and minnow, a hardbait, a plain hook and minnow, and a glide bait.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Pound the bottom so the lure puffs up a little cloud of sediment — that draws walleye in. And fish two rods with two jobs: an aggressive jigging rod to call them, and a deadstick or tip-up sitting still with a minnow. The loud rod brings them in; the quiet rod often catches them.

Read their mood from how they come in: if they rush in and stall, downsize and lengthen the pauses. If they follow but won't commit, raise the lure slowly. If they slide away, go quiet or deadstick. They usually eat on the pause.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: When a fish appears under you, don't reduce the show — keep the same energy that called it in. Half-hearted jigging loses more first-ice walleye than aggressive jigging ever scared.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: The same three presentations, a size smaller and a mood slower: jigging spoon tipped with a minnow head, jig and minnow, or a plain minnow on a deadstick beside the active rod.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Use the cadence loop: rush-and-stall from the fish means downsize and lengthen pauses; a follow without a commit means raise slowly; a slide-away means go quiet or deadstick. They eat on the pause.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Set the deadstick and trust it. Mid-winter walleye that refuse everything moving will still take a minnow that isn't doing anything at all.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Jigging spoons and jig-and-minnow combos lead again, with a deadstick minnow alongside — late-ice fish moving toward the spawn feed more willingly than mid-winter fish did.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: You can fish a little more aggressively than mid-winter, but keep the deadstick soaking — staging fish cruise, and the still rod intercepts the ones passing between your holes.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Move toward the spawning water, not away from it — if the staging spots are quiet, the fish are closer to the shoals than you think, especially at last light.
Move toward the spawning water, not away from it — if the staging spots are quiet, the fish are closer to the creeks than you think, especially at last light.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Walleye are gathering near where they'll spawn — rocky shoals, gravel bars. The males arrive first and stay shallow longest, in just a few feet of water. The bigger females hold a little deeper, just off the spawning area, and slide shallow in the morning, in the evening and after dark.

Walleye are gathering near where they'll spawn — the mouths of tributary creeks and rivers. The males arrive first and stay shallow longest, in just a few feet of water. The bigger females hold a little deeper, just off the spawning area, and slide shallow in the morning, in the evening and after dark.
In rivers, work the holes, the current breaks, the eddies and below wing dams — anywhere a fish can rest out of the push and still watch food come past.

movementSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: The spawn is done or winding down. The fish rest first, then start feeding again as the water warms — look just off the spawning shoals, then toward nearby flats. On the big lakes, postspawn walleye work flats roughly 7–20 ft deep before they scatter to summer structure.

The spawn is done or winding down. The fish rest first, then start feeding again as the water warms — look just off the spawning shoals, then toward river mouths and nearby flats. Postspawn walleye work river mouth water roughly 7–20 ft deep before they scatter to summer structure.

movementSeasons.heading: Fin de printemps
lines: Fish are moving out to the main lake — points, humps and reefs are turning on, and the first deep weedlines are worth checking. Expect them to use the same structure all summer from here; what changes is which side and how deep.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Main-lake points, humps, reefs and deep weedlines are the summer addresses — plus a pattern many anglers miss: walleye suspended over the basins, following baitfish. On the Great Lakes the bait stacks 30–50 ft down and the walleye hang halfway down to it. If you're marking bait over deep water with nothing under it, look halfway up.

movementSeasons.heading: Début d’automne
lines: Cooling water pulls walleye back onto the points, humps and reefs and bunches them up on baitfish. It's becoming an edges season again — the same structure that worked in summer, fished a little shallower and slower as the water drops.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Main-lake points, humps and reefs are the fall pattern — walleye bunch up on them, following the surviving baitfish and feeding up for winter. The biggest females use the deep edges: humps and points topping out around 25–35 ft are the classic spots.

Fish the windward side, where the wind is pushing in and the chop is. Save the tops of the points and the shallower breaks for the last hour of the day — big fall females slide up for short evening feeding sprees, then drop back down.

Fish the windward side, where the wind is pushing in and the chop is. Save the shallower breaks for the last hour of the day — big fall females slide up for short evening feeding sprees, then drop back down.

movementSeasons.heading: Fin d’automne
lines: The coldest open water of the year. Fish are on the deep edges of the points and humps, bunched tight and moving as little as they can get away with.
The coldest open water of the year. Fish are in the river holes and deep breaks, bunched tight and moving as little as they can get away with.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace précoce
lines: First ice is the fall pattern slowed down: start where the fish were in late fall, around any green weeds still standing — 10–16 ft is a good starting band, deeper by day, shallower at night. Dawn, dusk, and grey or snowy days are the feeding times, and overcast or snow stretches the midday bite.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace de mi-hiver
lines: Mid-winter, the fish have slid deeper — work the deeper breaks and basin edges off the same structure they used in fall, and lean harder on the dawn and dusk windows. Bright midday is the slowest ice fishing of the year; grey days and snowfall fish better through the middle hours.

Mid-winter, the fish have slid deeper — work the deeper breaks off the same structure they used in fall, and lean harder on the dawn and dusk windows. Bright midday is the slowest ice fishing of the year; grey days and snowfall fish better through the middle hours.

movementSeasons.heading: Glace tardive
lines: Late ice pulls walleye back toward the shallows and toward the shoals they'll spawn on — the reverse of the fall move. Fish the staging water near spawning areas, shallower than mid-winter, and expect the low-light windows to get stronger as the season runs out.

Late ice pulls walleye back toward the shallows and toward the creeks and rivers they'll spawn on — the reverse of the fall move. Fish the staging water near spawning areas, shallower than mid-winter, and expect the low-light windows to get stronger as the season runs out.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

movementDaily.heading: Through the ice
lines: Most active at dusk; quietest at midday.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 18–22 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.
Upper lethal temperature: about 27 °C, from the species' research file.
Wind: this species' feeding holds up best with wind 8–24 km/h — its own measured wind curve, not a generic one.

weatherOverlays.heading: Avant l’arrivée d’un front
lines: A front is coming and the fish know it — feed while it's on its way. The feeding areas you'd fish anyway produce better now, especially the shallower ones and the windward structure. Make these hours count; they're the best fishing before the change.
You can stay bigger and more active — crankbaits and spinner rigs cover water while fish are willing to chase.
Keep moving and check several spots instead of camping on one. This is the window to find the fish, because finding them after the front is harder.

weatherOverlays.heading: Au passage d’un front
lines: The front is passing now and the bite will stutter — the wind swings, the pressure bottoms out, and fish go unsettled. The spots that produced ahead of it deserve one more slow pass before you change anything; the fishing usually steadies once the new weather settles in.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: A cold front went through about a day ago, and it moves walleye: expect them several feet deeper than they were before it, bunched tight on the deep edges. Start on the deep edge of your best structure and only work shallower as the light fades — the tops and shallow breaks come back into play in the last hour.

Downsize — that's the post-front rule. A 1/16- or 1/8-oz jig with a small fathead or shiner, even down in 12–13 ft of water. Hook the minnow twice — through the mouth, out the gill, back into the side — so it stays on through the slow work. Blue is the jighead colour in clear water; gold if the water is tea-stained.

Drag it, long pause, drag it, slight hop. Post-front bites feel like plain weight on the line. When you feel it, let the fish load the rod two or three times, reel down until the tip bends, then set the hook. Before you leave any spot, fish it once more, slower.

Still tough? Go to the fallback that has saved more post-front days than anything: a small leech under a slip bobber, or on a dropshot — a #8 hook with the weight 12–18 in below it, 1/4-oz even in 8–10 ft of water, shaken in place. Small leeches beat jumbos on these days. And watch for the brief windows when the weather twitches — post-front fish feed in short bursts, and being on the shallow side at dusk catches one.

weatherOverlays.heading: Quelques jours après un front
lines: The front is a few days behind you and the fish are settling back — start where they were before it, a touch deeper than normal, and let them tell you how far back they've come.
You can quicken up a little from the post-front crawl and work back toward normal sizes, but keep the pauses in — recovering fish still don't chase far.

weatherOverlays.heading: Venteux
lines: Wind is a walleye's friend — anything that breaks up the mirror surface helps. Fish the windward side, where the chop is dimming the light and pushing food in.
On a windy shore, try moving baits first — crankbaits and rigs — then slow down with jigs and live bait. The chop lets you fish shallower than you'd dare on a calm day.

weatherOverlays.heading: Couvert
lines: Grey skies stretch the shallow feeding windows — fish that would be deep by mid-morning under sun stay up and feed longer. Take your dawn spots seriously well into the day.
Under grey skies and low light, UV and glow finishes earn their place in the crankbait box.

weatherOverlays.heading: Calme et brillant
lines: Bright sun and flat calm push walleye deeper and make them shy — lean on the deeper edges and the shaded sides, and save the shallows for the ends of the day.
Go natural with colours, and if you're rigging live bait, lengthen the leader — up to several metres on clear, pressured water (in dark water, 3–4 ft is plenty).

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: You're in the best light of the day. Be set up on your best spot before it arrives, start on the deeper side, and follow the fish shallower as the light fades toward dusk — reverse it at dawn.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: After dark, the shallows the fish avoided at noon come alive — the same shoals, points and weed edges, fished shallower. Females that held deep all day slide in to feed at night.
After dark, the shallows the fish avoided at noon come alive — the same shoals and weed edges, fished shallower. Females that held deep all day slide in to feed at night.
Slow everything down and keep baits close to the bottom or just above it — night fish are feeding, not chasing.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Dans le modèle complet du lac Escanaba, la pression n'avait aucun effet — succès des sorties p=0.122, taux de capture p=0.907. Une variation de taille de front vaut ~10–30 cm d'équivalent de profondeur d'eau, trivial à côté des mouvements verticaux courants.
Pleine lune non significative (p=0.578); les signaux gibbeux/de position se contredisent entre le succès et le taux de capture. Non utilisé.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Walleye are gathering near where they'll spawn — rocky shoals, gravel bars. The males arrive first and stay shallow longest, in just a few feet of water. The bigger females hold a little deeper, just off the spawning area, and slide shallow in the morning, in the evening and after dark.

Walleye are gathering near where they'll spawn — the mouths of tributary creeks and rivers. The males arrive first and stay shallow longest, in just a few feet of water. The bigger females hold a little deeper, just off the spawning area, and slide shallow in the morning, in the evening and after dark.
In rivers, work the holes, the current breaks, the eddies and below wing dams — anywhere a fish can rest out of the push and still watch food come past.
Work the jig slowly along the bottom — lift it a few inches to a foot, let it fall back, and rest it. Cold water means cold fish: short lifts, long pauses.
Time your best shallow spots for morning, evening, dark or a windy day — that's when the females visit. The males are there all day.

spawningSeasons.heading: Après-frai
lines: The spawn is done or winding down. The fish rest first, then start feeding again as the water warms — look just off the spawning shoals, then toward nearby flats. On the big lakes, postspawn walleye work flats roughly 7–20 ft deep before they scatter to summer structure.

The spawn is done or winding down. The fish rest first, then start feeding again as the water warms — look just off the spawning shoals, then toward river mouths and nearby flats. Postspawn walleye work river mouth water roughly 7–20 ft deep before they scatter to summer structure.
Cover water slowly and don't expect violence — these are recovering fish. Work a spot thoroughly before you move; a resting fish often eats on the third or fourth good pass, not the first.
The bait rotation turns with the season: minnows in spring, leeches as late spring arrives, crawlers into summer.

about: The white bass — sand bass in the south — is the striper's smaller, purely freshwater relative, a silver, dark-striped schooling fish of big lakes and rivers. Its year is ruled by one hard thermal trigger: the spring run, when the water reaches 12–14 °C and the fish pour up tributaries to spawn, males arriving as much as a month ahead of the females.

Outside the run, white bass are an open-water chase: schools roam the lake tracking baitfish rather than structure, herding shad to the surface in “jumps” where every cast connects, then vanishing. The skill is finding the forage, not the cover. Anglers target them for the spring river runs and the summer surface blitzes — fast limits, fast action — and rate them highly fresh from the water.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Match the forage the schools are following — this species is more sensitive to prey location than to habitat features in the habitat-suitability synthesis, and schools track baitfish concentrations rather than structure. No lure is named in the white bass literature, and none is invented here: baitfish-profile offerings sized to the local shiners are the supported pattern.

Feeding changes around the run rather than stopping for it: reservoir stomach work found contents differing significantly before, during and after spawning. Prespawn fish are feeding fish — present the baitfish profile actively, as a chased meal, not a bedside offering.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Fish the temperature build, not the calendar: the cold limb is anchored by behaviour — staging from about 7 °C, catch rates rising at 13 °C — and below that band feeding is genuinely depressed; age-0 fish held at 5 °C fed, but at rates too low to maintain body weight. A cold prespawn session over staging fish is a slow session by measurement, not by bad luck.

Time the day by the agency line the model is built on: most active at dawn and dusk, with a solid day value of 0.80 for a daylight-spawning, surface-chasing school fish. Be on the staging water at the light changes, and do not write off the bright hours the way you would for a night-feeding species.

Cover water: staging schools are mobile and prey-led, so a quiet pool is a reason to move along the staging route, not to wait. The run's shape also varies by year — unimodal one spring, bimodal the next in the Arkansas record — so expect waves, not a single day.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If staging fish will not take, check the thermometer first: below about 7 °C you are under the staging band and on the depressed part of the cold limb. Fish the warmest staging water, slow the presentation down, and expect the trigger temperatures to do what no bait change can.

If one staging area is empty, move toward the spawning water rather than away from it as the temperature climbs — the distribution loads progressively up the route, and the catch-rate rise at 13 °C was measured on fish moving into the tributary water, not sitting still.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Time the offering to the run's feeding rhythm, carried in the file as agency tradition and labelled as such: fish feed heavily immediately before and after spawning and bite little while actively spawning. The feeding fish are the arrivals and the spent fish — work the staging edges and the water just off the spawning ground for them, with the baitfish profile the schools follow.

There is no nest to fish and no guarding state to exploit — this is a broadcast spawner, and the nest-guarding playbook from the bass and panfish entries does not exist here. Present to moving, schooling fish: baitfish profiles worked through the run water at the depth the school is travelling.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: This is a daylight spawner, and the day is a real shift: the model's day value is 0.80, with dawn and dusk at the 1.0 peaks the agency account states. Fish the full day on the run, hardest at the light changes, instead of saving everything for dark.

Expect the run in waves and stay ready between them: the Arkansas record was unimodal in one year and bimodal the next, and males arrive up to a month ahead of females. A quiet day inside the temperature band is a gap between waves more often than it is the end of the run.

Keep moving with the fish: run schools distribute along the route and concentrate where the forage is, and the tributary record showed catch rates varying sharply between neighbouring tributaries in the same spring. If your reach is quiet at the right temperature, the next reach is a better bet than a new presentation.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If the fish on the spawning ground itself will not bite, you are probably casting at actively spawning fish — the one part of the run the tradition says bites little. Drop to the staging water below the ground or work its edges for arriving and spent fish, which are the feeding part of the run.

If the temperature is right and the run water is empty, check the shore side before you leave: the run splits between tributary gravel and windswept shores, and a year that loads one may slight the other. The trigger is thermal, not geographic — follow the 12–14 °C crossing to whichever spawning ground the fish chose.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Fish the shad season: in Lake Erie stomachs, the diet shifted from shiners, perch and midge larvae in June to gizzard shad at 56–97% of the diet from July through October, and threadfin shad made 56% frequency of occurrence in the Clarks Hill adults. Manitoba's version of the same menu is emerald shiners and perch, the forage the Lake Winnipeg adults share with walleye and sauger. Baitfish profiles matched to the local forage fish are the supported summer pattern; no specific lure is named in the literature, and none is invented here.

Size to the school, not the species average: this is a chase feeder taking prey in the open, so the offering should read as one of the forage fish the school is driving. When the bait is small shiners, a large profile is the wrong story however well it works on other species.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Dawn and dusk are the stated peaks — the agency account's most-active line, carried at 1.0 at both light changes — with day at 0.80 and night the low value at 0.40. The honest limit rides with the shape: diel structure is measured for this species, but the original studies' peak hours were not retrieved in the research, so the peaks here are the agency line and the schooling canon, not a stomach-by-hour curve.

Oxygen is a hard ladder for this fish, from one primary experiment: 1 mg/L was lethal at warm temperatures, 2 mg/L was extremely stressful, activity and colour fell off below 3 mg/L, and 5 mg/L is taken as the lower optimum. In a still, hot basin, fish the oxygenated water and passes the deep, depleted water by — below 3 mg/L the fish are not feeding, they are enduring.

Stay mobile and let the school tell you when to leave: summer schools follow concentrations of bait, and a school that was feeding hard can be gone with its food within the hour. Mark the bait, not the spot — tomorrow's fish are where tomorrow's forage gathers.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If summer schools will not take at midday, you are fishing the documented trough between two peaks, not a mystery: shift the session to the light changes before you change the tackle box. The day stays genuinely fishable at 0.80 — but dawn and dusk are where this entry puts its money.

If the heat has pushed the surface past about 30 °C, expect the measured decline — the curve steps down through the 30 °C chronic and 31 °C acute reference values toward an upper incipient lethal of 33.5 °C and a maximum tolerance of 35.3 °C. Fish early, late, and in the coolest oxygenated water; no single lethal point is quoted because the record holds three different quantities, not one.

Murk is a mild factor here, not a verdict: across five studies turbidity showed no observable effect on spawning, larval survival or growth, and the only directional finding is avoidance of continuously turbid water. In stained water, fish on — but give a permanently muddy basin a pass in favour of water that clears at least sometimes.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Keep the baitfish profile while the forage lasts: the shad-dominated diet runs July through October in the stomach record, so fall is not the moment to downsize to a panfish story. Match the size of the fall bait the schools are driving.

As the water cools into the low teens, slow the same profile down rather than replacing it: the fish are still chase feeders on the measured limb, but the chase shortens as the temperature falls. No fall-specific lure is named in the literature, and none is invented here.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: The fall surface season is part of the canon for a reason the diet record supports: schools driving bait to the surface are classically a dawn-and-dusk event in fall as in summer. Cover water at the light changes, watching for working schools, and fish found schools hard while the bait holds.

Use the warmest part of the cooling trend: fall activity rides the temperature curve down, so a mild spell that holds the water in the mid-teens is a genuine feeding window, and the first hard drop toward single digits is the signal to switch to the deep holding pattern.

Expect to re-find fish daily: fall schools are prey-led and mobile, and yesterday's concentration is a starting guess, not an address. Search the bait first — wind-worked shores and points are where the canon says bait gathers and schools follow, carried here as canon, not as a measured wind effect.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If fall fish have vanished from the summer water, follow the temperature and the bait downhill together: cooling water empties the shallows in order, and the deep holding pools on the corridor are the next address, not a smaller bait in the old one.

If the water has fallen below about 10 °C, you are on the low cold limb — 0.40 at 10 °C, 0.25 at 7 °C — and sessions become a located-school game. Fish slowly over found fish in the deep water and save the searching for the next warming trend.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Slow, small baitfish-profile presentations, delivered to located schools and given time: there is no measured winter feeding pattern to copy, so the honest winter tackle story is the summer forage pattern at its slowest, over fish you have found rather than fish you hope are there. No winter-specific lure is measured for this species.
Do not downsize your expectations along with the bait: a winter school that will not take is behaving the way the stomach record says winter fish behave. The offering is rarely the winter problem.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Sonar first, casts second: winter movement is minimal in the accounts, so a found school stays found — the reverse of the summer search. Spend the session's effort on locating deep stationary schools, then fish the warmest, most stable part of the short day over them.

Keep the light changes as your best hours even here — the open-water diel shape is the only diel evidence this species has, and winter has none of its own. That is an estimate carried into an unmeasured season, and the entry labels it as such rather than dressing it as a winter finding.

Treat every winter take as information, not a pattern: with mid-winter stomachs empty in the field record and juveniles losing weight while feeding, winter feeding — when it happens at all — is a brief, local event. Note the temperature and depth, because the literature cannot check your result against anything.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If deep winter schools will not take, that is the expected outcome on this species' own evidence, not a signal to change baits all afternoon. The sourced seasons for white bass are the spring run, the summer bait season and the fall — winter is the floor, and the entry says so plainly.

If you need a winter target with a measured winter pattern, this is the honest place to say this species is not it on current evidence. Stay with located deep schools in the warmest part of the day, or wait for the spring staging at 7 °C — the next measured event in this fish's year.

techniques.heading: À travers la saison de glace

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: No ice presentation is measured for white bass, and nothing is borrowed from another species to fill this space. The only tackle mention in the ice record is angler-grade — small spoons taken aggressively by schooled fish in the Winnebago account — carried here as canon with its label, not as a measured ice pattern.
Fish the winter forage story at its slowest if you fish at all: small baitfish profiles over located deep schools. A school that ignores them is consistent with everything the winter record holds.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Treat ice-season white bass as unstudied water: the winter scores for this species reuse the open-water model with a seasonal floor, and should be read as estimates. Fish the deep holding pattern if you fish them, relocate as the canon insists — the schools are described as highly mobile day to day, not where you found them yesterday — and know the library has no ice science to check your results against.

Weigh the one hard winter datum before you drill: every adult in the January–February field collection had an empty stomach, and laboratory juveniles at 5 °C lost condition while feeding. The ice season, on present evidence, is a season this fish endures at low ebb — plan effort accordingly.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: The sourced white bass seasons are the spring run, the summer bait season and the fall. The ice season is, on present evidence, a gap — this entry says so rather than papering over it, and the disposition reopens the moment any under-ice study or a proper winter creel dataset with effort and conditions exists for this species.

If deep schools under ice will not take, that result matches the winter record better than a hot bite would. Note it, fish the warmest stable part of the day over located fish, and save serious effort for the staging water when the temperature climbs back toward 7 °C.

movementSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn is a staging season with its own measured clock: migration begins as the water rises above about 7 °C, with males moving up to a month before females, toward the running water and spawning shores where the run will happen once the water reaches 12–14 °C. Fish the staging water below and beside the spawning ground — the fish are travelling and gathering, not yet spawning.

Stage on the lower reaches and the holding water below the gravel and rock spawning reaches. The run's catch rate in the Arkansas River work rose as temperatures reached 13 °C, so the staging pools closest to the spawning water load first as the thermometer climbs through the low teens.

Spawning happens on windswept shores as well as in tributary water, so the staging pattern has a shore version too: fish the points and gravel shores the wind works, off the deeper holding water, as the temperature builds toward the trigger.

movementSeasons.heading: Montaison de printemps
lines: The run has a hard thermal trigger, the best-documented fact in this file: the water must reach 12–14 °C before spawning begins, and tributary catch rates rose as temperatures reached 13 °C. In Manitoba the run is a May to late-June event at 14–21 °C in the Red and Winnipeg systems. When the thermometer crosses the trigger, be on the spawning water, not the staging water.

The spawning address in running water is gravel and rock, and the velocity record is specific — occurrence was highest in water moving at 0.6–0.7 m/s, intermediate at 0.2 m/s, and lowest at 0.4–0.5 and 0.9–1.0 m/s, in water 1–2 m deep. That is an occurrence pattern, not a measured bite rate, and this entry labels it as such — but as a place to start on a run, it is this species' own data.

The shore-spawning half of the run is real: this species also spawns on windswept shores, broadcasting eggs with no nest and no guarding. On shore-spawning water, fish the wind-worked gravel shores while the temperature sits in the 12–20 °C spawning range.

movementSeasons.heading: Été
lines: Summer white bass are an open-water, schooling chase: the schools track baitfish concentrations rather than structure, and the location skill is finding the forage, not the cover. In Manitoba the inshore feeding season runs from the early-to-late June arrival through September, with lakewide surveys finding the greatest biomass in summer — fish the bait, wherever the bait is.

Temperature sets the broad band: the model's plateau runs 20–27 °C, built openly as a construction between the two measured families — fish selected 18–30 °C through the year with summer selection at the warm end, while occupied summer habitat ran 19–28 °C and agency bands centre lower. Both families agree the fish is warm-water and active all summer; neither supports chasing the single hottest water in the system.

On open water, work the bait schools themselves — the surface breaks where schools drive bait upward are the classic sign, classically at dawn and dusk and again in fall. A located bait school with no white bass under it is worth one pass, not an hour: the predators move with the food, not with the map.

movementSeasons.heading: Automne
lines: Fall is the second schooling season: schools gather on the fall baitfish concentrations in the canon, and the diet record backs the timing — shad dominate the stomachs through October. In Manitoba the inshore season runs until September, so early fall fishes like a continuation of summer; the dispersal and the step down the cold limb come after.

Fish the cooling limb deliberately: the temperature curve still pays 0.85 at 17 °C and 0.70 at 14 °C, so mid-fall water is feeding water, and the season score holds 0.85 through September before stepping down. The fall fish are where the bait concentrates as the water cools, not where they were in August.

On running water, fall fish drop back toward the deeper holding water they will winter in as the temperature falls through the teens. Work the deep pools on the route down from the summer and spawning reaches — the same corridor as the spring run, travelled in reverse and at a feeding pace.

movementSeasons.heading: Hiver
lines: Winter is the floor of this species' year, and the record is blunt about it: the season score sits at 0.25, and in the one adult field record every fish collected in January and February had empty stomachs, at 7 °C — warmer water than any winter fishery here ever sees. The open-water winter address is the deep, stationary school: southern winter accounts describe schools holding deep, roaming little, with reduced metabolism for a few weeks.

Presence is not feeding, and this entry keeps them separate: winter white bass exist in the deep water and can be located — young fish at 5 °C in the laboratory did feed, but too little to maintain body weight, losing condition as they fed. Fish winter schools as a low-rate pattern at best, over located fish, and expect long odds.

The winter schools in the northern angler record hold deep — the biggest concentrations reported at 40–60 ft, smaller schools around 30 ft, sometimes several feet thick, and mixed with perch. That is angler-grade evidence for where fish are, carried with its grade: it locates fish; it does not promise they are feeding.

movementSeasons.heading: À travers la saison de glace
lines: No ice parameter set exists for this species, deliberately: no under-ice study of white bass exists in any form — no under-ice diel, no telemetry under ice, no catch-rate series against conditions — and issuing an ice template would invent one. If your water is ice-covered, the honest guidance is the winter open-water pattern, labelled as exactly that: deep, stationary schools in the holding water, fished as the low end of the open-water model, not as an ice measurement.

The ice fishery itself is real and is carried at its true grade: angler-grade accounts place winter schools deep — the biggest at 40–60 ft at Devils Lake, smaller schools near 30 ft, roaming flats around 18 ft on Winnebago, and backwater schools in 10–15 ft on the Mississippi system. Those numbers locate where anglers find fish through ice; the research is explicit that presence is the whole of what they prove.

movementDaily.heading: Open water
lines: Most active at first light and dusk; quietest at after dark.

weatherFacts: Feeding peaks in water 20–27 °C — the top of this species' temperature curve in the rating model.

weatherOverlays.heading: Le lendemain d’un front
lines: No front, barometric-pressure or moon effect has ever been measured for white bass — the falling-barometer material in the guides is lore, scored zero in the rating, and the one pressure item in the scientific record, caged fish ranking highly sensitive to pressure change, is blast physiology and is filed in the research against exactly the misreading that would turn it into fishing advice. Wind carries no term in this rating at all — it has never been measured for this species. The measured levers for this species are temperature, oxygen and the run calendar; a front matters here only as the temperature change it actually delivers.

weatherOverlays.heading: Lumière basse — aube et crépuscule
lines: The light changes are this species' stated peaks: the agency account puts maximum activity at dawn and dusk, and the schooling canon's surface breaks — schools driving bait upward — are classically light-change events. Be on the bait at the transitions, with the session built around them rather than through them.

weatherOverlays.heading: Après la tombée de la nuit
lines: Night is this species' low value at 0.40 — not zero, because night fishing under lights is an established method for these schooling fish, and that fishery is what bounds the value up from nothing. After dark, fish located schools and lit bait concentrations, and know that dawn is the better bet on the evidence: no telemetry or stomach-by-hour night peak exists for white bass, and none is claimed here.

weatherNotCounted.reason: Aucun test d'alimentation barométrique ou de passage frontal n'existe pour le white bass dans aucune source cherchée — zéro avec frontExposure 0, la disposition du striped bass pour la même absence documentée. Le seul élément de pression au registre (des white bass en cage classés très sensibles au CHANGEMENT de pression) est de la physiologie d'explosion, classé à-ne-pas-utiliser contre le lire comme un coefficient de front.
Même absence documentée que le front; aucune étude de réponse barométrique n'existe pour cette espèce.

Jamais testé chez le white bass. La seule revendication lunaire trouvée (vagues de frai aux pleines/nouvelles lunes) est un message de forum — grade D, à-ne-pas-utiliser. Toute la littérature « lunar white seabass » concerne Atractoscion nobilis, une espèce différente.

La photopériode conditionne démontrablement le frai en culture (Kohler et al. 1994), mais l'effet de terrain est entièrement confondu avec le déclencheur de température 12–14 °C que l'ensemble note déjà; un terme séparé compterait le seuil deux fois.

weatherNotCounted.factor: Moment du jour sous la glace
weatherNotCounted.reason: La glace est un repli d'eau libre : aucune observation journalière sous la glace n'existe contre laquelle noter.
Le risque d'OD sous la glace est non observé chez cette espèce (aucun travail d'OD sous la glace n'existe); l'échelle d'OD d'eau libre est notée sous l'oxygène.

Le modérateur réel dominant (la disponibilité de l'alose guide les bancs; régime 56–97% d'alose en saison) mais aucune entrée du moteur ne le mesure et aucune dose–réponse n'existe; un a priori permanent serait une supposition portant une citation (un précédent permanent du programme). Partiellement représenté par la saison et le débit.
Jamais isolé pour cette espèce; entre seulement par la voie de lumière déjà notée.

spawningSeasons.heading: Avant-frai
lines: Prespawn is a staging season with its own measured clock: migration begins as the water rises above about 7 °C, with males moving up to a month before females, toward the running water and spawning shores where the run will happen once the water reaches 12–14 °C. Fish the staging water below and beside the spawning ground — the fish are travelling and gathering, not yet spawning.

Stage on the lower reaches and the holding water below the gravel and rock spawning reaches. The run's catch rate in the Arkansas River work rose as temperatures reached 13 °C, so the staging pools closest to the spawning water load first as the thermometer climbs through the low teens.

Spawning happens on windswept shores as well as in tributary water, so the staging pattern has a shore version too: fish the points and gravel shores the wind works, off the deeper holding water, as the temperature builds toward the trigger.

Fish the temperature build, not the calendar: the cold limb is anchored by behaviour — staging from about 7 °C, catch rates rising at 13 °C — and below that band feeding is genuinely depressed; age-0 fish held at 5 °C fed, but at rates too low to maintain body weight. A cold prespawn session over staging fish is a slow session by measurement, not by bad luck.

Time the day by the agency line the model is built on: most active at dawn and dusk, with a solid day value of 0.80 for a daylight-spawning, surface-chasing school fish. Be on the staging water at the light changes, and do not write off the bright hours the way you would for a night-feeding species.

Cover water: staging schools are mobile and prey-led, so a quiet pool is a reason to move along the staging route, not to wait. The run's shape also varies by year — unimodal one spring, bimodal the next in the Arkansas record — so expect waves, not a single day.

spawningSeasons.heading: Montaison de printemps
lines: The run has a hard thermal trigger, the best-documented fact in this file: the water must reach 12–14 °C before spawning begins, and tributary catch rates rose as temperatures reached 13 °C. In Manitoba the run is a May to late-June event at 14–21 °C in the Red and Winnipeg systems. When the thermometer crosses the trigger, be on the spawning water, not the staging water.

The spawning address in running water is gravel and rock, and the velocity record is specific — occurrence was highest in water moving at 0.6–0.7 m/s, intermediate at 0.2 m/s, and lowest at 0.4–0.5 and 0.9–1.0 m/s, in water 1–2 m deep. That is an occurrence pattern, not a measured bite rate, and this entry labels it as such — but as a place to start on a run, it is this species' own data.

The shore-spawning half of the run is real: this species also spawns on windswept shores, broadcasting eggs with no nest and no guarding. On shore-spawning water, fish the wind-worked gravel shores while the temperature sits in the 12–20 °C spawning range.

This is a daylight spawner, and the day is a real shift: the model's day value is 0.80, with dawn and dusk at the 1.0 peaks the agency account states. Fish the full day on the run, hardest at the light changes, instead of saving everything for dark.

Expect the run in waves and stay ready between them: the Arkansas record was unimodal in one year and bimodal the next, and males arrive up to a month ahead of females. A quiet day inside the temperature band is a gap between waves more often than it is the end of the run.

Keep moving with the fish: run schools distribute along the route and concentrate where the forage is, and the tributary record showed catch rates varying sharply between neighbouring tributaries in the same spring. If your reach is quiet at the right temperature, the next reach is a better bet than a new presentation.

about: Yellow perch are the walleye's smaller perch-family cousins — golden, dark-barred and almost always found in company. They are schooling fish of the middle temperatures, feeding most actively around 20 °C in the rating model, and they are a cornerstone forage fish: pike, walleye and bass all hunt them, which makes perch schools a signpost for everything else in the lake.

Perch work weedlines, flats and the bases of offshore structure, spawning in the shallows in early spring over weeds a few feet down. They travel in age-matched schools, so the run of small fish and the jumbos rarely mix — find the right school and the day changes. Anglers target them for steady action, for kids' first fish, through the ice all winter, and for a plate of fillets that rivals walleye.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Shiner minnows are the top ice-out bait — surprisingly, the size of the shiner matters less than you'd think. Small teardrop ice-style jigs in the 3–4.5 mm tungsten class, in glow, black, chartreuse or orange, match the early season's small food.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Early schools are often sorted by sex — if you're only catching small males under one dock, move a few docks over before you change baits; the jumbos may be clustered separately. And don't try to sort for size with bigger baits at ice-out: upsizing doesn't sort bigger perch in this window, whatever it does later.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: The spawn is brief — a week to ten days — and then they vanish back out. If the shallows suddenly empty, the show is over: follow them to the first deeper water off the spawning coves.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Live bait and small jigs are the two standard methods, all season: minnows or a 1/32- to 1/8-oz jig. When you want the bigger fish specifically, minnows select for size — small fatheads as the general bait, a medium shiner when you're hunting jumbos.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Keep moving until you find the right school — perch schools are sorted by size and age, so the school of small fish is telling you where the big ones aren't. A few docks or a hundred metres of weedline can be the whole difference.
Keep moving until you find the right school — perch schools are sorted by size and age, so the school of small fish is telling you where the big ones aren't. A few docks can be the whole difference.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: If they're looking but not biting, deadstick a minnow — perch that refuse flashy lures will often take a still bait hanging near bottom.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Whole minnow near the structure; waxworms or maggots farther out on the flats — that's the pro split. On the structure itself, small spoons in the 1/16- to 1/4-oz range and small jigging baits are the active offerings, and rattling baits call jumbos in from a distance. Golden Shiner, Shiner, Perch and Rainbow are the near-universal colour patterns.
For finding them: drift with a crawler or pull a spinner harness to locate a school — then anchor and work them properly.

groups.label: How to fish it
lines: Once you've located them, anchor and fish a slip bobber with the bait 6–12 in off the bottom — the classic perch float lies on its side and stands up when a fish takes. Duwe's rig: a small ½- to ¾-in float, a 6½–7 ft medium-light rod, 4–6 lb line.
On deep Great Lakes water the perch spreader — minnows on a vertical two-hook rig — is the classic, though no book we found gives its dimensions; fish it straight down over the school.

groups.label: If it's still tough
lines: Catching small perch is information, not bad luck: the schools are size-sorted, so keep moving — jumbos range farther afield than the small fish. And if flashy baits get looks but no bites, deadstick a minnow beside the active rod.

groups.label: What to tie on
lines: Minnows for size, small jigs for numbers — the same split as summer. This is also when one pro's contrarian system produces his biggest perch of the year: deep-diving crankbaits off 12–16 ft weedlines, and late in the fall a heavy 3/4-oz football jig on the bottom in deep water. It's a big-lure exception to the small-bait rule, and it belongs to this season.
